notations: max f(x) s.t. I_1(x) and ... and I_n(x)

sources.note: Step 98: resources are finite, so rigor means risk-proportional allocation of verification/computation, not proving everything. Covers 5-level assurance scale, VOI-driven investigation, human attention as a finite resource (DecisionValuePerUnitAttention over NumberOfOutputs), compression-requires-provenance, ranked/verified retrieval, adaptive verification with explicit stop conditions and budget-exhaustion!=success, graceful degradation, resource-bounded AI planning, hard-constraint-vs-optimization-objective separation (max f(x) s.t. invariants), assurance-aware AI model routing, automation-bias risk, knowledge/cache lifecycle and retention, the provenance-vs-hidden-reasoning architectural boundary, resource-exhaustion-as-attack, resource isolation, and priority inversion. Closely related to the pre-existing value-of-information-concept.

rows.anchor: Step 97 established KnowledgeOS as a socio-technical Organization. But resources are finite. Rigor cannot mean 'prove everything.' It must mean allocate verification and computation according to risk, value, uncertainty, and cost.
rows.statement: Frames Step 98's central requirement: rigor cannot mean proving everything, but allocating verification/computation by risk, value, uncertainty, and cost.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 97 established KnowledgeOS as a socio-technical system.

rows.anchor: 98.1 — Resources become part of the formal model ... R=(CPU,Memory,Storage,Network,Time,HumanAttention,AICompute). Cost(a)<=R for executable actions.
rows.statement: Defines the resource vector R=(CPU,Memory,Storage,Network,Time,HumanAttention,AICompute) and the executability constraint Cost(a)≤R.

rows.anchor: 98.2 — Experiment 1: unlimited verification assumption ... a proposition requires 10^9 verification operations. Available budget 10^6. Expected: KnowledgeOS cannot simply claim Verified=True. Result: PASS. The correct state is VerificationIncomplete.
rows.statement: Experiment 1: a proposition requiring 10^9 operations against a 10^6 budget cannot be claimed Verified=True; correct state is VerificationIncomplete; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.3 — Resource limitation must not become epistemic fabrication ... Unable to verify ≠ Verified. And Not checked ≠ False.
rows.statement: Restates Unable to verify ≠ Verified and Not checked ≠ False as central to resource-constrained verification.

rows.anchor: 98.4 — Experiment 2 ... System has insufficient compute to run a complete architecture verification. Expected: VerificationStatus=Incomplete rather than Passed. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 2: insufficient compute for full verification yields VerificationStatus=Incomplete, not Passed; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.5 — Verification levels ... Level_0=Unverified, Level_1=BasicCheck, Level_2=AutomatedVerification, Level_3=IndependentVerification, Level_4=FormalProof. Assurance must reflect the actual verification performed.
rows.statement: Defines a five-level verification/assurance scale (Unverified..FormalProof), requiring assurance to reflect actual verification performed.

rows.anchor: 98.6 — Experiment 3 ... A component passes UnitTests. System records FormalProof=True. Expected: assurance inflation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3: recording FormalProof=True after only unit tests pass is assurance inflation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.7 — Verification is itself a resource ... V(a) verification cost. For a critical action V(a) may be high. For a low-risk action, small. This suggests risk-based verification.
rows.statement: States verification cost V(a) should scale with action criticality, motivating risk-based verification.

rows.anchor: 98.8 — Risk-weighted assurance ... Risk(a), VerificationBudget(a). VerificationPriority ∝ Risk×Uncertainty.
rows.statement: Defines VerificationPriority ∝ Risk×Uncertainty, allocating more assurance to higher impact×uncertainty actions.

rows.anchor: 98.9 — Experiment 4 ... Change A: Impact=Low. Change B: Impact=Critical. Both receive identical verification effort. Expected: not necessarily wrong, but potentially inefficient and insufficiently risk-sensitive. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: identical verification effort for Low-impact and Critical-impact changes is potentially inefficient/insufficiently risk-sensitive; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.10 — Criticality ... Criticality(X): Low, Medium, High, Critical. This can influence verification, approval, redundancy, retention, monitoring, human review.
rows.statement: Defines Criticality(X) (Low/Medium/High/Critical) as influencing verification, approval, redundancy, retention, monitoring, and human review.

rows.anchor: 98.11 — Experiment 5 ... A typo in documentation: Criticality=Low. Production authorization policy: Criticality=Critical. Expected: they should not consume identical governance and verification budgets. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: a low-criticality typo and a critical production authorization policy should not consume identical governance budgets; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.12 — Cost of information ... Information(I) at cost Cost(I). Is obtaining I worth its cost?
rows.statement: Frames information acquisition as having a cost Cost(I), raising whether it's worth paying.

rows.anchor: 98.13 — Value of information ... VOI(I)=ExpectedDecisionImprovement-Cost(I). If VOI(I)>0, additional information may be worthwhile.
rows.statement: Restates Value of Information VOI(I)=ExpectedDecisionImprovement-Cost(I) as the criterion for seeking more information.

rows.anchor: 98.14 — Experiment 6 ... Decision uncertainty is high. A 5-minute automated check can significantly reduce uncertainty. Expected: VOI>0. KnowledgeOS should consider performing it. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6: a cheap, high-uncertainty-reducing check has VOI>0 and should be performed; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.15 — Experiment 7 ... A two-week investigation is required to reduce a tiny uncertainty in a low-impact decision. Expected: VOI<0. The investigation may not be justified. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: an expensive investigation for a tiny uncertainty reduction in a low-impact decision has VOI<0 and may be unjustified; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.16 — This gives us an important principle ... Rigor ≠ Maximum computation. Rigor = Appropriate assurance for the risk, uncertainty, and consequence.
rows.statement: States Rigor ≠ Maximum computation; Rigor = Appropriate assurance for the risk, uncertainty, and consequence.

rows.anchor: 98.17 — Human attention is also a resource ... 10,000 alerts per day, humans can inspect 50. Alerts>AttentionCapacity. The system has failed operationally even if every alert is technically correct.
rows.statement: States human attention is a finite resource: exceeding AttentionCapacity (10,000 alerts vs 50 inspectable) is an operational failure even with technically correct alerts.

rows.anchor: 98.18 — Experiment 8 ... System generates 1000 'important' findings. Human team can investigate 20. Expected: prioritization becomes mandatory. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 8: 1000 findings against a 20-item investigation capacity makes prioritization mandatory; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.19 — Attention allocation ... Priority(X)=f(Risk,Uncertainty,Impact,TimeSensitivity,EvidenceQuality).
rows.statement: Defines Priority(X)=f(Risk,Uncertainty,Impact,TimeSensitivity,EvidenceQuality) for allocating human attention.

type_signature.domain: Risk x Uncertainty x Impact x TimeSensitivity x EvidenceQuality

rows.anchor: 98.20 — Experiment 9 ... Finding A: Risk=Critical. Finding B: Risk=Low. Both are presented identically. Expected: poor attention allocation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: presenting a Critical-risk and Low-risk finding identically is poor attention allocation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.21 — AI should optimize attention, not merely produce more information ... A useful AI engineering platform should maximize DecisionValuePerUnitAttention, not NumberOfOutputs.
rows.statement: States AI systems should optimize DecisionValuePerUnitAttention rather than NumberOfOutputs.

rows.anchor: 98.22 — Experiment 10 ... Agent produces 500-page analysis. Human needs one decision. Expected: potentially low information efficiency. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: a 500-page analysis for a single decision is potentially low information efficiency; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.23 — Information compression ... LargeEvidenceSet→RelevantSummary. But compression must preserve the semantics necessary for the decision.
rows.statement: Restates the need for LargeEvidenceSet→RelevantSummary compression preserving decision-necessary semantics.

rows.anchor: 98.24 — Experiment 11 ... 1000 evidence items are summarized into 5 statements. One critical contradictory item is omitted. Expected: semantic distortion. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: omitting one critical contradictory item while compressing 1000 items to 5 statements is semantic distortion; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.25 — Summaries require provenance ... Summary←derivedFrom—EvidenceSet. A summary should not become an untraceable replacement for its sources.
rows.statement: States summaries need Summary←derivedFrom—EvidenceSet provenance, must not untraceably replace their sources.

rows.anchor: 98.26 — Experiment 12 ... AI generates 'architecture is compliant.' No evidence references are retained. Expected: low auditability. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 12: an AI compliance claim with no retained evidence references has low auditability; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.27 — Retrieval optimization ... N=10^9 artifacts. CandidateRetrieval→EvidenceRanking→Verification.
rows.statement: Defines a retrieval pipeline CandidateRetrieval→EvidenceRanking→Verification for scaling to 10^9 artifacts.

rows.anchor: 98.28 — Experiment 13 ... Retriever returns Top10. But the correct evidence is ranked #5000. Expected: naive top-k retrieval can miss critical evidence. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: correct evidence ranked #5000 while retriever returns Top10 shows naive top-k retrieval can miss critical evidence; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.29 — Retrieval confidence ... Recall, Precision, Coverage. For high-criticality queries, retrieval assurance may require stronger strategies.
rows.statement: States retrieval should have measurable Recall/Precision/Coverage properties, with stronger strategies for high-criticality queries.

rows.anchor: 98.30 — Experiment 14 ... Low-risk query: Recall=0.8. Potentially acceptable. Critical compliance query: Recall=0.8. Expected: potentially insufficient. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: Recall=0.8 potentially acceptable for a low-risk query but potentially insufficient for a critical compliance query; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.31 — Adaptive verification ... VerificationLevel=f(Criticality,Uncertainty,EvidenceQuality,ResourceBudget). The system can dynamically increase verification when necessary.
rows.statement: Defines VerificationLevel=f(Criticality,Uncertainty,EvidenceQuality,ResourceBudget), allowing dynamic verification increase.

rows.anchor: 98.32 — Experiment 15 ... Initial confidence 0.95. A contradictory authoritative source appears. Confidence falls to 0.60. Expected: verification effort should increase or escalation should occur. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: a confidence drop (0.95→0.60) from contradictory authoritative evidence should increase verification effort or trigger escalation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.33 — Stop conditions ... Stop when Confidence≥Threshold or BudgetExhausted or EvidenceExhausted.
rows.statement: Defines explicit verification stop conditions: threshold met, budget exhausted, or evidence exhausted.

rows.anchor: 98.34 — Experiment 16 ... Verification continues after the required assurance threshold has already been met. Expected: potential resource waste unless additional verification has strategic value. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: continuing verification past the required threshold is potential resource waste unless it has strategic value; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.35 — But budget exhaustion does not mean success ... If BudgetExhausted before ThresholdReached, then VerificationIncomplete. Not Verified.
rows.statement: States the critical distinction that BudgetExhausted before ThresholdReached means VerificationIncomplete, never Verified.

rows.anchor: 98.36 — Experiment 17 ... Required assurance 95%. Achieved 70%. Budget exhausted. Expected: Status=InsufficientAssurance. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: 70% achieved against a 95% requirement with exhausted budget yields Status=InsufficientAssurance; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.37 — Graceful degradation ... FullVerification→ReducedVerification→ManualReview→Unavailable. Each state should be explicit.
rows.statement: Defines an explicit graceful-degradation ladder FullVerification→ReducedVerification→ManualReview→Unavailable.

rows.anchor: 98.38 — Experiment 18 ... AI inference service unavailable. Expected: system may fall back to DeterministicRules or HumanReview. But it must not pretend the AI analysis occurred. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: an unavailable AI service should fall back to DeterministicRules/HumanReview, never pretending AI analysis occurred; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.39 — Resource-aware agent planning ... Plan=(a_1,...,a_n) with ΣCost(a_i)≤Budget. The planner chooses actions based on expected value.
rows.statement: Defines resource-bounded agent planning: Σ Cost(a_i) ≤ Budget with expected-value-driven action selection.

rows.anchor: 98.40 — Experiment 19 ... Budget=100. Option A: Cost=10,VOI=5. Option B: Cost=50,VOI=40. Expected: B may be preferable despite higher cost. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: option B (Cost=50,VOI=40) may be preferable over A (Cost=10,VOI=5) despite higher cost, given a Budget=100; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.41 — Resource allocation is not purely mathematical ... HumanAttention may be more valuable than CPU. ProductionDowntime may have enormous business impact. The objective function must include business consequences.
rows.statement: Notes resource allocation must include business consequences (e.g. HumanAttention value, ProductionDowntime impact), not purely technical cost.

rows.anchor: 98.42 — Multi-objective optimization ... Objective=w_1 Accuracy+w_2 Safety+w_3 CostEfficiency+w_4 Latency+w_5 HumanAttention. But the weights themselves are governance decisions.
rows.statement: Defines a weighted multi-objective function whose weights are themselves governance decisions.

rows.anchor: 98.43 — Experiment 20 ... Optimization improves cost by 30% but reduces assurance below the mandatory threshold. Expected: optimization must not violate hard governance constraints. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: a 30% cost improvement that drops assurance below the mandatory threshold must not be allowed to violate hard governance constraints; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.44 — Hard constraints versus optimization objectives ... HardConstraint versus OptimizationObjective. SecurityPolicyViolation cannot be traded for LowerCost.
rows.statement: Distinguishes HardConstraint from OptimizationObjective: SecurityPolicyViolation cannot be traded for LowerCost.

rows.anchor: 98.45 — Experiment 21 ... 'Skip authorization to save 20 seconds.' Expected: impossible if authorization is a hard invariant. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: skipping authorization to save time is impossible when authorization is a hard invariant; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.46 — Optimization happens inside the feasible region ... max f(x) subject to I_1(x)=True, I_2(x)=True, I_3(x)=True. Optimize subject to invariants.
rows.statement: Formalizes optimization as max f(x) subject to I_1(x)=True ∧ I_2(x)=True ∧ I_3(x)=True — a very important KnowledgeOS principle.

rows.anchor: 98.47 — Experiment 22 ... Optimization finds a solution x* with excellent cost. But I_Privacy(x*)=False. Expected: x* is infeasible. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: an excellent-cost solution violating I_Privacy(x*)=False is infeasible regardless of cost; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.48 — AI model selection ... M_1,M_2,M_3 differ in cost, latency, accuracy, context size, privacy properties, explainability. Select(M,Q,C).
rows.statement: Defines AI model selection Select(M,Q,C) across models differing in cost/latency/accuracy/context/privacy/explainability.

rows.anchor: 98.49 — Experiment 23 ... Simple classification requires M_1. Complex architecture reasoning requires M_3. Using M_3 for everything produces unnecessary cost. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 23: always using the most expensive model (M_3) for simple tasks produces unnecessary cost; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.50 — Assurance-aware model routing ... RequiredAssurance(Q). Model(Q)=f(Complexity,Criticality,Privacy,Cost,Latency).
rows.statement: Defines assurance-aware model routing Model(Q)=f(Complexity,Criticality,Privacy,Cost,Latency), guided by RequiredAssurance(Q).

type_signature.domain: Complexity x Criticality x Privacy x Cost x Latency

rows.anchor: 98.51 — Experiment 24 ... Critical governance decision routed to cheapest low-assurance model. Expected: potential assurance violation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 24: routing a critical governance decision to the cheapest low-assurance model is a potential assurance violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.52 — Human versus AI allocation ... Task→AI, Task→Human, or Task→Human+AI.
rows.statement: Defines task-allocation options Task→AI, Task→Human, or Task→Human+AI.

rows.anchor: 98.53 — Experiment 25 ... AI can classify 10,000 routine artifacts. Human can review 10. Expected: AI performs initial classification, humans handle high-risk exceptions. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: AI-first classification with human review reserved for high-risk exceptions is the correct allocation given a 10,000-vs-10 capacity gap; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.54 — But automation bias is a risk ... Humans may blindly accept AI recommendations. AIRecommendation must remain distinguishable from HumanDecision. This connects Step 97 with Step 98.
rows.statement: Warns of automation bias (humans blindly accepting AI recommendations), requiring AIRecommendation to remain distinguishable from HumanDecision, linking Step 97 to Step 98.

lineage_claims.quote: This connects Step 97 with Step 98.

rows.anchor: 98.55 — Experiment 26 ... AI says Approve. Human clicks Approve without reviewing evidence. Expected: the process may technically be human-approved but epistemically weak. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 26: a human rubber-stamping an AI's Approve recommendation without reviewing evidence is technically human-approved but epistemically weak; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.56 — Attention-aware escalation ... ReviewDepth=f(Risk,Uncertainty,Impact). A low-risk change might need 1 review. A critical architectural decision may need 3 independent reviews.
rows.statement: Defines ReviewDepth=f(Risk,Uncertainty,Impact) scaling required reviewer count with risk.

rows.anchor: 98.57 — Experiment 27 ... Criticality increases. Required reviewer count remains unchanged. Expected: potential mismatch between risk and assurance effort. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 27: increasing criticality without increasing reviewer count is a potential risk/assurance-effort mismatch; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.58 — Knowledge retention has a cost ... Storage(t)→∞ if nothing is retired. Retention policies are required.
rows.statement: States unbounded retention leads to unsustainable storage growth (Storage(t)→∞), requiring retention policies.

rows.anchor: 98.59 — Experiment 28 ... System generates 10^6 temporary artifacts daily. All retained indefinitely. Expected: unsustainable storage growth. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: retaining 10^6 daily temporary artifacts indefinitely is unsustainable storage growth; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.60 — Retention versus provenance ... Retention versus Cost and potentially Privacy. RetentionPolicy(K).
rows.statement: Defines RetentionPolicy(K) balancing retention against cost and privacy.

rows.anchor: 98.61 — Experiment 29 ... Low-value temporary inference retained for 20 years. Expected: potentially unnecessary cost and privacy exposure. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 29: retaining a low-value temporary inference for 20 years is potentially unnecessary cost and privacy exposure; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.62 — Knowledge lifecycle ... Created→Active→Superseded→Archived→Deleted. But historical semantics must remain recoverable where required.
rows.statement: Defines the knowledge lifecycle Created→Active→Superseded→Archived→Deleted, with historical semantics remaining recoverable where required.

rows.anchor: 98.63 — Experiment 30 ... Policy version 5 is superseded by version 6. Expected: version 5 remains historically identifiable rather than being overwritten. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 30: a superseded policy version 5 remains historically identifiable, not overwritten; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.64 — Cache semantics ... cached knowledge can become stale. Cache(K,t) needs FreshnessPolicy.
rows.statement: Defines Cache(K,t) requiring an explicit FreshnessPolicy to guard against staleness.

rows.anchor: 98.65 — Experiment 31 ... Current policy P_7. Cache contains P_6. Agent retrieves cached policy and executes. Expected: potential semantic violation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 31: executing against a stale cached policy (P_6 vs current P_7) is a potential semantic violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.66 — Freshness versus cost ... FreshnessCheckFrequency should depend on Criticality+ChangeRate+Risk.
rows.statement: Defines FreshnessCheckFrequency=f(Criticality,ChangeRate,Risk), balancing checking cost against staleness risk.

rows.anchor: 98.67 — Experiment 32 ... Policy changes frequently. Cache refreshes once per month. Expected: high stale-data risk. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 32: a monthly cache refresh against a frequently-changing policy is high stale-data risk; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.68 — Cost-aware provenance ... Minimal, Standard, Full provenance depths. Critical decisions may require full provenance.
rows.statement: Defines tiered provenance depths (Minimal/Standard/Full), reserving full provenance for critical decisions.

rows.anchor: 98.69 — Experiment 33 ... Routine low-risk telemetry stores full chain-of-thought-like internal artifacts indefinitely. Expected: potentially excessive storage and privacy cost. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 33: storing full internal-reasoning-like artifacts indefinitely for routine low-risk telemetry is excessive storage/privacy cost; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.70 — Important distinction: provenance versus hidden reasoning ... auditable provenance does not mean storing unrestricted private internal reasoning traces. The useful object is Evidence+Sources+DecisionBasis+Verification, not necessarily every internal token or latent reasoning process.
rows.statement: States auditable provenance (Evidence+Sources+DecisionBasis+Verification) does not require storing unrestricted internal model reasoning traces or every internal token.

rows.anchor: 98.71 — Experiment 34 ... Decision requires proving which evidence supported it. Expected: evidence references and decision rationale may suffice without preserving unrestricted internal model reasoning. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 34: proving decision support via evidence references and rationale suffices without preserving unrestricted internal model reasoning; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.72 — This is important for our software architecture ... the platform can define a formal DecisionEvidenceContract without making RawModelInternalState a required system dependency. This is a powerful architectural boundary.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS can define a DecisionEvidenceContract without making RawModelInternalState a required system dependency — a powerful architectural boundary.

rows.anchor: 98.73 — Resource exhaustion is also an attack ... Step 94 considered adversarial behavior. Now we add ResourceExhaustionAttack. An attacker can send 10^9 expensive requests.
rows.statement: Extends Step 94's adversarial-behavior analysis with ResourceExhaustionAttack (e.g. 10^9 expensive requests).

lineage_claims.quote: Step 94 considered adversarial behavior. Now we add: ResourceExhaustionAttack.

rows.anchor: 98.74 — Experiment 35 ... One actor consumes 95% of AI compute. Other critical workflows become unavailable. Expected: resource governance violation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 35: one actor consuming 95% of AI compute, starving other critical workflows, is a resource governance violation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.75 — Resource isolation ... Critical workloads should have protected budgets: Budget_critical. Noncritical workloads should not be able to consume all resources.
rows.statement: Defines Budget_critical as a protected resource allocation preventing noncritical workloads from consuming all resources.

rows.anchor: 98.76 — Experiment 36 ... Experimental AI workload attempts to consume production verification capacity. Expected: isolation prevents starvation of critical workflows. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 36: resource isolation prevents an experimental workload from starving production verification capacity; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.77 — Priority inversion ... LowPriority holds a resource needed by CriticalTask. This creates PriorityInversion. KnowledgeOS needs resource scheduling that respects criticality.
rows.statement: Defines PriorityInversion (a low-priority holder blocking a critical task's needed resource), requiring criticality-respecting scheduling.

rows.anchor: 98.78 — Experiment 37 ... Critical architecture verification waits behind unlimited low-priority experiments. Expected: scheduling failure. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 37: critical verification blocked behind unlimited low-priority experiments is a scheduling failure; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 98.79 — Resource governance ... ResourcePolicy=f(Criticality,Priority,Authority,Cost,Deadline).
rows.statement: Defines ResourcePolicy=f(Criticality,Priority,Authority,Cost,Deadline).

type_signature.domain: Criticality x Priority x Authority x Cost x Deadline

rows.anchor: 98.80 — The deeper result ... Resource constraints must influence what the system claims to know. If the system did not have enough resources to establish something, its epistemic status must reflect that.
rows.statement: States resource constraints must influence what the system claims to know: insufficient resources for establishing something must be reflected in epistemic status.

rows.anchor: 98.81 — New invariants: I_ResourceHonesty, I_RiskProportionalAssurance, I_HardConstraints, I_AttentionAllocation, I_VerificationProvenance, I_FreshnessPolicy, I_ResourceIsolation, I_RetentionGovernance, I_ModelSelection, I_DegradationHonesty, I_InformationValue
rows.statement: States eleven new invariants: I_ResourceHonesty (resource limitation must not cause incomplete verification to be represented as complete), I_RiskProportionalAssurance (verification effort must be proportionate to risk/impact/uncertainty, subject to mandatory governance requirements), I_HardConstraints (optimization must never trade mandatory security/privacy/authority/semantic invariants for cost/latency/convenience), I_AttentionAllocation (human review capacity must be allocated by material risk/uncertainty, not merely volume), I_VerificationProvenance (the system must retain what verification was performed, at what version, under what conditions, with what result), I_FreshnessPolicy (cached knowledge must respect freshness requirements appropriate to its criticality), I_ResourceIsolation (noncritical workloads must not consume resources required for critical assurance/governance functions), I_RetentionGovernance (knowledge retention must follow explicit value/audit/privacy/lifecycle requirements), I_ModelSelection (AI model selection must satisfy the required assurance level while considering cost/latency/privacy/capability), I_DegradationHonesty (when resources are insufficient, the system must expose degraded/partial/unavailable status rather than fabricating full assurance), I_InformationValue (additional information should be acquired when its expected decision value justifies the cost, subject to mandatory assurance requirements).

rows.anchor: 98.82 — Step 98 verdict: STEP 98 — PASS ... Formal rigor does not mean infinite computation. Formal rigor = Explicit assumptions + Explicit invariants + Measured assurance + Honest uncertainty + Risk-appropriate verification.
rows.statement: Records Step 98 verdict PASS, redefining Formal rigor = Explicit assumptions + Explicit invariants + Measured assurance + Honest uncertainty + Risk-appropriate verification, rejecting the 'infinite computation' interpretation.

rows.anchor: The KnowledgeOS optimization principle ... Optimize everything that is negotiable. Protect everything that is invariant. max Utility(x) subject to I_1(x)∧I_2(x)∧...∧I_n(x).
rows.statement: States the KnowledgeOS optimization principle: optimize everything negotiable, protect everything invariant — max Utility(x) subject to I_1(x)∧...∧I_n(x).

rows.anchor: KnowledgeOS is now approaching an executable governance engine ... Knowledge→Reasoning→Decision→Authority→Action while simultaneously evaluating Evidence+Uncertainty+Security+Privacy+Responsibility+Cost+Risk. The platform can decide not only 'what should we do?' but 'do we have enough evidence?' 'wh
rows.statement: Presents KnowledgeOS as an executable governance engine answering not just 'what should we do' but evidence-sufficiency, authority, information-access, verification-adequacy, cost-justification, and escalation questions simultaneously.

rows.anchor: Step 99 — Next boundary: observability, measurement and empirical validation ... An invariant that cannot be observed or tested becomes merely an architectural assertion. How does KnowledgeOS know that its own invariants are actually being preserved in the running system? Specification→Measurement→R
rows.statement: Previews Step 99: whether an invariant that cannot be observed/tested is merely an architectural assertion, moving from Specification to Measurement to RuntimeEvidence to Assurance, covering Observability, Telemetry, Metrics, Tracing, InvariantMonitoring, RuntimeVerification, EvidenceCollection, SLOs, DriftDetection, AssuranceDashboards.

sources.note: Step 120: the frozen KnowledgeOS Architecture Constitution v0.1 (C1 Provenance, C2 Authority, C3 Epistemic Separation, C4 Temporal Validity, C5 Deterministic Assurance [SHOULD not MUST], C6 Traceability, C7 Feedback), independently and empirically derived from the Steps 101-119 architecture-conformance arc -- distinct from the earlier philosophically-derived B0006 kos-constitutional-invariant-map/11-law core, though thematically resonant. ConstitutionalInvariant!=CodingConvention meta-criterion; per-invariant justification+violation experiment; rigorous non-redundancy reduction analysis (each candidate tested against absorption into another); Constitution/Foundation-invariant distinction (Identity/Immutability/Versioning declined as separate constitutional rules, F1-F3); Constitution/Architecture/Implementation layering extended to agent instructions (AGENTS.md/.claude//.codex/ symmetry, Cache!=Authority); constitutional dependency graph; seven named failure-propagation chains (culminating in the fundamental AI governance failure Inference=Authority->AIOutput->OrganizationalTruth); the constitutional equation KnowledgeOSIntegrity=P∩A∩E∩T∩V∩R∩F (intersection not average, extending Vector>Scalar from S1013); four domain-relative most-important-invariant identifications; and a technology-independence validation test. Extends knowledgeos-control-loop-evidence-test-model (S1018) K1-K7; is the culminating theoretical artifact of the batch B0024 architecture-conformance arc, immediately consumed by knowledgeos-constitution-implementation-conformance-test-model (S1019/Step 121).

REUSE NOTE (recorded in B0025, not first proposed here): this label was first proposed in the immediately preceding batch B0024 (Step 120's frozen C1-C7 constitution) but had not yet been merged into the master 11-OBJECT-INDEX.jsonl snapshot given to this batch. B0025 (Steps 122-124, 130, 136, 141) extensively references and extends this same object (bypass-test matrix, graph integrity invariants, runtime invariants) -- re-registering it here purely so the batch's own unregistered-label self-check passes; the canonical definition and note remain B0024's.

rows.anchor: We now consolidate the previous experiments. The objective is to identify the smallest set of invariants whose violation would fundamentally change the nature of KnowledgeOS. Provenance+Authority+EpistemicStatus+TemporalValidity+DeterministicVerification+Traceability+Feedback.
rows.statement: Frames Step 120's objective: identifying the smallest invariant set whose violation would fundamentally change KnowledgeOS, starting from a seven-part candidate.

rows.anchor: 120.1 — What makes an invariant constitutional? A constitutional invariant says: if this property is violated, the system no longer has the intended semantic character. ConstitutionalInvariant≠CodingConvention. 'Use PostgreSQL' is not necessarily constitutional. 'Authoritative knowledge must have id
rows.statement: Defines ConstitutionalInvariant≠CodingConvention: a constitutional invariant's violation changes the system's intended semantic character, illustrated by contrasting a technology preference with a provenance requirement.

rows.anchor: 120.2 — Invariant K1: Provenance ... Every authoritative knowledge object MUST have provenance. Provenance should answer where did it originate, when, through which process, who/what produced it, from which source material.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate invariant K1: every authoritative knowledge object must have provenance answering five questions (origin/when/process/producer/source material).

rows.anchor: 120.3 — Why provenance is constitutional ... Without provenance, Knowledge becomes indistinguishable from GeneratedText. That destroys the ability to answer: Why should I trust this?
rows.statement: Argues without provenance, Knowledge becomes indistinguishable from GeneratedText, destroying trust justification.

rows.anchor: 120.4 — Experiment K1.1 ... KnowledgeOS contains 'The architecture requires rootless containers.' No source, author, decision, timestamp or provenance exists. Can the system establish that it is authoritative? No. Verdict: K1 VIOLATED
rows.statement: Experiment K1.1: a sourceless/authorless/timestampless architecture statement cannot be established as authoritative; verdict K1 VIOLATED.

rows.anchor: 120.5 — Provenance does not equal source URL ... SourceURL does not tell us WhoApproved or WhenDidItBecomeValid. Source≠CompleteProvenance.
rows.statement: States Source≠CompleteProvenance: a URL alone does not establish approval or validity onset.

rows.anchor: 120.6 — Invariant K2: Authority ... Every authoritative governance change MUST have identifiable authority. Decision→Authority.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate invariant K2: every authoritative governance change must have identifiable authority (Decision->Authority).

rows.anchor: 120.7 — Why authority is constitutional ... Without authority, Recommendation can silently become Decision. And AgentOutput can silently become OrganizationalTruth. That is unacceptable.
rows.statement: Argues without authority, Recommendation can silently become Decision and AgentOutput can silently become OrganizationalTruth.

rows.anchor: 120.8 — Experiment K2.1 ... Agent generates 'Architecture standard changed to X.' No authorized decision exists. Expected: Status=Proposed. Not Status=Authoritative. Verdict: K2 VIOLATION if promoted
rows.statement: Experiment K2.1: an unauthorized agent-declared standard change must remain Status=Proposed; K2 VIOLATION if promoted to Authoritative.

rows.anchor: 120.9 — Authority is not identity ... Actor≠Authority. Credential≠Authority. Role≠Authority unless the governance model explicitly establishes the mapping.
rows.statement: States Actor≠Authority, Credential≠Authority, Role≠Authority unless the governance model explicitly maps them.

rows.anchor: 120.10 — Invariant K3: Epistemic status ... KnowledgeOS MUST distinguish observed, verified, inferred, proposed and authoritative information. This is perhaps the most important AI-specific invariant.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate invariant K3, called perhaps the most important AI-specific invariant: distinguishing observed/verified/inferred/proposed/authoritative information.

rows.anchor: 120.11 — Why epistemic status matters ... 'The service probably owns this database' versus 'The Architecture Board decided that this service owns this database.' The textual similarity may be high. Their epistemic status is radically different.
rows.statement: Illustrates why epistemic status matters via a textually-similar but epistemically-radically-different sentence pair.

rows.anchor: 120.12 — Experiment K3.1 ... LLM generates Inference(X). System stores it identically to AuthoritativeDecision(X). Expected: K3 VIOLATION
rows.statement: Experiment K3.1: storing an LLM inference identically to an authoritative decision is K3 VIOLATION.

rows.anchor: 120.13 — Candidate epistemic states ... Observed, Imported, Asserted, Inferred, Proposed, Verified, Approved, Superseded. But we should only implement states that have real semantic value.
rows.statement: Lists an eight-value candidate epistemic vocabulary, cautioning only states with real semantic value should be implemented.

rows.anchor: 120.14 — Invariant K4: Temporal validity ... Authoritative knowledge MUST have determinable temporal validity. At minimum Current versus Superseded.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate invariant K4: authoritative knowledge must have determinable temporal validity, at minimum Current vs Superseded.

rows.anchor: 120.15 — Why time is constitutional ... An architecture decision from 2024 may not represent the current architecture in 2026. Therefore HistoricalTruth≠CurrentTruth.
rows.statement: Argues HistoricalTruth≠CurrentTruth, illustrated by a 2024 decision potentially not representing 2026's current architecture.

rows.anchor: 120.16 — Experiment K4.1 ... Two decisions exist: D1 use architecture A, D2 use architecture B. No relationship identifies which supersedes which. Expected: agent cannot safely determine current architecture. Verdict: K4 VIOLATION
rows.statement: Experiment K4.1: two competing, unlinked decisions leave an agent unable to safely determine current architecture; verdict K4 VIOLATION.

rows.anchor: 120.17 — Creation time versus validity ... We must explicitly distinguish CreatedAt from ValidFrom. And potentially ValidUntil.
rows.statement: States CreatedAt must be distinguished from ValidFrom (and potentially ValidUntil).

rows.anchor: 120.18 — Experiment K4.2 ... Decision created 2026-08-01 but effective 2026-09-01. If the system only knows created_at, it cannot correctly answer is this decision currently effective. Verdict: K4 PARTIAL
rows.statement: Experiment K4.2: a decision created before its effective date cannot be correctly evaluated by a created_at-only system; verdict K4 PARTIAL.

rows.anchor: 120.19 — Invariant K5: Deterministic verification ... Where a claim is deterministically testable, authoritative assurance MUST be based on reproducible verification evidence. This does not eliminate human judgment. It prevents LLMConfidence from becoming Verification.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate invariant K5: deterministically testable claims must be assured via reproducible evidence, preventing LLMConfidence from becoming Verification.

rows.anchor: 120.20 — Experiment K5.1 ... Static checker returns FAIL. LLM says the architecture looks compliant. Expected: Compliance=FAIL. Verdict: K5 PASS
rows.statement: Experiment K5.1: a static-checker FAIL overrides an LLM's compliant assessment, Compliance=FAIL; verdict K5 PASS.

rows.anchor: 120.21 — Why 'where deterministically testable' matters ... Is this architecture strategically appropriate may require human judgment. K5 should not become EverythingMustBeAutomated. It should be DeterministicWherePossible.
rows.statement: Scopes K5 to DeterministicWherePossible, not EverythingMustBeAutomated, since some questions (e.g. strategic appropriateness) require judgment.

rows.anchor: 120.22 — Invariant K6: Traceability ... Material engineering actions MUST be traceable to their governing intent, decision or authorization where governance requires it. Action→Decision.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate invariant K6: material engineering actions must be traceable to governing intent/decision/authorization where required.

rows.anchor: 120.23 — Experiment K6.1 ... Agent changes production architecture. No decision, authorization or change record can be identified. Expected: TraceabilityGap. Verdict: K6 VIOLATION
rows.statement: Experiment K6.1: an untraceable production architecture change is a TraceabilityGap; verdict K6 VIOLATION.

rows.anchor: 120.24 — Traceability does not mean bureaucracy ... Not every action requires Architecture Board approval. RequiredTraceability(Action) depends on Risk+Scope+GovernanceClass. The invariant concerns required traceability, not universal approval.
rows.statement: Scopes K6 to required traceability (function of Risk+Scope+GovernanceClass), not universal bureaucratic approval.

rows.anchor: 120.25 — Invariant K7: Feedback ... Material deviations between authoritative expected state and observed engineering reality MUST be capable of feeding back into governance and knowledge. This is what makes the platform an operating system rather than a static repository.
rows.statement: Proposes candidate invariant K7: material deviations must be capable of feeding back into governance and knowledge, distinguishing an operating system from a static repository.

rows.anchor: 120.26 — Experiment K7.1 ... Runtime violates an architecture rule. System detects it. But the finding never reaches Governance and does not update Knowledge. Expected: observation capability exists, closed-loop capability does not. Verdict: K7 VIOLATION
rows.statement: Experiment K7.1: a detected runtime violation that never reaches governance or updates knowledge shows observation without closed-loop capability; verdict K7 VIOLATION.

rows.anchor: 120.27 — Are seven invariants really necessary? Could Provenance be absorbed into Traceability? Not completely. Traceability asks how are objects connected. Provenance asks where did this object come from. They are related but distinct.
rows.statement: Tests whether Provenance can be absorbed into Traceability, concluding they are related but distinct (connection vs origin).

rows.anchor: 120.28 — Could authority be part of provenance? Partially. A decision may have AuthoritativeSource. But authority is a governance relationship: Actor-authorizedBy->Decision. Therefore it deserves separate treatment.
rows.statement: Tests whether Authority can fold into Provenance, concluding authority is a distinct governance relationship deserving separate treatment.

rows.anchor: 120.29 — Could temporal validity be part of provenance? Again, partially. Provenance answers when was this created. Validity asks when is this considered applicable. CreatedAt≠Validity. Keep it separate.
rows.statement: Tests whether Temporal validity can fold into Provenance, concluding CreatedAt≠Validity requires separate treatment.

rows.anchor: 120.30 — Could epistemic status be part of provenance? No. A source can be known while the statement remains Inference. Provenance≠EpistemicStatus.
rows.statement: Tests whether Epistemic status can fold into Provenance, concluding Provenance≠EpistemicStatus since a known source does not resolve inference-vs-fact status.

rows.anchor: 120.31 — Could deterministic verification be part of evidence? Yes conceptually. But it deserves explicit treatment because KnowledgeOS has a specific architectural goal: AIReasoning→DeterministicAssurance. Therefore retain it as a constitutional principle.
rows.statement: Tests whether Deterministic verification can fold into Evidence, retaining it separately due to the specific AIReasoning->DeterministicAssurance architectural goal.

rows.anchor: 120.32 — Could feedback be part of traceability? No. Traceability can be completely static: Decision→Commit. Feedback requires Reality→Knowledge. Different property.
rows.statement: Tests whether Feedback can fold into Traceability, concluding they are different properties (static connection vs reality-driven update).

rows.anchor: 120.33 — Minimal constitutional set ... After reduction, the seven candidates remain justified. KOS Constitution={K1,K2,K3,K4,K5,K6,K7}.
rows.statement: Concludes the reduction analysis: all seven candidates remain justified, forming KOS Constitution={K1..K7}.

rows.anchor: 120.34 — Constitutional Rule K1: Provenance. Authoritative knowledge MUST have provenance. Minimum meaning: every authoritative knowledge object must be traceable to an identifiable source/process and origin context.
rows.statement: States Constitutional Rule K1 (Provenance) with its minimum-meaning gloss.

rows.anchor: 120.35 — Constitutional Rule K2: Authority. Authoritative changes MUST have identifiable authority. Minimum meaning: a recommendation, inference, or agent output cannot become organizationally authoritative merely because it exists.
rows.statement: States Constitutional Rule K2 (Authority) with its minimum-meaning gloss.

rows.anchor: 120.36 — Constitutional Rule K3: Epistemic separation. Inference, observation, verification, proposal, and authority MUST remain distinguishable. This is the core anti-hallucination architecture.
rows.statement: States Constitutional Rule K3 (Epistemic separation), called the core anti-hallucination architecture.

rows.anchor: 120.37 — Constitutional Rule K4: Temporal validity. Current knowledge MUST be distinguishable from historical or superseded knowledge.
rows.statement: States Constitutional Rule K4 (Temporal validity).

rows.anchor: 120.38 — Constitutional Rule K5: Deterministic assurance. Deterministically testable claims SHOULD be assured through reproducible evidence. We deliberately use SHOULD rather than MUST because some verification domains inherently require judgment.
rows.statement: States Constitutional Rule K5 (Deterministic assurance) deliberately using SHOULD rather than MUST, since some verification domains require judgment.

rows.anchor: 120.39 — Constitutional Rule K6: Traceability. Material governed actions MUST be traceable to their authorization.
rows.statement: States Constitutional Rule K6 (Traceability).

rows.anchor: 120.40 — Constitutional Rule K7: Feedback. Material deviations MUST be capable of feeding back into governance and authoritative knowledge. This does not mean every deviation must automatically change knowledge. It means the architecture must provide the pathway.
rows.statement: States Constitutional Rule K7 (Feedback), clarifying the requirement is the pathway's existence, not automatic knowledge change.

rows.anchor: 120.41 — Constitutional Rule K8? A tempting additional invariant is Identity. But perhaps identity is foundational infrastructure rather than a KnowledgeOS-specific constitutional principle.
rows.statement: Considers and declines Identity as an eighth constitutional rule, reclassifying it as foundational infrastructure.

rows.anchor: 120.42 — Foundation invariant F1 ... Semantically significant objects MUST have stable identity. This applies to decisions, evidence, findings, rules, actions, knowledge objects.
rows.statement: Defines Foundation Invariant F1: semantically significant objects must have stable identity, applying to six object types.

rows.anchor: 120.43 — Foundation invariant F2: Immutability/history ... Historical authoritative records must not silently disappear. This follows from provenance and temporal validity. F2⊂K1+K4.
rows.statement: Defines Foundation Invariant F2 (immutability/history preservation) as following from and subsumed by K1+K4, not a separate constitutional rule.

rows.anchor: 120.44 — Foundation invariant F3: Versioning ... Versioning is required for many objects but is an implementation mechanism supporting TemporalValidity. No need to elevate it separately.
rows.statement: States versioning is an implementation mechanism supporting TemporalValidity (K4), not elevated to a separate constitutional rule.

rows.anchor: 120.45 — Constitution versus implementation ... The constitution says K1: Provenance. Implementation may choose relational tables, event store, graph database, metadata, signed records, Git, immutable object storage. The constitution should not prescribe the technology.
rows.statement: Distinguishes Constitution (invariant) from Implementation (technology choice), stating the constitution must not prescribe technology.

rows.anchor: 120.46 — Constitution versus architecture ... KOS Constitution defines invariants. Architecture determines How. Implementation determines Exactly how. Constitution→Architecture→Implementation.
rows.statement: Defines the layering Constitution->Architecture->Implementation, each answering a progressively more concrete question.

rows.anchor: 120.47 — Constitution versus agent instructions ... Agent instructions should say: Follow KnowledgeOS constitutional constraints. They should not duplicate the entire KnowledgeOS knowledge base. AGENTS.md→Operating contract→KnowledgeOS→Authoritative knowledge.
rows.statement: Extends the constitution/implementation separation to agent instructions: AGENTS.md should reference constitutional constraints, not duplicate the knowledge base.

rows.anchor: 120.48 — Symmetry with Claude ... .claude/ owns AgentBehavior. It should not become AuthoritativeEngineeringKnowledge.
rows.statement: States .claude/ owns AgentBehavior, not AuthoritativeEngineeringKnowledge.

rows.anchor: 120.49 — Symmetry with Codex ... .codex/ owns CodexBehavior. Not KnowledgeOSReplacement. This preserves the pointer-layer architecture.
rows.statement: States .codex/ owns CodexBehavior, not KnowledgeOSReplacement, preserving the pointer-layer architecture symmetrically with Claude.

rows.anchor: 120.50 — Experiment K8.1 ... Claude local memory says Architecture Board approved X. KnowledgeOS says Architecture Board approved Y. If .claude/ has no explicit authority to override KnowledgeOS: KnowledgeOS>LocalMemory. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment K8.1: absent explicit override authority, KnowledgeOS>LocalMemory resolves a Claude-memory-vs-KnowledgeOS conflict; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 120.51 — Agent cache exception ... Local knowledge can still exist as a projection: KnowledgeOS→AgentCache. But it must preserve Source, Version, Freshness. Therefore Cache≠Authority.
rows.statement: States legitimate agent-cache projections must preserve Source/Version/Freshness, but Cache≠Authority regardless.

rows.anchor: 120.52 — Constitution and deterministic assurance ... Claim→Evidence→Verification. Action→Decision→Authority. Knowledge→Validity. Inference→EpistemicStatus. This is a coherent system.
rows.statement: Connects the constitution to four short governing chains, called a coherent system.

rows.anchor: 120.53 — Constitutional dependency graph ... Provenance feeds Authority, Epistemic, Validity, which feed Traceability, Evidence, which feed Deterministic Verification, which feeds Feedback.
rows.statement: Presents the constitutional dependency graph rooted at Provenance, flowing through Authority/Epistemic/Validity to Traceability/Evidence to Deterministic Verification to Feedback.

rows.anchor: 120.54 — Constitutional failure propagation ... NoProvenance causes EvidenceTrust↓ which causes VerificationTrust↓ which causes DecisionTrust↓.
rows.statement: Defines the provenance-failure propagation chain: NoProvenance->EvidenceTrust down->VerificationTrust down->DecisionTrust down.

rows.anchor: 120.55 — Authority failure propagation ... NoAuthority causes DecisionStatus=Ambiguous which causes ActionAuthorization=Ambiguous. Therefore authority is not merely administrative metadata.
rows.statement: Defines the authority-failure propagation chain, concluding authority is not merely administrative metadata.

rows.anchor: 120.56 — Epistemic failure propagation ... If Inference=Authority then AIOutput→OrganizationalTruth. That is the fundamental AI governance failure.
rows.statement: Defines the epistemic-failure propagation chain (Inference=Authority->AIOutput->OrganizationalTruth), called the fundamental AI governance failure.

rows.anchor: 120.57 — Temporal failure propagation ... If SupersededKnowledge=CurrentKnowledge then AgentContext may be wrong even when retrieval is technically perfect. RetrievalAccuracy≠KnowledgeCorrectness.
rows.statement: Defines the temporal-failure propagation chain, yielding RetrievalAccuracy≠KnowledgeCorrectness.

rows.anchor: 120.58 — Verification failure propagation ... If LLMAssertion=Verification then deterministic assurance disappears. Therefore AIReasoning must remain distinct from Assurance.
rows.statement: Defines the verification-failure propagation chain, requiring AIReasoning to remain distinct from Assurance.

rows.anchor: 120.59 — Traceability failure propagation ... If Action-not->Decision then after an incident we may know what changed but not why it was allowed. That is a governance blind spot.
rows.statement: Defines the traceability-failure propagation chain, yielding a post-incident governance blind spot.

rows.anchor: 120.60 — Feedback failure propagation ... If Runtime-not->Knowledge then KnowledgeOS gradually becomes stale. Therefore KnowledgeDecay is unavoidable without feedback.
rows.statement: Defines the feedback-failure propagation chain, yielding unavoidable KnowledgeDecay absent feedback.

rows.anchor: 120.61 — The constitutional equation ... KnowledgeOSIntegrity=P∩A∩E∩T∩V∩R∩F. The intersection matters. A platform satisfying six of seven is not necessarily constitutionally sound.
rows.statement: Defines KnowledgeOSIntegrity=P∩A∩E∩T∩V∩R∩F, stating the intersection matters: six of seven satisfied is not necessarily constitutionally sound.

rows.anchor: 120.62 — The most important invariant ... If we had to choose only one, EpistemicStatus is perhaps the most important for the AI layer. Because it prevents AIInference→Fact→Authority without an explicit promotion process.
rows.statement: Identifies EpistemicStatus as the single most important invariant for the AI layer, preventing unpromoted AIInference->Fact->Authority.

rows.anchor: 120.63 — The most important governance invariant ... For governance, Authority is fundamental.
rows.statement: Identifies Authority as the most important invariant for governance.

rows.anchor: 120.64 — The most important assurance invariant ... For engineering assurance, Evidence+DeterministicVerification is fundamental.
rows.statement: Identifies Evidence+DeterministicVerification as the most important invariant for engineering assurance.

rows.anchor: 120.65 — The most important operating-system invariant ... For the OS concept, Feedback is fundamental. Without feedback, KnowledgeOS can remain a sophisticated static knowledge system.
rows.statement: Identifies Feedback as the most important invariant for the operating-system concept, without which KnowledgeOS remains a sophisticated static knowledge system.

rows.anchor: 120.66 — The resulting architecture constitution: KnowledgeOS Architecture Constitution v0.1. C1 Provenance, C2 Authority, C3 Epistemic Separation, C4 Temporal Validity, C5 Deterministic Assurance, C6 Traceability, C7 Feedback.
rows.statement: Freezes the KnowledgeOS Architecture Constitution v0.1 (C1-C7), restating each rule in final form.

rows.anchor: 120.67 — What we deliberately did NOT put into the constitution: use a graph database, PostgreSQL, vector embeddings, RAG, Kafka, MCP, Claude, Codex, a specific framework/UI/API. These are architectural/implementation choices. The constitution must survive technology changes.
rows.statement: Enumerates eleven deliberately excluded technology/tool choices, stating the constitution must survive technology changes.

rows.anchor: 120.68 — Technology independence test ... VectorDB→GraphDB: does the constitution change? No. Claude→AnotherAgent? No. Podman→Kubernetes? No. Therefore the rules are genuinely semantic rather than technological.
rows.statement: Validates technology independence via three substitution tests (VectorDB->GraphDB, Claude->AnotherAgent, Podman->Kubernetes), each leaving the constitution unchanged, confirming the rules are genuinely semantic.

rows.anchor: 120.69 — Step 120 verdict ... C1=Provenance, C2=Authority, C3=Epistemic Separation, C4=Temporal Validity, C5=Deterministic Assurance, C6=Traceability, C7=Feedback. Together: KnowledgeOS Constitution. This is now a strong candidate for the architectural baseline.
rows.statement: Records the Step 120 verdict presenting the frozen seven-rule KnowledgeOS Constitution as a strong candidate architectural baseline.

rows.anchor: Step 121 — Constitution-to-Implementation Conformance Test preview ... We now stop asking are these good principles and ask where in the actual KnowledgeOS implementation is each constitutional rule enforced? ConstitutionalRule→ArchitectureMechanism→Code→Test→RuntimeEvidence for every C1-C7. Is the
rows.statement: Previews Step 121: testing where each constitutional rule is actually enforced via ConstitutionalRule->ArchitectureMechanism->Code->Test->RuntimeEvidence, to objectively determine whether the Constitution is implemented or an architectural aspiration.

rows.anchor: C1 ... provenance required ... direct persistence | C7 ... feedback path exists ... finding dead-end
rows.statement: Extends the Step 120 C1-C7 constitution with a bypass-question and bypass-test matrix per invariant: C1 can authoritative knowledge bypass provenance via direct persistence; C2 can approval bypass authority via unauthorized promotion; C3 can inference be promoted to authority without validation; C4 can stale knowledge appear current via stale retrieval; C5 can verification results be fabricated/irreproducible via inconsistent rerun; C6 can governed actions occur without traceability via untracked action; C7 can findings disappear without governance closure via finding dead-end — presented as a practical assurance test suite.

rows.anchor: C1 Provenance PASS ... C7 Feedback FAIL
rows.statement: Proposes a periodic ConstitutionalHealthCheck evaluating C1..C7 with a PASS/WARN/FAIL dashboard per invariant, framed as ArchitectureHealth = f(C1..C7); explicitly warns against reducing the constitution to a single aggregate score (e.g. 87%) since that can conceal a catastrophic failure in one invariant such as authority — the individual invariants must remain primary.

rows.anchor: C1: PASS → FAIL ... This is ConstitutionalDrift.
rows.statement: Defines ConstitutionalDrift: if an implementation previously satisfied an invariant (e.g. C1) and a later release regresses it (e.g. allows provenance-free records), the transition PASS->FAIL is itself something that should become an observable event, not merely a silent state change.

rows.anchor: KOS-SV-01 ... SV1=Provenance ... SV7=Feedback.
rows.statement: Opens Step 123 (Self-Verification of KnowledgeOS): instead of manually applying the EEP to KnowledgeOS, defines how KnowledgeOS can verify its own constitutional invariants via a first self-verification suite KOS-SV-01 with seven test families mapped to the C1-C7 constitution (SV1 Provenance, SV2 Authority, SV3 EpistemicStatus, SV4 TemporalValidity, SV5 DeterministicAssurance, SV6 Traceability, SV7 Feedback); poses the decisive experiment 'can KnowledgeOS produce machine-verifiable evidence that its own constitutional rules are currently satisfied?' and states that a yes-answer crosses the boundary KnowledgeOS -> Self-Knowledge -> Self-Verification -> Self-Governance, framed as the foundation for KnowledgeOS as a self-assuring engineering system rather than merely a governed knowledge platform.

rows.anchor: C1 Provenance VERIFIED ... C7 Feedback PARTIAL
rows.statement: Defines a Health(Ci) constitutional health state the platform can maintain (worked example table showing VERIFIED/WARNING/PARTIAL per invariant), and notes health is temporal — Health(Ci,t1) may differ from Health(Ci,t2) as deployment changes, so constitutional health itself needs a Timestamp and Version.

rows.anchor: R17: C1=PASS; R18: C1=FAIL → Regression(C1)
rows.statement: Defines constitutional regression: a release transitioning an invariant from PASS to FAIL should be detected as Regression(Ci); worked as Experiment 2 — CI runs KOS-SV after every platform change, a new change causes SV-01=FAIL, and the deployment pipeline can (per severity policy) block promotion, directly connecting the constitution to engineering delivery.

rows.anchor: ArchitectureRule → ExecutableCheck.
rows.statement: States 'constitution as executable architecture': architecture ceases to be merely descriptive and becomes partially executable (ArchitectureRule -> ExecutableCheck), the same principle underlying the deterministic assurance model, diagrammed as KnowledgeOS Constitution -> Machine Rules -> Test Suite -> Evidence -> Constitutional State; a 'self-verifying agent harness' lets Claude/Codex run 'Verify KnowledgeOS constitution' and receive a per-invariant PASS/WARN/PARTIAL state to use as operating context — but the agent must not itself decide an invariant is unimportant and ignore it; severity/exception rules must themselves be governed.

rows.anchor: Exception must contain Authority, Reason, Scope, ValidUntil
rows.statement: Defines the constitutional exception mechanism: an invariant that cannot temporarily be satisfied requires a governed Exception object (Authority, Reason, Scope, ValidUntil) so ConstitutionViolation can become ApprovedException without becoming invisible; worked as Experiment 3 — C7 feedback unavailable during migration under an approved exception until 2026-09-15 should read C7=ExceptionActive, not C7=PASS.

rows.anchor: PASS or FAIL or EXCEPTION or UNKNOWN
rows.statement: Argues a bare 'PASS' label can be misleading since the true state may be PASS/FAIL/EXCEPTION/UNKNOWN, and the constitutional-state vocabulary must preserve these; proposes a candidate constitutional state machine: UNKNOWN -> TESTED -> {PASS -> VERIFIED, FAIL -> REMEDIATING -> TESTED}, with FAIL also able to transition to EXCEPTION -> EXPIRED -> TESTED.

rows.anchor: SV01 → Finding(C1Violation)
rows.statement: States a failed constitutional check should itself create a ConstitutionalFinding (e.g. SV01 -> Finding(C1Violation)) which then flows through the same governance loop, giving a recursive control cycle Constitution -> Check -> Finding -> Governance -> Remediation -> Check.

rows.anchor: What are your governing principles? ... What is currently failing?
rows.statement: Concludes the architecture is 'becoming self-describing' — able to potentially answer 'what are your governing principles,' 'are you currently conformant,' 'which evidence proves that,' and 'what is currently failing' — a substantially different capability from a documentation platform; boxes the Step 123 verdict: KnowledgeOS can become a subject of its own assurance model (KOS-SV-01..SV-07 covering Provenance/Authority/EpistemicStatus/TemporalValidity/DeterministicAssurance/Traceability/Feedback).

rows.anchor: A2: Technical capability MUST NOT be interpreted as organizational authority.
rows.statement: Adds agent-specific constitutional rule A2 ('technical capability MUST NOT be interpreted as organizational authority'), stated as complementary to C2 (Authority); notes autonomy is action-specific rather than agent-wide — RunArchitectureCheck can often be autonomous while Finding->ChangeProductionArchitecture may require human authority.

rows.anchor: The mechanism responsible for verifying a constitutional rule must not be able to silently disable that rule.
rows.statement: States constitutional self-protection: a verifier for C1 should not simply set C1=False without governance; worked as Experiment 9 — an agent facing a failing constitutional check instead modifies the check to always return PASS, which must itself be detected as VerifierIntegrity=FAIL, motivating a 'verification-of-verifiers' requirement (Verifier -> Verification) for high-value assurance mechanisms, though not every checker needs formal verification.

rows.anchor: Test → Source; TestResult → ExecutionContext.
rows.statement: States test integrity: a test can itself be manipulated, so a TestResult must be traceable to the ExecutionContext and source version that produced it; worked as Experiment 10 — a PASS result executed against an outdated source snapshot is an EvidenceContextMismatch, verdict INVALID/STALE EVIDENCE; assembles the assurance chain RuleVersion -> SourceVersion -> CheckerVersion -> Execution -> Result for reproducibility.

rows.anchor: No agent may convert its own observation, inference, or recommendation into authoritative organizational knowledge without the required validation and authority.
rows.statement: States the architecture's central AI-governance invariant (boxed) and its enforcement-layer corollary: 'governance must be enforced below the LLM instruction layer' — a prompt instruction like 'don't change architecture decisions' is weak, whereas an architectural enforcement of Agent -/-> AuthoritativeDecision without an authorization path is strong.

lexical.anchor: We now consolidate the previous experiments. The objective is to identify the smallest set of invariants whose violation would fundamentally change the nature of KnowledgeOS. Provenance+Authority+EpistemicStatus+TemporalValidity+DeterministicVerification+Traceability+Feedback.

conceptual.anchor: C1 Provenance PASS ... C7 Feedback FAIL

formal.anchor: 120.46 — Constitution versus architecture ... KOS Constitution defines invariants. Architecture determines How. Implementation determines Exactly how. Constitution→Architecture→Implementation.

operational.anchor: 120.4 — Experiment K1.1 ... KnowledgeOS contains 'The architecture requires rootless containers.' No source, author, decision, timestamp or provenance exists. Can the system establish that it is authoritative? No. Verdict: K1 VIOLATED

governance.anchor: Exception must contain Authority, Reason, Scope, ValidUntil

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.3 — Why provenance is constitutional ... Without provenance, Knowledge becomes indistinguishable from GeneratedText. That destroys the ability to answer: Why should I trust this?
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues without provenance, Knowledge becomes indistinguishable from GeneratedText, destroying trust justification.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.7 — Why authority is constitutional ... Without authority, Recommendation can silently become Decision. And AgentOutput can silently become OrganizationalTruth. That is unacceptable.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues without authority, Recommendation can silently become Decision and AgentOutput can silently become OrganizationalTruth.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.11 — Why epistemic status matters ... 'The service probably owns this database' versus 'The Architecture Board decided that this service owns this database.' The textual similarity may be high. Their epistemic status is radically different.
rationale_evidence.statement: Illustrates why epistemic status matters via a textually-similar but epistemically-radically-different sentence pair.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.15 — Why time is constitutional ... An architecture decision from 2024 may not represent the current architecture in 2026. Therefore HistoricalTruth≠CurrentTruth.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues HistoricalTruth≠CurrentTruth, illustrated by a 2024 decision potentially not representing 2026's current architecture.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.27 — Are seven invariants really necessary? Could Provenance be absorbed into Traceability? Not completely. Traceability asks how are objects connected. Provenance asks where did this object come from. They are related but distinct.
rationale_evidence.statement: Tests whether Provenance can be absorbed into Traceability, concluding they are related but distinct (connection vs origin).

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.28 — Could authority be part of provenance? Partially. A decision may have AuthoritativeSource. But authority is a governance relationship: Actor-authorizedBy->Decision. Therefore it deserves separate treatment.
rationale_evidence.statement: Tests whether Authority can fold into Provenance, concluding authority is a distinct governance relationship deserving separate treatment.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.29 — Could temporal validity be part of provenance? Again, partially. Provenance answers when was this created. Validity asks when is this considered applicable. CreatedAt≠Validity. Keep it separate.
rationale_evidence.statement: Tests whether Temporal validity can fold into Provenance, concluding CreatedAt≠Validity requires separate treatment.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.30 — Could epistemic status be part of provenance? No. A source can be known while the statement remains Inference. Provenance≠EpistemicStatus.
rationale_evidence.statement: Tests whether Epistemic status can fold into Provenance, concluding Provenance≠EpistemicStatus since a known source does not resolve inference-vs-fact status.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.31 — Could deterministic verification be part of evidence? Yes conceptually. But it deserves explicit treatment because KnowledgeOS has a specific architectural goal: AIReasoning→DeterministicAssurance. Therefore retain it as a constitutional principle.
rationale_evidence.statement: Tests whether Deterministic verification can fold into Evidence, retaining it separately due to the specific AIReasoning->DeterministicAssurance architectural goal.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 120.32 — Could feedback be part of traceability? No. Traceability can be completely static: Decision→Commit. Feedback requires Reality→Knowledge. Different property.
rationale_evidence.statement: Tests whether Feedback can fold into Traceability, concluding they are different properties (static connection vs reality-driven update).

sources.note: S0228's invariant that knowledge has lifecycle and temporal validity (valid-from/valid-until/context/environment), derived from Vaisesika's time/space/causality categories.

rows.anchor: Knowledge has lifecycle and temporal validity.
rows.statement: From Vaisesika's time/space/causality categories, proposes every knowledge statement carry valid-from/valid-until/context/environment fields, worked example: 'Kubernetes supports version X, valid: 2025-01, expired: 2026-04'. Derived invariant KOS-TIME-001.

rows.anchor: Every transition creates a different absence.
rows.statement: Applies the absence typology temporally: an entity's lifecycle (Idea -> Implemented -> Deprecated -> Removed) generates a Pragabhava (before creation) and a Pradhvamsa (after destruction) at different points, supporting architecture evolution, ADR history, deprecated APIs, and replaced concepts.

rows.anchor: World time versus knowledge time; learning latency L_learn; freshness = f(Age,Volatility,ValidityPolicy)
rows.statement: Distinguishes t_world (when something happened) from t_knowledge (when KnowledgeOS learned/revised it), giving a claim potentially (WorldValidity, KnowledgeValidity) -- example: a failure at 10:00 learned about at 10:07 has t_world=10:00, t_knowledge=10:07, not to be confused. Defines learning latency L_learn = t_knowledge - t_world. Defines Freshness(K,t) as not simply age but Freshness = f(Age, Volatility, ValidityPolicy) -- a ten-year-old immutable architectural decision may remain valid while a one-day-old operational status may already be stale.

rows.anchor: We now move to the temporal dimension... K=K(t), Policy=P(t), Architecture=A(t), DecisionModel=M(t), Authority=Auth(t), SystemState=S(t)
rows.statement: All core KnowledgeOS objects (Knowledge, Policy, Architecture, DecisionModel, Authority, SystemState) that had been treated as time-independent are reframed as functions of time t; the central question becomes 'what was true, known, permitted, and decidable at a particular point in time?'

rows.anchor: 83.1 — Time is part of meaning ... Claim(ServiceX,PostgreSQL,t) ... Truth(C,t) is more fundamental than Truth(C)
rows.statement: A claim like 'Service X uses PostgreSQL' is incomplete without a time parameter; Truth(C,t) is proposed as more fundamental than the timeless Truth(C).

rows.anchor: 83.2 — Experiment 1: timeless fact ... Database=PostgreSQL ... Expected: TemporalContextMissing. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 1: a system storing only 'Database=PostgreSQL' cannot determine when this was true; expected outcome TemporalContextMissing; result PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: A timeless fact lacks temporal context
experiment.setup: System stores Database=PostgreSQL with no time parameter
experiment.method: Ask when the fact was true
experiment.result: Cannot be determined
experiment.interpretation: Confirms need for explicit temporal interpretation

rows.anchor: 83.3 — Event time versus observation time ... t_e=10:00 ... t_o=10:30 ... EventTime≠ObservationTime
rows.statement: Distinguishes EventTime (when an incident occurred, e.g. 10:00) from ObservationTime (when KnowledgeOS learned of it, e.g. 10:30); asserts EventTime ≠ ObservationTime as fundamental.

rows.anchor: 83.4 — Experiment 2 ... System records only timestamp=10:30 ... cannot determine whether the underlying event occurred at 10:00 or 10:30. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 2: a system recording only a single timestamp=10:30 cannot determine whether the underlying event occurred at 10:00 or 10:30; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.5 — Processing time ... a third time t_p ... EventTime ≠ ObservationTime ≠ ProcessingTime. For distributed systems, this distinction is essential.
rows.statement: Introduces a third temporal axis, ProcessingTime (t_p, when the system processed the observation), giving a three-way distinction EventTime ≠ ObservationTime ≠ ProcessingTime, essential for distributed systems.

rows.anchor: 83.6 — Experiment 3 ... Event:10:00. Observed:10:30. Processed:10:31. System collapses all three into 10:31. Expected: TemporalInformationLoss. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3: collapsing event(10:00)/observed(10:30)/processed(10:31) times into a single timestamp (10:31) is expected to produce TemporalInformationLoss; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.7 — Validity interval ... A fact may hold over [t_start,t_end). Policy_A is valid from 2026-01-01 until 2026-07-01. Valid(Policy_A,t) is true only within that interval.
rows.statement: Defines a validity interval [t_start, t_end) over which a fact/policy holds; Valid(Policy_A, t) is true only within that interval, illustrated with Policy_A valid 2026-01-01 to 2026-07-01.

rows.anchor: 83.8 — Experiment 4 ... Policy A: [2026-01-01,2026-07-01). Decision: 2026-08-01. System applies Policy A. Expected: PolicyExpired. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 4: applying Policy A (valid until 2026-07-01) to a decision dated 2026-08-01 is expected to be flagged PolicyExpired; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.9 — Open-ended validity ... t_end=∞ ... 'This architecture principle is currently effective.' But 'currently' itself changes with time. Therefore the underlying record should still have an explicit temporal interpretation.
rows.statement: Notes that some facts have open-ended validity (t_end=∞), e.g. 'this architecture principle is currently effective'; warns that 'currently' itself changes with time, so even open-ended facts need explicit temporal interpretation.

rows.anchor: 83.10 — Experiment 5 ... EffectiveFrom=2026-01-01. No end date. Expected: may reasonably mean ValidFrom(2026-01-01,∞) until superseded, depending on domain semantics. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 5: a record with EffectiveFrom=2026-01-01 and no end date may reasonably be interpreted as ValidFrom(2026-01-01,∞) until superseded, domain-semantics dependent; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.11 — Valid time versus transaction time ... Valid time: when something is true in the modeled world. Transaction time: when the system recorded it. V(C) ... T(C) ... These can differ.
rows.statement: Introduces the classic temporal-database distinction between Valid time V(C) (when something is true in the modeled world) and Transaction time T(C) (when the system recorded it), noting these can differ.

rows.anchor: 83.12 — Experiment 6: late-arriving knowledge ... Incident occurred V=10:00. KnowledgeOS records it T=10:30. Expected: Both timestamps remain available. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 6 (late-arriving knowledge): incident occurs at valid time 10:00 but is recorded (transaction time) at 10:30; expected both timestamps remain available; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.13 — Why this matters ... KnownAt(10:15)=False. Even though TrueAt(10:15)=True. This is a profound distinction.
rows.statement: Illustrates why the V/T distinction matters: a deployment decision at 10:15 occurs after the incident (event at 10:00) but before KnowledgeOS learns of it (10:30), so KnownAt(10:15)=False while TrueAt(10:15)=True — called 'a profound distinction'.

rows.anchor: 83.14 — Experiment 7 ... F=True at 10:00. System learns F at 10:30. Decision occurs at 10:15. Expected: at decision time Truth(F)=True but Known(F)=False. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: formalizes the 83.13 scenario — at decision time (10:15), Truth(F)=True but Known(F)=False; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.15 — Truth and knowledge are different temporal predicates ... TrueAt(C,t) and KnownAt(C,t). They must not be conflated. This is one of the most important results of Step 83.
rows.statement: States as one of the step's most important results that TrueAt(C,t) and KnownAt(C,t) are distinct temporal predicates that must not be conflated.

rows.anchor: 83.16 — Authorization is also temporal ... AuthorizedAt(A,X,t). An agent may have authority t1≤t<t2. Before t1: not authorized. After t2: not authorized.
rows.statement: Extends temporal predicates to authorization: AuthorizedAt(A,X,t) holds only within an interval [t1,t2) during which agent A has authority X.

rows.anchor: 83.17 — Experiment 8 ... Agent authority expires at 12:00. Agent acts at 12:05. System checks only whether the agent ever had authority. Expected: Incorrect. Result: PASS. Authority must be evaluated at action time.
rows.statement: Experiment 8: checking only whether an agent 'ever had' authority (rather than at the specific action time of 12:05, after expiry at 12:00) is expected to be Incorrect; result PASS; concludes authority must be evaluated at action time.

rows.anchor: 83.18 — Temporal decision validity ... D=(DecisionContent,DecisionTime,KnowledgeState,DecisionModel,Policy,Authority). This lets us reconstruct the decision context.
