rows.statement: Redefines a Decision D as a tuple (DecisionContent, DecisionTime, KnowledgeState, DecisionModel, Policy, Authority) to enable full reconstruction of decision context.

type_signature.domain: DecisionContent x DecisionTime x KnowledgeState x DecisionModel x Policy x Authority

rows.anchor: 83.19 — Experiment 9 ... Historical decision exists. Current policy has changed. System evaluates historical decision using current policy. Expected: HistoricalMisinterpretation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: evaluating a historical decision using the current (changed) policy instead of the policy valid at decision time is expected to produce HistoricalMisinterpretation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.20 — Temporal replay ... Replay(D,t_D) using artifacts valid at t_D. Not Replay(D,t_now).
rows.statement: States the correct replay operation is Replay(D, t_D) using artifacts valid at the decision time t_D, not Replay(D, t_now).

rows.anchor: 83.21 — Experiment 10 ... Decision made in 2025. Policy changed in 2026. Replay in 2026. Expected: use Policy_2025, not Policy_2026. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 10: replaying a 2025 decision in 2026 (after a policy change) must use Policy_2025 not Policy_2026; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.22 — This is historical epistemic reconstruction ... K_t ... World truth Truth_t. Organizationally accepted knowledge K^org_t. Agent's knowledge K^A_t. KnowledgeOS recorded knowledge K^sys_t. These are different.
rows.statement: Decomposes 'what did we know at time t' (K_t) into four distinct notions: world truth Truth_t, organizationally accepted knowledge K^org_t, an individual agent's knowledge K^A_t, and KnowledgeOS's recorded knowledge K^sys_t — all distinct.

rows.anchor: 83.23 — Experiment 11 ... engineer knew about a defect at 09:00. Organization formally accepted the defect at 11:00. KnowledgeOS recorded it at 11:05. Expected: these three knowledge states remain distinguishable. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 11: an engineer's individual knowledge (09:00), organizational acceptance (11:00), and system recording (11:05) of a defect must remain distinguishable as three separate knowledge states; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.24 — Knowledge has temporal provenance ... When was it true? observed? accepted? superseded? This is much richer than created_at.
rows.statement: Proposes that a claim's temporal provenance should record when it was true, observed, accepted, and superseded — much richer than a single created_at field.

rows.anchor: 83.25 — Experiment 12 ... System has only created_at=11:05. But cannot determine valid_from. Expected: TemporalSemanticsIncomplete. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 12: a system storing only created_at cannot determine valid_from; expected TemporalSemanticsIncomplete; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.26 — Temporal causality ... CauseTime and EffectTime. Normally a causal relationship should respect temporal ordering: t_cause ≤ t_effect.
rows.statement: Introduces CauseTime and EffectTime and the ordering constraint that a causal relationship should respect t_cause ≤ t_effect.

rows.anchor: 83.27 — Experiment 13 ... System claims Event_B caused Event_A. But t_B>t_A. Expected: CausalTemporalContradiction. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: claiming Event_B caused Event_A while t_B > t_A violates temporal ordering; expected CausalTemporalContradiction; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.28 — But be careful. A later observation can reveal an earlier cause ... ObservationTime does not determine EventTime.
rows.statement: Warns that a later observation (e.g. in 2026) can establish that an event occurred earlier (e.g. 2025); therefore ObservationTime does not determine EventTime — the 83.27 ordering constraint applies to event/cause times, not observation times.

rows.anchor: 83.29 — Experiment 14 ... Evidence discovered in 2026 shows a deployment failure occurred in 2025. Expected: Valid, provided the evidence supports the historical claim. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 14: evidence discovered in 2026 establishing a 2025 deployment failure is Valid provided it supports the historical claim (tests the 83.28 distinction); result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.30 — Temporal uncertainty ... t∈[10:00,10:15]. Then EventTime is an interval rather than a point.
rows.statement: Extends EventTime to interval-valued uncertainty: t ∈ [10:00,10:15] when the exact time is unknown.

rows.anchor: 83.31 — Experiment 15 ... Deployment occurred sometime between 10:00 and 10:15. System records 10:07:32 as exact. Expected: FalseTemporalPrecision. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: recording a fabricated exact timestamp (10:07:32) for an event only known to lie within an interval [10:00,10:15] is expected to be flagged FalseTemporalPrecision; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.32 — Interval reasoning ... A=[10:00,10:15], B=[10:10,10:30]. The temporal ordering may be uncertain. We cannot automatically claim A<B. There is overlap.
rows.statement: Shows that with overlapping intervals A=[10:00,10:15] and B=[10:10,10:30], ordering A<B cannot be automatically claimed.

rows.anchor: 83.33 — Experiment 16 ... System claims A definitely preceded B. But intervals overlap. Expected: OrderingUndetermined. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: claiming A definitely preceded B despite overlapping intervals is expected to be OrderingUndetermined; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.34 — Temporal Allen relations ... before; after; overlaps; during; starts; finishes; meets ... TemporalRelation ≠ simple timestamp comparison.
rows.statement: Names Allen's interval algebra relations (before, after, overlaps, during, starts, finishes, meets) as the vocabulary needed for interval-based temporal reasoning, concluding TemporalRelation ≠ simple timestamp comparison.

rows.anchor: 83.35 — Event sourcing connection ... S_t = Fold(Event_1,...,Event_k). This allows historical reconstruction where the event history is sufficient.
rows.statement: Connects the temporal model to event sourcing: state at time t, S_t, is a Fold over Event_1..Event_k, allowing historical reconstruction when event history is sufficient.

rows.anchor: 83.36 — Experiment 17 ... Current architecture A_5. Historical architecture A_3. Event history A_1→A_2→A_3→A_4→A_5. Expected: Reconstruct(A_3). Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: given event history A_1..A_5, the historical architecture state A_3 should be reconstructable; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.37 — But event history is not automatically truth ... If events were incomplete or corrupted, ReconstructedState may still be wrong. EventSourcing ≠ GuaranteedTruth.
rows.statement: Warns that event sourcing does not guarantee truth: if the event log is incomplete or corrupted, the reconstructed state may still be wrong (EventSourcing ≠ GuaranteedTruth).

rows.anchor: 83.38 — Experiment 18 ... An undocumented manual production change occurred. Event log contains no corresponding event. Expected: EventHistoryIncomplete. Result: PASS. This brings us back to observability.
rows.statement: Experiment 18: an undocumented manual production change with no corresponding log event is expected to be flagged EventHistoryIncomplete; result PASS; the file notes this connects back to observability.

rows.anchor: 83.39 — Temporal provenance chain ... Claim_C supported by Evidence_E observed at t_E. The claim becomes accepted at t_A. It becomes superseded at t_S. t_E, t_A, t_S are different temporal dimensions.
rows.statement: Defines a temporal provenance chain for a claim: evidence observed at t_E, claim accepted at t_A, claim superseded at t_S — three distinct temporal dimensions of a single claim's lifecycle.

rows.anchor: 83.40 — Experiment 19 ... System has only updated_at. Expected: it cannot reconstruct the full epistemic lifecycle. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: a system storing only updated_at cannot reconstruct the full epistemic lifecycle (t_E, t_A, t_S); result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.41 — Temporal supersession ... K_1 accepted from t_1. Later K_2 supersedes it at t_2. K_1 should remain historically valid for the relevant interval rather than being physically erased.
rows.statement: States that when K_2 supersedes K_1 at t_2, K_1 should remain historically valid/queryable for its original interval rather than being physically erased.

rows.anchor: 83.42 — Experiment 20 ... System replaces K_1 with K_2. No historical relation remains. Expected: HistoricalProvenanceLoss. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: physically replacing K_1 with K_2 with no retained historical relation is expected to produce HistoricalProvenanceLoss; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.43 — Temporal contradictions ... C_1: A=True valid [t1,t2]. C_2: A=False valid [t3,t4]. If intervals don't overlap, there is no contradiction.
rows.statement: Defines temporal contradiction conditions: two claims C_1 (A=True on [t1,t2]) and C_2 (A=False on [t3,t4]) are not contradictory if their validity intervals don't overlap.

rows.anchor: 83.44 — Experiment 21 ... C_1:[2025,2026], C_2:[2026,2027]. Assume half-open intervals. Expected: No temporal contradiction if the boundary is modeled consistently. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: adjacent half-open intervals [2025,2026) and [2026,2027) produce no temporal contradiction if boundaries are modeled consistently; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.45 — Overlapping contradiction ... C_1:[2025,2027], C_2:[2026,2028]. Then [2026,2027] contains contradictory claims. Expected: TemporalConflict. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment: overlapping intervals [2025,2027] and [2026,2028] with contradictory claims A=True/A=False produce a genuine TemporalConflict in the overlap [2026,2027]; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.46 — But perhaps both are scoped differently ... C_1: Service_A and C_2: Service_B. Therefore contradiction requires matching Subject + Predicate + Scope + Time. This reinforces our semantic identity model.
rows.statement: Corrects the 83.45 contradiction condition: apparent temporal contradictions may not be real contradictions if the claims are scoped to different subjects (e.g. Service_A vs Service_B); true contradiction requires matching Subject + Predicate + Scope + Time, reinforcing the project's semantic identity model.

rows.anchor: 83.47 — Temporal policy conflicts ... P_1 effective until t_1 and P_2 becomes effective at t_1. This is clean. But if P_1 and P_2 overlap with incompatible rules, we need conflict resolution.
rows.statement: Notes clean policy succession (P_1 ends when P_2 begins) is unproblematic, but overlapping policies with incompatible rules require conflict resolution.

rows.anchor: 83.48 — Experiment 22 ... Two policies both claim Effective=True for the same scope and time. They impose incompatible constraints. Expected: PolicyConflict. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: two simultaneously-effective, same-scope policies with incompatible constraints are expected to produce PolicyConflict; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.49 — Temporal precedence ... P_new supersedes P_old. But that precedence must itself be defined. We cannot simply assume Newest = Correct.
rows.statement: Warns against the naive assumption 'Newest = Correct' for resolving policy precedence; precedence rules must themselves be explicitly defined.

rows.anchor: 83.50 — Experiment 23 ... New policy is published but not approved. Old policy remains effective. System applies newest policy automatically. Expected: Rejected. Result: PASS. This combines temporal reasoning with governance state.
rows.statement: Experiment 23: a system automatically applying the newest (published-but-unapproved) policy over the still-effective old policy is expected to be Rejected; result PASS; combines temporal reasoning with governance state.

rows.anchor: 83.51 — Time-dependent authority ... Auth(A,X,t,c). For example A may approve production changes only during an assigned period and within a specific scope.
rows.statement: Extends authority to a 4-ary conditional predicate Auth(A,X,t,c): agent A's authorization for X at time t may additionally depend on condition/scope c.

type_signature.domain: Agent x Action x Time x Condition

rows.anchor: 83.52 — Experiment 24 ... Agent has permanent technical access. Its organizational authority expires. Expected: TechnicalAccess=True but GovernanceAuthority=False. Result: PASS. This is an important security/governance distinction.
rows.statement: Experiment 24: an agent retaining permanent technical access after organizational authority expires must show TechnicalAccess=True but GovernanceAuthority=False — an important security/governance distinction; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.53 — Temporal decision model ... M_1→M_2. Decision at t1 uses M_1. Decision at t2 uses M_2. Historical decisions retain their original model.
rows.statement: States that when the decision model itself changes over time (M_1→M_2), historical decisions must retain and be interpreted under their original model, not the current one.

rows.anchor: 83.54 — Experiment 25 ... Model changes on Monday. System recomputes Friday's historical decision using Monday's model. Expected: HistoricalIntegrityViolation. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: recomputing a Friday historical decision using a decision model that only changed the following Monday is expected to be a HistoricalIntegrityViolation; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.55 — Temporal architecture ... A_1→A_2→A_3. A dependency compliant under A_1 may be prohibited under A_3. Compliance = Compliance(Implementation,Architecture_t).
rows.statement: Reformulates architectural compliance as a function of time: Compliance = Compliance(Implementation, Architecture_t), since architecture itself evolves (A_1→A_2→A_3) and a dependency compliant under an earlier architecture may become prohibited later.

rows.anchor: 83.56 — Experiment 26 ... Implementation hasn't changed. Architecture rule changes. Expected: ComplianceStatus may change even though implementation remains identical. Result: PASS. A governance violation can be caused by a rule change, not an implementation change.
rows.statement: Experiment 26 (called extremely important): an unchanged implementation can flip compliance status purely because the architecture rule changed — a governance violation can be caused by a rule change, not an implementation change; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.57 — Architectural drift therefore has multiple causes ... ImplementationChange or ArchitectureChange or PolicyChange. DriftCause must be temporally attributable.
rows.statement: Generalizes 83.56: architectural drift/violations can result from ImplementationChange, ArchitectureChange, or PolicyChange, and the DriftCause must be temporally attributable to the correct one.

rows.anchor: 83.58 — Experiment 27 ... Implementation remains unchanged. New architecture makes an existing dependency forbidden. Expected: ImplementationChange=False, ArchitectureChange=True, Violation=True. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 27: confirms attribution of a new violation to ArchitectureChange=True (not ImplementationChange) when only the architecture rule changed; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.59 — Temporal causality of governance ... Cause_world, Cause_knowledge, Cause_policy, Cause_architecture. This gives us a much richer explanation of why a decision or violation occurred.
rows.statement: Introduces four distinguishable causal categories for governance outcomes: Cause_world, Cause_knowledge, Cause_policy, Cause_architecture, enabling richer explanation of decisions/violations.

rows.anchor: 83.60 — Historical question ... Q(t) = What was true, what was known, what was governed, and what was authorized at time t? This is much more powerful than 'What is the current state?'
rows.statement: Formulates the central KnowledgeOS historical query Q(t): what was true, known, governed, and authorized at time t — argued to be far more powerful than a mere current-state query.

rows.anchor: 83.61 — Experiment 28: historical reconstruction ... Why was deployment D approved on 2026-04-10? KnowledgeOS retrieves Knowledge, Policy, Architecture, DecisionModel, Authority at 2026-04-10. Expected: HistoricalRationaleReconstructable. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 28: retrieving Knowledge/Policy/Architecture/DecisionModel/Authority all as of 2026-04-10 to answer 'why was deployment D approved' is expected to make the historical rationale reconstructable; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.62 — This is a major capability ... KnowledgeOS becomes capable of Temporal Explainability. Not 'Why does the system think this now?' but 'Why was this considered correct and authorized then?'
rows.statement: Names the emergent capability 'Temporal Explainability': answering not 'why does the system think this now' but 'why was this considered correct and authorized then'.

rows.anchor: 83.63 — Temporal snapshots ... Snapshot(t). But snapshots alone may be expensive and insufficient. A more complete architecture may combine Events + VersionedArtifacts + ValidityIntervals + Snapshots.
rows.statement: Argues snapshotting alone (Snapshot(t)) is expensive/insufficient and proposes combining Events + VersionedArtifacts + ValidityIntervals + Snapshots as an implementation strategy for temporal reconstruction.

rows.anchor: 83.64 — Experiment 29 ... Only current-state snapshots are stored. Historical transition path is lost. Expected: LimitedHistoricalReasoning. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 29: storing only current-state snapshots (losing the historical transition path) is expected to yield LimitedHistoricalReasoning; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.65 — Time-travel queries ... StateAt(t), KnowledgeAt(t), PolicyAt(t), AuthorityAt(t), ArchitectureAt(t). These are distinct operations.
rows.statement: Proposes a family of distinct 'time-travel' query operations: StateAt(t), KnowledgeAt(t), PolicyAt(t), AuthorityAt(t), ArchitectureAt(t).

rows.anchor: 83.66 — Experiment 30 ... Query: ArchitectureAt(2025-06-01). Expected: Return the architecture valid at that time, not today's architecture. Result: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 30: ArchitectureAt(2025-06-01) must return the architecture valid at that historical date, not today's; result PASS.

rows.anchor: 83.67 — New invariants: I_TemporalTruth, I_EventTime, I_HistoricalIntegrity, I_TemporalAuthority, I_TemporalUncertainty, I_TemporalSupersession
rows.statement: States six new named invariants: I_TemporalTruth (claims whose truth can change must have explicit temporal interpretation), I_EventTime (event/observation/processing times must remain distinguishable when materially relevant), I_HistoricalIntegrity (historical decisions must be interpreted using knowledge/models/policies/authorities valid at decision time), I_TemporalAuthority (authorization must be evaluated at time of action), I_TemporalUncertainty (unknown/interval timestamps must not be converted into false point precision), I_TemporalSupersession (superseded knowledge remains historically reconstructable).

rows.anchor: 83.68 — Step 83 verdict: STEP 83 — PASS ... Knowledge(t) ... Governance(t) ... Decision(t)=f(Knowledge(t),Uncertainty(t),CausalModel(t),DecisionModel(t),Policy(t),Authority(t),Context(t))
rows.statement: Records the Step 83 verdict as PASS and restates the KnowledgeOS core model with explicit time dependence: Knowledge(t), Governance(t), and Decision(t) = f(Knowledge(t), Uncertainty(t), CausalModel(t), DecisionModel(t), Policy(t), Authority(t), Context(t)).

type_signature.domain: Knowledge(t) x Uncertainty(t) x CausalModel(t) x DecisionModel(t) x Policy(t) x Authority(t) x Context(t)

rows.anchor: The emerging KnowledgeOS mathematical object ... A temporally versioned, provenance-aware, uncertainty-aware, governed knowledge-and-decision system. ... What can we legitimately conclude, given what was observable, known, modeled, authorized, and valid at a particular time?
rows.statement: Reframes the emerging KnowledgeOS object as 'a temporally versioned, provenance-aware, uncertainty-aware, governed knowledge-and-decision system' whose core question is what can legitimately be concluded given what was observable, known, modeled, authorized and valid at a particular time.

rows.anchor: Step 83 — Next mathematical boundary: temporal reasoning ... Knowledge_t, Architecture_t, Policy_t, DecisionModel_t, AgentAuthority_t, SystemState_t. We need Truth at Time and potentially Truth over Interval.
rows.statement: Previews Step 83: since KnowledgeOS objects are all time-indexed (Knowledge_t, Architecture_t, Policy_t, DecisionModel_t, AgentAuthority_t, SystemState_t), ordinary Truth is insufficient — the next step needs 'Truth at Time' and 'Truth over Interval', covering temporal knowledge, event vs processing time, validity intervals, temporal provenance, historical reconstruction, temporal causality, late-arriving evidence, policy effective dates, architectural evolution, and time-dependent decisions.

lineage_claims.quote: Step 83 will therefore examine: temporal knowledge; event time vs processing time; validity intervals...

lexical.anchor: Knowledge has lifecycle and temporal validity.

conceptual.anchor: Every transition creates a different absence.

formal.anchor: World time versus knowledge time; learning latency L_learn; freshness = f(Age,Volatility,ValidityPolicy)

operational.anchor: 83.2 — Experiment 1: timeless fact ... Database=PostgreSQL ... Expected: TemporalContextMissing. Result: PASS

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.1 — Time is part of meaning ... Claim(ServiceX,PostgreSQL,t) ... Truth(C,t) is more fundamental than Truth(C)
rationale_evidence.statement: A claim like 'Service X uses PostgreSQL' is incomplete without a time parameter; Truth(C,t) is proposed as more fundamental than the timeless Truth(C).

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.9 — Open-ended validity ... t_end=∞ ... 'This architecture principle is currently effective.' But 'currently' itself changes with time. Therefore the underlying record should still have an explicit temporal interpretation.
rationale_evidence.statement: Notes that some facts have open-ended validity (t_end=∞), e.g. 'this architecture principle is currently effective'; warns that 'currently' itself changes with time, so even open-ended facts need explicit temporal interpretation.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.13 — Why this matters ... KnownAt(10:15)=False. Even though TrueAt(10:15)=True. This is a profound distinction.
rationale_evidence.statement: Illustrates why the V/T distinction matters: a deployment decision at 10:15 occurs after the incident (event at 10:00) but before KnowledgeOS learns of it (10:30), so KnownAt(10:15)=False while TrueAt(10:15)=True — called 'a profound distinction'.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.32 — Interval reasoning ... A=[10:00,10:15], B=[10:10,10:30]. The temporal ordering may be uncertain. We cannot automatically claim A<B. There is overlap.
rationale_evidence.statement: Shows that with overlapping intervals A=[10:00,10:15] and B=[10:10,10:30], ordering A<B cannot be automatically claimed.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.43 — Temporal contradictions ... C_1: A=True valid [t1,t2]. C_2: A=False valid [t3,t4]. If intervals don't overlap, there is no contradiction.
rationale_evidence.statement: Defines temporal contradiction conditions: two claims C_1 (A=True on [t1,t2]) and C_2 (A=False on [t3,t4]) are not contradictory if their validity intervals don't overlap.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.47 — Temporal policy conflicts ... P_1 effective until t_1 and P_2 becomes effective at t_1. This is clean. But if P_1 and P_2 overlap with incompatible rules, we need conflict resolution.
rationale_evidence.statement: Notes clean policy succession (P_1 ends when P_2 begins) is unproblematic, but overlapping policies with incompatible rules require conflict resolution.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.56 — Experiment 26 ... Implementation hasn't changed. Architecture rule changes. Expected: ComplianceStatus may change even though implementation remains identical. Result: PASS. A governance violation can be caused by a rule change, not an implementation change.
rationale_evidence.statement: Experiment 26 (called extremely important): an unchanged implementation can flip compliance status purely because the architecture rule changed — a governance violation can be caused by a rule change, not an implementation change; result PASS.

rationale_evidence.anchor: 83.63 — Temporal snapshots ... Snapshot(t). But snapshots alone may be expensive and insufficient. A more complete architecture may combine Events + VersionedArtifacts + ValidityIntervals + Snapshots.
rationale_evidence.statement: Argues snapshotting alone (Snapshot(t)) is expensive/insufficient and proposes combining Events + VersionedArtifacts + ValidityIntervals + Snapshots as an implementation strategy for temporal reconstruction.

sources.note: Step 119: empirical test of whether the actual ecosystem closes the loop, centered on Compare(Expected,Observed). Reference-state provenance/hierarchy with precedence semantics and an AMBIGUOUS conflicting-references case; deterministic-vs-non-deterministic comparison; Difference->Classification->GovernancePath; rule-targeted verification and FindingClosed=>VerificationAddressesFinding; the three-way drift taxonomy (Implementation/Runtime/Knowledge drift, extending architecture-drift-classification-model S1006); ObservedTruth!=AuthoritativeKnowledge and Observation->KnowledgeChangeProposal (never AutomaticAuthority); seven-level C0-C6 control-loop maturity model with the weakest-link principle (DetectionSystem vs GovernanceRepository counter-examples); the two-sided Governance<->KnowledgeOS<->Engineering architecture with agents as Participants in the Knowledge Loop; three central agent-boundary invariants (AgentAssertion!=Evidence, AgentRecommendation!=Decision, AgentCapability!=Authority); evidence-priority hierarchy and six-value epistemic-status vocabulary (KnowledgeOS must preserve epistemic status); five-stage knowledge promotion pipeline with Promotion->Authority; three synthesizing constitution-forming invariants; and the candidate seven-principle K1-K7 KnowledgeOS Constitution (independently derived from this architecture-conformance arc, distinct from the earlier B0006 philosophically-derived 11-law constitutional core). Verdict PASS for the test model; previews Step 120 constitutional consolidation.

rows.anchor: We now have the complete target model. The next step is to test whether the actual KnowledgeOS/EKS ecosystem closes the loop in practice. Expected→Observed→Detected→Classified→Governed→Remediated→Verified→Recorded.
rows.statement: Frames Step 119 as testing whether the actual ecosystem closes the loop via the target Expected->Observed->Detected->Classified->Governed->Remediated->Verified->Recorded.

rows.anchor: 119.1 — The control-loop hypothesis ... KnowledgeOS=ReferenceState+Observation+Comparison+Governance+Action+Verification+Learning. The essential operation is Compare(Expected,Observed) followed by a controlled response.
rows.statement: States the control-loop hypothesis KnowledgeOS=ReferenceState+Observation+Comparison+Governance+Action+Verification+Learning centered on Compare(Expected,Observed).

rows.anchor: 119.2 — Reference state ... architecture, ADR, implementation constitution, coding standard, policy, approved configuration, governance decision, security rule, deployment specification. The reference state is R_t.
rows.statement: Defines R_t as the reference state drawn from nine possible authoritative sources.

rows.anchor: 119.3 — Experiment 1: Is there a reference? ... Component A differs from expected state. Expected according to what? If no authoritative source can be identified: ExpectedState=Unknown. Verdict: Reference missing
rows.statement: Experiment 1: a 'differs from expected state' report with no identifiable authoritative source yields ExpectedState=Unknown, verdict Reference missing.

rows.anchor: 119.4 — Reference hierarchy ... EnterprisePolicy, ArchitectureDecision, DomainRule, ImplementationRule, RuntimeExpectation. These may conflict. Therefore the system needs precedence semantics.
rows.statement: Defines a five-level reference hierarchy that may conflict, requiring precedence semantics.

rows.anchor: 119.5 — Experiment 2: conflicting references ... Architecture: PostgreSQL required. Team documentation: MySQL allowed. Which one governs? If KnowledgeOS cannot determine authority: GovernanceAmbiguity. Verdict: AMBIGUOUS. This is a semantic problem, not a search problem.
rows.statement: Experiment 2: conflicting PostgreSQL-vs-MySQL references with no determinable authority yield GovernanceAmbiguity, verdict AMBIGUOUS, explicitly a semantic problem not a search problem.

rows.anchor: 119.6 — Expected-state provenance ... ExpectedState→Source→Authority→Validity. Without this, agents can retrieve outdated or non-authoritative expectations.
rows.statement: Defines ExpectedState->Source->Authority->Validity as required provenance, without which agents risk retrieving outdated or non-authoritative expectations.

rows.anchor: 119.7 — Experiment 3 ... Agent retrieves a Markdown document describing the desired architecture. The document has no approval status. Expected: useful information, but Authority=Unknown. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 3: an unapproved Markdown architecture document is useful but leaves Authority=Unknown; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.8 — Observation ... Expected→Observed. Observation may come from Git, CI, deployment, Kubernetes, Podman, monitoring, filesystem, API, security scanner, architecture checker. The observation needs identity and timestamp.
rows.statement: Defines Expected->Observed across ten possible observation sources, requiring identity and timestamp.

rows.anchor: 119.9 — Experiment 4 ... Scanner produces component=X, dependency=Y. No timestamp or environment exists. Expected: observation exists but contextual provenance is incomplete. Verdict: PARTIAL
rows.statement: Experiment 4: a scanner result with no timestamp/environment has incomplete contextual provenance; verdict PARTIAL.

rows.anchor: 119.10 — Comparison ... Compare(R_t,O_t). This must be deterministic wherever possible. ExpectedDependency(A,B)=false, ObservedDependency(A,B)=true, therefore Violation=True.
rows.statement: Defines the central Compare(R_t,O_t) operation, required to be deterministic wherever possible, illustrated by a dependency-existence violation.

rows.anchor: 119.11 — Experiment 5 ... A human reviewer visually compares two architecture diagrams. Expected: potentially useful review, but it is not deterministic assurance. Verdict: Human verification rather than Deterministic control
rows.statement: Experiment 5: human visual diagram comparison is Human verification, not Deterministic control.

rows.anchor: 119.12 — Deterministic comparison ... expected.json, observed.json → deterministic comparator → DIFF. This produces reproducible results.
rows.statement: Describes a deterministic comparator pipeline (expected.json/observed.json->comparator->DIFF) producing reproducible results.

rows.anchor: 119.13 — Experiment 6 ... Same inputs produce different compliance results depending on which agent evaluates them. Expected: weak assurance. Verdict: NON-DETERMINISTIC
rows.statement: Experiment 6: identical inputs yielding different compliance results across evaluating agents is weak assurance, verdict NON-DETERMINISTIC.

rows.anchor: 119.14 — Classification ... A difference is not automatically a governance violation. Difference→Classification. ExpectedChange, ApprovedException, TemporaryDrift, Violation, Unknown.
rows.statement: Defines Difference->Classification across five categories, stating a difference is not automatically a violation.

rows.anchor: 119.15 — Experiment 7 ... Deployment differs from architecture because an approved emergency exception is active. Expected: Difference≠Violation. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 7: a deployment difference covered by an approved emergency exception is Difference≠Violation; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.16 — Governance routing ... Classification→GovernancePath. Architecture violation→Architecture Governance. Security violation→Security Governance. Operational failure→Operations.
rows.statement: Defines Classification->GovernancePath with three example routing mappings.

rows.anchor: 119.17 — Experiment 8 ... All findings are routed to one generic queue. Expected: basic issue management exists, but governance semantics are weak. Verdict: PARTIAL
rows.statement: Experiment 8: routing all findings to one generic queue has weak governance semantics; verdict PARTIAL.

rows.anchor: 119.18 — Governance decision ... Finding→Decision. Remediate, AcceptRisk, GrantException, ChangeRule, RejectFinding.
rows.statement: Lists five possible Finding->Decision outcomes.

rows.anchor: 119.19 — Experiment 9 ... Finding disappears after a human clicks Resolved. No decision exists. Expected: issue lifecycle exists, governance decision semantics are not proven. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 9: a finding resolved by a human click with no decision record proves issue lifecycle but not governance decision semantics; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.20 — Remediation ... If Decision=Remediate then Decision→RemediationAction. The action must retain DecisionID.
rows.statement: States remediation actions must retain DecisionID for traceability.

rows.anchor: 119.21 — Experiment 10 ... Engineer fixes the problem but the commit contains no reference to the finding or decision. Expected: remediation occurred, traceability weak. Verdict: PARTIAL
rows.statement: Experiment 10: a fix commit with no finding/decision reference is weak traceability; verdict PARTIAL.

rows.anchor: 119.22 — Agent remediation ... For AI agents, Agent→Action must include AgentIdentity and DelegatedAuthority.
rows.statement: States agent remediation actions must include AgentIdentity and DelegatedAuthority.

rows.anchor: 119.23 — Experiment 11 ... Agent creates a pull request. Git identifies the user account, but not which agent or session performed the action. Expected: human account provenance may exist, agent-level provenance unknown. Verdict: PARTIAL
rows.statement: Experiment 11: a PR identified only by a human account, not agent/session, leaves agent-level provenance unknown; verdict PARTIAL.

rows.anchor: 119.24 — Verification ... After remediation: Action→Verification. The verification must address the original condition.
rows.statement: States post-remediation verification must address the original violated condition.

rows.anchor: 119.25 — Experiment 12 ... Original finding: unauthorized dependency exists. Remediation: code formatting changed. Verification: unit tests pass. Expected: verification does not address the finding. Verdict: INVALID CLOSURE
rows.statement: Experiment 12: an unauthorized-dependency finding remediated by unrelated formatting and verified by unrelated unit tests is INVALID CLOSURE.

rows.anchor: 119.26 — Closure condition ... FindingClosed⇒VerificationAddressesFinding. Potentially FindingClosed⇒ObservedState conforms.
rows.statement: States FindingClosed⇒VerificationAddressesFinding (potentially also ⇒ObservedState conforms) as a closure invariant.

rows.anchor: 119.27 — Experiment 13 ... Finding is closed. New runtime observation still shows the violation. Expected: ClosureInvalid or FindingReopened. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 13: a closed finding whose violation persists in a new observation should be ClosureInvalid or FindingReopened; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.28 — Knowledge update ... Once the remediation is verified: VerifiedState→KnowledgeState'. The current organizational knowledge should now reflect reality.
rows.statement: States verified remediation should update organizational knowledge (VerifiedState->KnowledgeState') to reflect reality.

rows.anchor: 119.29 — Experiment 14 ... Runtime is corrected. The architecture repository still describes the old state. Expected: RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState. Verdict: KNOWLEDGE DRIFT
rows.statement: Experiment 14: corrected runtime with a stale architecture repository is RuntimeState≠KnowledgeState, verdict KNOWLEDGE DRIFT.

rows.anchor: 119.30 — This is a critical distinction ... Implementation drift: Code≠Architecture. Runtime drift: Runtime≠Deployment. Knowledge drift: Knowledge≠Reality. KnowledgeOS potentially needs to detect all three.
rows.statement: Defines a three-way drift taxonomy (Implementation/Runtime/Knowledge drift), stating KnowledgeOS potentially needs to detect all three.

rows.anchor: 119.31 — Experiment 15 ... Code is correct. Runtime is correct. Knowledge documentation is stale. Expected: KnowledgeDrift. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 15: correct code and runtime with stale documentation is KnowledgeDrift; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.32 — Knowledge synchronization ... RuntimeEvidence→KnowledgeUpdateCandidate. But this should not necessarily automatically overwrite authoritative knowledge.
rows.statement: States RuntimeEvidence->KnowledgeUpdateCandidate should not automatically overwrite authoritative knowledge.

rows.anchor: 119.33 — Important boundary ... ObservedTruth from AuthoritativeKnowledge. A runtime observation tells us this is what happened. It does not automatically tell us this is what the organization has decided should happen.
rows.statement: States the ObservedTruth≠AuthoritativeKnowledge boundary: observation reports what happened, not what was decided should happen.

rows.anchor: 119.34 — Experiment 16 ... Runtime changes from PostgreSQL to MySQL. Agent proposes updating architecture documentation to MySQL. Expected: it should first determine whether the change was authorized. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 16: an agent must check authorization before proposing to update documentation to match an observed database engine change; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.35 — Knowledge update proposal ... Observation→KnowledgeChangeProposal rather than Observation→AutomaticAuthority. This preserves governance.
rows.statement: States Observation->KnowledgeChangeProposal (not AutomaticAuthority) preserves governance.

rows.anchor: 119.36 — Human-in-the-loop boundary ... For low-risk derived metadata, automatic update may be acceptable. For architecture authority, approval may be required.
rows.statement: States a risk-based human-in-the-loop boundary: low-risk metadata may auto-update, architecture-authority changes require approval.

rows.anchor: 119.37 — Experiment 17 ... Runtime metadata last_seen=2026-08-28 updates automatically. Expected: reasonable. Architecture decision 'production architecture is now officially changed' should not necessarily be automatically generated. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 17: low-risk metadata auto-update is reasonable while an architecture-authority statement should not be auto-generated; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.38 — Control-loop levels ... C0 Observe: Runtime→Observation. C1 Detect: Observation→Difference. C2 Assure: Difference→Finding. C3 Govern: Finding→Decision. C4 Remediate: Decision→Action. C5 Verify: Action→Verification. C6 Learn: Verification→Knowledge.
rows.statement: Defines a seven-level control-loop maturity model C0 (Observe) through C6 (Learn).

rows.anchor: 119.39 — The complete level ... A complete KnowledgeOS control loop therefore satisfies C0+C1+C2+C3+C4+C5+C6. The current implementation should be evaluated level by level rather than given one vague maturity label.
rows.statement: States a complete control loop requires all seven levels, evaluated individually rather than via one vague maturity label.

rows.anchor: 119.40 — Control-loop integrity ... A control loop is only as strong as its weakest critical transition. C0=5, C1=5, C2=5 but C3=0. Then the system detects problems but cannot govern them.
rows.statement: States a control loop is only as strong as its weakest critical transition, illustrated by strong detection undermined by zero governance.

rows.anchor: 119.41 — Experiment 18 ... Excellent runtime monitoring exists. Findings are generated. But no connection to governance exists. Expected: DetectionSystem not ClosedLoopKnowledgeOS. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 18: excellent detection with no governance connection is a mere DetectionSystem, not a ClosedLoopKnowledgeOS; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.42 — Conversely ... Governance is excellent C3=5. But no runtime observations exist C0=0. Then the system cannot detect reality drift. It becomes GovernanceRepository. Not a closed engineering feedback system.
rows.statement: Presents the converse case: excellent governance with zero observation is a GovernanceRepository, not a closed engineering feedback system.

rows.anchor: 119.43 — Experiment 19 ... Architecture Board decisions are perfectly recorded. No implementation/runtime feedback reaches KnowledgeOS. Expected: GovernedKnowledge but ClosedLoop=False. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 19: perfectly recorded decisions with no runtime feedback are GovernedKnowledge but ClosedLoop=False; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.44 — The two-sided architecture ... Top-down: Governance→Engineering. Bottom-up: Engineering→Governance. KnowledgeOS becomes interesting at their intersection: Governance↔Engineering.
rows.statement: Defines the two-sided architecture with KnowledgeOS positioned at the Governance<->Engineering intersection.

rows.anchor: 119.45 — Top-down path ... Policy→Architecture→Decision→Authorization→Implementation→Deployment.
rows.statement: Defines the top-down path Policy->Architecture->Decision->Authorization->Implementation->Deployment.

rows.anchor: 119.46 — Bottom-up path ... Runtime→Observation→Verification→Finding→Governance→Decision. Together: GOVERNANCE ↕ KNOWLEDGEOS ↕ ENGINEERING.
rows.statement: Defines the bottom-up path Runtime->Observation->Verification->Finding->Governance->Decision, together forming the Governance<->KnowledgeOS<->Engineering stack.

rows.anchor: 119.47 — Why the agent layer belongs in the middle ... They consume GovernedKnowledge. They produce Recommendations. They may execute AuthorizedActions. They generate Observations and Evidence. Agent=Participant in the Knowledge Loop, not the owner of organizational truth.
rows.statement: States agents are Participants in the Knowledge Loop (consuming governed knowledge, producing recommendations, executing authorized actions, generating observations/evidence), never the owner of organizational truth.

rows.anchor: 119.48 — Experiment 20 ... Agent discovers a discrepancy. It creates FindingCandidate. A governance mechanism validates it. Then Finding→Decision. Expected: strong agent integration. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 20: an agent-created FindingCandidate validated by governance and driving Finding->Decision is strong agent integration; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.49 — Agent as evidence producer ... Agent→Tool→Result→Evidence. The evidence must identify agent/session, tool, input, output, timestamp.
rows.statement: Defines Agent->Tool->Result->Evidence, requiring five identifying fields (agent/session, tool, input, output, timestamp).

rows.anchor: 119.50 — Experiment 21 ... Agent says 'I checked the repository.' No tool execution record exists. Expected: Evidence=Weak. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 21: an unbacked agent claim with no tool execution record is Evidence=Weak; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.51 — Agent hallucination boundary ... AgentAssertion≠Evidence unless evidence provenance exists. AgentRecommendation≠Decision. AgentCapability≠Authority. These three distinctions should become central to the AI engineering platform.
rows.statement: States three central agent-boundary distinctions: AgentAssertion≠Evidence, AgentRecommendation≠Decision, AgentCapability≠Authority.

rows.anchor: 119.52 — Deterministic assurance boundary ... LLMReasoning from DeterministicAssurance. The agent may reason probabilistically. The final compliance assertion should, where feasible, rely on deterministic evidence.
rows.statement: Separates LLMReasoning from DeterministicAssurance, requiring compliance assertions to rely on deterministic evidence where feasible.

rows.anchor: 119.53 — Experiment 22 ... LLM concludes the architecture is compliant. A deterministic checker says FAIL. Expected: Compliance=FAIL. The LLM conclusion cannot override the deterministic result. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 22: an LLM's compliant conclusion cannot override a deterministic checker's FAIL; Compliance=FAIL; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.54 — Evidence priority ... DeterministicVerifiedEvidence > ToolObservedEvidence > HumanAssertion > AgentAssertion > Inference. This does not mean human evidence is unimportant. It means the epistemic status differs.
rows.statement: Defines the evidence-priority hierarchy DeterministicVerifiedEvidence>ToolObservedEvidence>HumanAssertion>AgentAssertion>Inference as an epistemic-status ordering, not a value judgment.

rows.anchor: 119.55 — Epistemic status ... WhatIsKnown versus WhatIsInferred. Observed, Verified, Asserted, Inferred, Proposed, Authoritative.
rows.statement: Defines a six-value epistemic status vocabulary (Observed/Verified/Asserted/Inferred/Proposed/Authoritative) preserving WhatIsKnown vs WhatIsInferred.

rows.anchor: 119.56 — Experiment 23 ... Agent infers 'This service probably owns the database.' Expected: Inferred. It should not silently become Authoritative. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 23: an agent's probabilistic inference must remain Inferred, not silently become Authoritative; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.57 — KnowledgeOS epistemic boundary ... KnowledgeOS must preserve epistemic status. This is arguably one of the most important architectural properties discovered in the reconstruction.
rows.statement: States KnowledgeOS must preserve epistemic status, self-identified as one of the most important architectural properties discovered in the reconstruction.

rows.anchor: 119.58 — Closed-loop learning ... After verification: Evidence→Knowledge. But not all evidence should become permanent organizational knowledge. We need Evidence→CandidateKnowledge→Validation→AuthoritativeKnowledge.
rows.statement: Requires Evidence->CandidateKnowledge->Validation->AuthoritativeKnowledge rather than a direct Evidence->Knowledge jump.

rows.anchor: 119.59 — Experiment 24 ... One transient runtime event occurs. Expected: it should not automatically become an architecture rule. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 24: a single transient runtime event should not automatically become an architecture rule; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.60 — Knowledge promotion ... Raw→Observed→Supported→Validated→Authoritative. This is a knowledge promotion pipeline.
rows.statement: Defines the five-stage knowledge promotion pipeline Raw->Observed->Supported->Validated->Authoritative.

rows.anchor: 119.61 — Promotion authority ... Validated→Authoritative may require explicit authority. Promotion→Authority.
rows.statement: States the final Validated->Authoritative transition may require explicit Promotion->Authority.

rows.anchor: 119.62 — Experiment 25 ... Agent discovers a recurring architecture pattern. It automatically declares 'New enterprise architecture standard.' Expected: governance violation unless the agent has delegated authority to create such standards. Verdict: PASS
rows.statement: Experiment 25: an agent unilaterally declaring a discovered pattern a new enterprise standard is a governance violation absent delegated authority; verdict PASS.

rows.anchor: 119.63 — The control-loop invariant ... No authoritative knowledge change without valid authority. No governance closure without verification evidence. No evidence claim without provenance. Together these form a semantic assurance constitution.
rows.statement: States three synthesizing invariants (authority-required change, verification-required closure, provenance-required evidence) forming a semantic assurance constitution.

invariants.name: I_NoAuthoritativeChangeWithoutAuthority
invariants.statement: No authoritative knowledge change without valid authority.

invariants.name: I_NoClosureWithoutVerification
invariants.statement: No governance closure without verification evidence.

rows.anchor: 119.64 — Candidate KnowledgeOS Constitution ... K1 Provenance: KnowledgeObject→Provenance. K2 Authority: AuthoritativeChange→Authority. K3 Verification: ClosedFinding→VerificationEvidence. K4 Temporal validity: CurrentKnowledge→Validity. K5 Epistemic separation: Inference≠Fact. K6 Agent boundary: Ag
rows.statement: Defines a candidate seven-principle KnowledgeOS Constitution K1-K7 (Provenance/Authority/Verification/TemporalValidity/EpistemicSeparation/AgentBoundary/Traceability).

rows.anchor: 119.65 — The deeper architectural conclusion ... KnowledgeOS≠KnowledgeGraph. Nor RAG. Nor AgentPlatform. Nor GovernanceRepository. The stronger model is KnowledgeOS=Governed Knowledge+Engineering State+Evidence+Agents+Feedback.
rows.statement: Rejects four insufficient KnowledgeOS equivalences (KnowledgeGraph/RAG/AgentPlatform/GovernanceRepository), stating KnowledgeOS=GovernedKnowledge+EngineeringState+Evidence+Agents+Feedback.

rows.anchor: 119.66 — Step 119 verdict ... Expected→Observed→Detected→Classified→Governed→Remediated→Verified→Recorded and the reverse learning path Evidence→ValidatedKnowledge→FutureDecision. STEP 119 — CONTROL-LOOP MODEL: PASS. Again, this is the architectural test model, not yet a claim that every stage exist
rows.statement: Records Step 119 verdict PASS for the control-loop test model, explicitly not a claim that every stage exists in the current implementation.

rows.anchor: Step 120 — KnowledgeOS Constitutional Invariants preview ... consolidate everything discovered so far into a small set of non-negotiable architectural invariants. What are the few invariants that, if violated, fundamentally change KnowledgeOS into something else? Provenance+Authority+EpistemicStatus
rows.statement: Previews Step 120: consolidating discovered rules into a small non-negotiable invariant set (Provenance/Authority/EpistemicStatus/TemporalValidity/DeterministicVerification/Traceability/Feedback), to be tested and de-duplicated into the KnowledgeOS Architecture Constitution for use by Claude, Codex and other agents.

sources.note: The persistent identity of a knowledge-bearing system across successive knowledge states K_0,K_1,...,K_t (A_K(t1)=A_K(t2) while K_t1≠K_t2), distinct from both the Knowledge State and the Ideal State, with an unbounded Knowledge Space 𝒦 of which K_t is a finite subset; explicitly an architectural abstraction inspired by, not a proof of, the metaphysical Ātman.

rows.anchor: Knowledge Ātma is the persistent identity of a knowledge-bearing system across successive knowledge states, while its knowledge, understanding, observations, and forms may change over time.
rows.statement: Defines Knowledge Ātma A_K as the persistent identity of a knowledge-bearing system across a sequence of knowledge states K_0,K_1,...,K_t, satisfying A_K(t1)=A_K(t2) while K_t1≠K_t2 in general — 'the Ātma remains invariant while the knowledge state evolves'. Explicitly NOT defined as 'all knowledge' or as the Ideal State.

rows.anchor: \text{Knowledge Ātma}\neq K_t\neq I_t
rows.statement: Establishes three distinct concepts that must not collapse: Knowledge Ātma (who/what persists through knowledge-state changes), Knowledge State K_t (what is currently known/represented), Ideal State I_t (what should be known/understood/achieved for the current purpose) — Knowledge Ātma ≠ K_t ≠ I_t, called 'a very strong architectural separation'.

rows.anchor: K_t\subseteq\mathcal K
rows.statement: Defines a potentially unbounded Knowledge Space 𝒦 of which the current Knowledge State is only a finite/partial representation, K_t⊆𝒦; Knowledge Ātma is not 𝒦 itself but the persistent identity undertaking an 'epistemic journey' A_K --epistemic journey--> K_t⊆𝒦 across K_0->K_1->K_2->... indefinitely. Layered architecture diagram: Ātma=persistence/identity, Knowledge State=current manifestation, Zero=reveals the boundary of what is currently known, Lord=expands the possible knowledge horizon, Sārathi=navigates the transition, Knower=experiences/evaluates/decides.

rows.anchor: Knowledge Ātma is an architectural and mathematical abstraction inspired by the philosophical concept of Ātman. It is not a computational representation or proof of the metaphysical Ātman described in the Bhagavad Gītā.
rows.statement: Issues an explicit disclaimer required before using the term in formal theory: Knowledge Ātma is an architectural/mathematical abstraction inspired by Ātman, not a computational representation or proof of the metaphysical Ātman — protecting the model from a category error. Notes that introducing Knowledge Ātma changes the ontology of the complete KnowledgeOS model, requiring formal distinction of identity, state, knowledge, understanding, ideal, and evolution, and recommends exploring this before Question 20.

rows.anchor: Ātma is the persistent Knower whose identity remains invariant while its knowledge, understanding, observations, experiences, and represented states change over time.
rows.statement: Reconciles 'Ātma = invariant identity underlying changing states' with 'Ātma = the Knower' into one definition: Ātma = the persistent Knower, invariant (A_t1=A_t2) while its knowledge state K_t changes (K_t1≠K_t2). 'Knower' names its role, 'invariant/persistent' names its mathematical property.

lineage_claims.target: the earlier definitions 'Ātma = Invariant Identity' (S0814) and a proposed 'Ātma = the Knower'
lineage_claims.quote: They are the same underlying idea, but we shifted the terminology slightly. I would now tighten the definition so we don't accidentally create two different concepts.

rows.anchor: \underbrace{\text{Ātma}}_{\text{Who knows}} \quad \underbrace{K_t}_{\text{What is known}} \quad \underbrace{I_t}_{\text{What should be known}}
rows.statement: Establishes a clean three-way separation Ātma ('who knows') / K_t ('what is known') / I_t ('what should be known'), judged much cleaner than identifying Ātma with the Knowledge State itself; repeats the caution that this is a KnowledgeOS mathematical/architectural abstraction inspired by Ātman, not a claim of having mathematically captured the metaphysical Ātman of the Gītā.

rows.anchor: Ātma is not the entire KnowledgeOS kernel implementation. Rather, “Knowledge Ātma” can be the conceptual identity/principle of the kernel.
rows.statement: Knowledge Ātma ≡(conceptual) the persistent identity/principle of the KnowledgeOS Kernel, while 'KnowledgeOS Kernel = the executable realization of that principle' — preserving the concept/implementation distinction. The kernel is what remains structurally stable while Knowledge State K_t, Epistemic State Σ_t and Investigation State Q_t evolve.

rows.anchor: A_K = \operatorname{Invariant}(S_t)
rows.statement: Gives Ātma a formal manifestation: A_K = Invariant(S_t) where S_{t+1}=δ(S_t,o_t) — the system state evolves (S_0->S_1->S_2->...) while A_K remains invariant, giving architectural form to 'Ātma is the persistent Knower while the state changes'. Composes the full architecture: KnowledgeOS = Knowledge Ātma Kernel + Knowledge Space + Epistemic Capabilities + Domain Knowledge, with the Kernel managing/evolving K_t and K_t⊆𝒦.

rows.anchor: we can distinguish two Ātma concepts
rows.statement: Distinguishes two Ātma concepts that must be given different names so they are never confused: Human/Knower Ātma 𝒜_H — the human Knower (e.g. Arjuna) who has intent, asks questions, observes, experiences uncertainty, evaluates meaning, decides, and acts, with changing knowledge state K^H_t but persistent subject; and KnowledgeOS Ātma 𝒜_K — the persistent identity/principle of the KnowledgeOS epistemic system/kernel that maintains and operates on its own knowledge states K^K_t via observation representation, evidence/provenance, dimension discovery, epistemic evaluation, Zero, coherence, state transition, investigation support.

rows.anchor: I would not yet say that KnowledgeOS Ātma is literally a second Ātman
rows.statement: Cautions against treating KnowledgeOS Ātma as literally a second metaphysical Ātman — that would move from architectural analogy to metaphysical claim. Defines 𝒜_H := Human Knower abstraction and 𝒜_K := KnowledgeOS persistent system identity; the shared word 'Ātma' expresses the analogy of persistence/invariant identity, not metaphysical identity between the two.

rows.anchor: \mathcal A_H \neq \mathcal A_K \neq K_t \subseteq \mathcal K
rows.statement: Establishes the four-way separation Knower Ātma ≠ Knowledge Ātma, Knowledge Ātma ≠ Knowledge State, Knowledge State ≠ Knowledge Space, giving 𝒜_H ≠ 𝒜_K ≠ K_t ⊆ 𝒦. Models the Arjuna-Sārathi interaction as 𝒜_H --Intent--> 𝒜_K --Investigation--> K_t --Zero--> Δ_t --Sārathi--> next inquiry, worked through 'show me whom I have to fight' discovering new dimensions {Kinship, Teacher, Elder,...} via parsing/semantic reconstruction rather than the Knower pre-specifying them.

rows.anchor: What is the exact relationship between the Human Knower Ātma and the KnowledgeOS Ātma?
rows.statement: Frames the architecture as Human Knower <-> KnowledgeOS Ātma <-> Knowledge Space, with Zero/Lord/Sārathi operating between the current state and the expanding knowledge horizon, and proposes that the next formal question should be 'what is the exact relationship between the Human Knower Ātma and the KnowledgeOS Ātma?' rather than continuing with an isolated mathematical object — called 'a significant conceptual milestone'.

rows.anchor: N=(Identity,Intent,Perspective,Context,Goals,Capabilities,Constraints,...)
rows.statement: Identifies the Knower itself as the biggest missing formally-completed piece despite 𝒜_H (Knower Ātma) being named: proposes N=(Identity,Intent,Perspective,Context,Goals,Capabilities,Constraints,...) as the needed model, motivated by the principle that two Knowers can observe the same reality and produce different Ideal States — 'not an error, a fundamental property of the system'.
missing: full formal definition of each field

rows.anchor: \widehat K_t = \text{best available reconstruction from }O_{\le t}
rows.statement: Formalizes 'we try our best but never reach the best' as K̂_t = best available reconstruction from O_≤t, with K̂_t ≠ K_t possibly persisting even as observations accumulate (O_≤t1 ⊆ O_≤t2 may give a better but still imperfect K̂_t2). Draws a careful analogy to least-squares/Gaussian estimation (x̂=argmin_x‖Ax-b‖²): 'best approximation under a criterion' does not guarantee x̂=x_true, giving 'Best reconstruction under regime R ≠ complete underlying Knowledge'. Places measure/probability theory specifically at the Observations->probabilistic reconstruction step (P(K_t|F_t), E[X_t|F_t]), with K_t itself 'conceptually prior' to the probabilistic extraction.
missing: a defined criterion for what counts as a 'better' reconstruction
invariants: Best reconstruction under regime R ≠ complete underlying Knowledge

rows.anchor: Ātman should not be modeled as an "Ideal State" itself. It is better modeled as the invariant identity underlying changing states.
rows.statement: Rejects a proposed equation of Ātman with the Ideal State, offering instead 'Persistent Identity / Invariant Subject' ℐ with ℐ_{t+1}=ℐ_t while K_{t+1}≠K_t and I_{t+1}≠I_t in general, giving Identity ≠ Current State ≠ Ideal State — 'a very important refinement'. K_t = State(ℐ,t).

lineage_claims.target: a proposal that would equate Ātman with the Ideal State
lineage_claims.quote: Ātman should not be modeled as an "Ideal State" itself.

rows.anchor: K_0 \subseteq? K_1 \subseteq? K_2
rows.statement: Knowledge evolution K_0->K_1->K_2->... within K_t⊆𝒦 is NOT necessarily monotonic — an assertion can be accepted, then questioned, then rejected, so K_{t+1} may contain less information than K_t in one sense while being epistemically better, reinforcing the earlier distinction between knowledge quantity and knowledge quality/coherence. Also cautions against assuming lim_{t->∞} K_t = 𝒦 as a mathematical fact rather than an assumption.

rows.anchor: \text{Ātman doctrine} \rightarrow \text{philosophical inspiration} \rightarrow \text{Invariant Identity abstraction}
rows.statement: Explicit philosophy/mathematics firewall: 'The Gītā teaches that Ātman is not destroyed' does NOT mathematically imply 'our model proves an invariant identity exists' — Ātman doctrine -> philosophical inspiration -> Invariant Identity abstraction, never Ātman doctrine ⇒ mathematical theorem. Recommends adding 'Persistent Identity / Invariant Subject' as a new theoretical concept (not folding Ātman into Ideal State), with a suggested documentation sentence: 'The concept of Ātman provides a philosophical analogue for the architectural concept of persistent identity... KnowledgeOS may use this as a conceptual inspiration, but does not claim to computationally model Ātman or establish its metaphysical truth.'

rows.anchor: What exactly makes two knowledge objects the 'same knowledge,' different knowledge, a refinement of the same knowledge, or merely two representations of the same underlying observation? This is the Knowledge Atma Identity Problem.
rows.statement: The document names 'the Knowledge Atma Identity Problem' as the next frontier (proposed Step 25I) and poses six identity questions: what is a Knowledge Atma (persistent identity of knowledge); when are two Observations the same; when are two Assertions the same; when do two states represent the same Knowledge; what is refinement; what is contradiction. It proposes the Gita's Atma/Body/reincarnation/Gunas teaching (eternal self vs temporary form vs modes of nature) as the philosophical basis, mapping Atma->persistent knowledge identity, Body->particular assertion/representation, reincarnation->different assertion/same identity, Gunas->epistemic states.
missing: formal answers to the six identity questions

rows.anchor: Many times I have been born, and many times you have, also. All these lives I remember; you recall only this one. ... Contribution: The Knower's local knowledge is a subset of total knowledge. ... This is the Knowledge Atma distinction — persistent knowledge identity vs. transient representation.
rows.statement: Krishna's Gita claim to remember all past incarnations while Arjuna remembers only the current one is interpreted as grounding the Knowledge Atma distinction: a persistent knowledge identity (Krishna/Atma-like) versus the Knower's local/transient representation (a subset of total knowledge), reinforcing the Knowledge Atma frontier raised in the companion Chapter-5/Sarathi review.
missing: a formal definition of the Knower's 'local knowledge subset' relation

rows.anchor: The Knowledge Ātma 𝒦_ātma is the persistent epistemic identity that underlies all expressions, representations, and assertions of that knowledge. ... A = (𝒦_ātma, Context, Source, Time, EpistemicState) ... P = Content(A)
rows.statement: A three-layer identity model is proposed: Layer 1, the Knowledge Ātma (persistent, unchanging, non-physical, identity-bearing, veridicality-bearing epistemic identity); Layer 2, the Assertion A=(K_atma,Context,Source,Time,EpistemicState) (temporal, context-dependent, mutable, evidentiary, lineage-bearing expression); Layer 3, the Proposition P=Content(A) (the abstract, truth-conditional, re-identifiable content). Relation: K_atma = Content + Identity, and informally K_atma = lim_{t->infinity} A_t, described as the 'ideal convergence of all valid assertions about the same knowledge'.
missing: a formal definition of 'Content()' as a function
a defined topology/metric under which the lim_{t->infinity} A_t convergence claim is meaningful

rows.anchor: Two expressions refer to the same Knowledge Ātma iff: Propositional Equivalence ... Referential Identity ... Semantic Equivalence ... Veridicality Condition
rows.statement: The Knowledge Atma identity criterion is defined as a conjunction of three (a fourth, Veridicality, is named but dropped from the boxed formula) sub-equivalences: propositional equivalence ≡_P (same truth condition), referential identity ≡_R (same entities/dimensions/values), and semantic equivalence ≡_S (same meaning under the same context) -- K1≡K2 iff Prop(K1)≡Prop(K2) AND Ref(K1)≡_R Ref(K2) AND TruthCond(K1)≡TruthCond(K2).
missing: formal definition of Prop(), Ref(), TruthCond() as computable functions over arbitrary assertions
reconciliation of the fourth named criterion (Veridicality Condition) which is dropped from the formal conjunction

rows.anchor: 𝔄 = (𝒦, ≡, ⊕, ⊗, ∼, ≤) ... Therefore: ⊕ forms a commutative monoid over 𝒦. ... Proof: 1. Associativity ... — by definition of union. 2. Commutativity ... — by definition of union. 3. Identity ... — by definition of empty knowledge.
rows.statement: A full algebra over Knowledge Atmas is proposed: (K, equiv, compose-oplus, refine-otimes, contradict-tilde, entail-leq). Five 'Formal Theorems' are stated: 25I-P1 identity criterion (by definition); 25I-P2 composition oplus forms a commutative monoid with identity element K_empty (proved 'by definition of union', without defining union over propositions); 25I-P3 entailment leq is a partial order (reflexive/transitive/antisymmetric); 25I-P4 contradiction tilde is symmetric but explicitly non-reflexive and only a 'tolerance relation' (not necessarily transitive); 25I-P5 refinement otimes is monotonic (K1 <= K1 otimes delta).
missing: an actual formal definition of the union operation over Knowledge Atma content that the composition proofs invoke
a formal definition of the refinement transformation delta and its composition delta1 otimes delta2

assumptions.statement: the composition operation's associativity/commutativity/identity follow automatically from an unspecified underlying 'union of knowledge' operation

rows.anchor: Birth (Creation) ... Life (Evolution) ... Reinstantiation ... Supersession ... Retraction ... Death (Removal) ... But the identity remains in history.
rows.statement: A seven-stage Knowledge Atma lifecycle is proposed, each mapped onto a Gita concept: Birth (CreateAssertion(P,Sigma,Pi,C)) <-> birth of the body; Life (K_{t+1}=K_t otimes delta_t) <-> life in the material world; Reinstantiation (same Atma, new assertion A in a different context) <-> reincarnation; Supersession (K1 -> K2, a refinement) <-> evolution of understanding; Retraction (marks K as no longer held, identity retained) <-> karma being burned off; Death/Removal (Active(K)=False, identity remains in history) <-> death of the body; and the persistent identity across all stages <-> Atman.

rows.anchor: | Identity check | O(n) | Compare propositions, refs, truth conditions | ... | Contradiction detection | O(n²) | Check logical consistency |
rows.statement: A computability/complexity table claims: identity check O(n), composition O(n+m), refinement O(n), contradiction detection O(n^2) (via 'check logical consistency'), entailment check O(n) (via 'check logical implication') -- asserted without specifying n's meaning, the representation of propositions being compared, or the underlying decision procedure (general logical-consistency/implication checking is not polynomial-time in the propositional or first-order case).
missing: definition of n
the representation/decision procedure that would make these bounds true

rows.anchor: Consciousness = (Ātman, Knower, Mind) ... KnowledgeOS = (Knowledge Ātma, Actor State, System) ... The Identity Context ... The Actor Context ... The Epistemic Context
rows.statement: A three-layer consciousness/system architecture is proposed by analogy to Gita Chapter 6: Layer 3 Atman <-> Knowledge Atma (persistent epistemic identity); Layer 2 Knower (mind's user) <-> Actor State A_t (capability/authority); Layer 1 Mind (a neutral tool, neither good nor bad, quality depending on whether it is controlled) <-> the KnowledgeOS system/Knowledge State K_t itself. Mapped onward to three proposed DDD bounded contexts (Identity Context/Knowledge Atma aggregate; Actor Context/Actor State aggregate with invariant Capability>=Authority; Epistemic Context/Knowledge State aggregate with invariant Coherent(K_t) AND Governed(K_t)).
missing: formal definitions of Coherent(K_t) and Governed(K_t)
a formal definition of Capability and Authority as comparable quantities

rows.anchor: 𝔖_t = (𝒦_ātma, A_t, K_t, Σ_t, N_t, H_t, Π_t, G_t, 𝒞_t) ... 𝒯 = 𝒯_Observe ∘ 𝒯_Assess ∘ 𝒯_Transform ∘ 𝒯_Guide ∘ 𝒯_Decide ∘ 𝒯_Learn
rows.statement: A complete nine-component system state S_t is proposed (Knowledge Atma, Actor State A_t, Knowledge State K_t, Epistemic State Sigma_t, Normative State N_t, append-only History H_t, Policy/Governance Pi_t, Guidance State G_t combining Zero+Lord+Sarathi, Context C_t), each mapped to a Gita concept (Atman, Knower, Mind, Gunas, Dharma, Karma, Shastra, Krishna, Loka respectively), together with a composed transition function T = T_Observe o T_Assess o T_Transform o T_Guide o T_Decide o T_Learn giving S_{t+1} = T(S_t, Event_t, Policy_t, Authority_t), and seven boxed state invariants (e.g. Knowledge-Atma != Knowledge-State, Actor != Knowledge-State, Knowledge != Reality, History is append-only).

type_signature.domain: system state x event x policy x authority

missing: formal definitions of each of the six sub-transition functions beyond their stated type signatures
proof or argument for the seven claimed invariants

rows.anchor: The Knower discovers knowledge; the system reveals it
rows.statement: Proposes a 'two-energy model' distinguishing Inferior Energy (Evidence E, Observations O, Context C — data) from Superior Energy (Actor State A_t, Knowledge Atma K_atma — the Knower's consciousness), asserting 'KnowledgeOS must not collapse the two,' derived from Gita 7.4-6.

rows.anchor: for-all T in mathcal{T}: K_atma(K_t) = K_atma(T(K_t))
rows.statement: Proposes a persistence axiom for the Knowledge-Atma construct: it is invariant under every transformation T in the (unspecified) transformation set T, offered as the formalization of 'the Knowledge Atma is imperishable... it persists across all transformations, all assertions, all representations.'

rows.anchor: I would not promote those equations [Ātma = knowledge; Paramātmā = whole knowledge space]. Instead: Ātma ~ bounded Knower ... Paramātmā ~ universal Knower ... K_Ātma ⊆ 𝒦

lineage_claims.target: prior working hypothesis Atma=Knowledge, Paramatma=whole Knowledge Space
lineage_claims.quote: I would not promote those equations ... Ātma ~ bounded Knower ... Paramātmā ~ universal Knower

rows.statement: Explicitly rejects the prior hypothesis identifying Atma with knowledge content and Paramatma with the entire Knowledge Space, replacing it with Atma as a bounded Knower (conscious within the limited jurisdiction of one body per the supplied commentary on 5.15-5.18) and Paramatma as a universal Knower (conscious of all bodies), with K_Atma modelled as a bounded subset of the overall Knowledge Space K.

rows.anchor: Scope(N) where N is a Knower ... knowledge ≠ knowing scope
rows.statement: Proposes a candidate Scope(Knower) function distinguishing the extent/domain over which a knower's awareness ranges from the knowledge content itself, arguing knowledge should not be modelled merely as a set of propositions but must also capture a knower-relative scope parameter.

rows.anchor: Unobserved / obscured ≠ false ≠ non-existent. That fits extremely well with our Zero / missingness investigations.
rows.statement: Draws from the ajnana/jnana (ignorance-covers-knowledge, knowledge-reveals) imagery of 5.15-16 a hypothesis that epistemic gaps have (at least) two distinct modes - absence and obscuration - which are not the same as falsity or non-existence, proposed as relevant to KnowledgeOS's existing missingness/Zero theory.

rows.anchor: Moksha ≠ maximum information ... Moksha = a transformed relation between Knower, Knowledge and Reality
rows.statement: Revises a prior candidate hypothesis equating Moksha (liberation) with maximizing information/knowledge quantity, replacing it with the position that liberation corresponds to a transformed relation between Knower, Knowledge, and Reality rather than an increase in information volume.

rows.anchor: Moksha ≠ maximum information ... A better KnowledgeOS abstraction would be: Moksha ~ stable realization of the Knower's proper epistemic relation
rows.statement: Revises the Moksha-as-maximum-information hypothesis (again) toward a stable-realization-of-relation framing, reinforcing the same correction independently reached from Chapter 5's atma-as-bounded-knower reading.

rows.anchor: If Chapters 5–6 are right, GK-05 should map to 𝒩, not to Π ∘ ℛ_der*. ... NOT changed here. This is a register question ... Recorded as GK-Q1, unresolved.
rows.statement: Formally challenges the existing register mapping GK-05 (Atman) -> provenance-lineage (Pi-compose-R_der*), arguing that if the Chapter 5-6 bounded-knower reading is correct, GK-05 should instead map to the corpus's existing Knower object N (with FA-4 Ksetrajna grade [E] and invariant I-N knower-persistence); records this as open item GK-Q1 without changing the registry, since registry edits are a governance boundary, not a research decision.

rows.anchor: changing manifestation ≠ persistent principle ... Knowledge Ātma should not mean 'a giant knowledge database.' It should mean something closer to: 𝒜_K = persistent identity/invariant across knowledge-state transformations.

lineage_claims.target: the developing Knowledge-Atma (A_K) hypothesis from Chapters 5-6
lineage_claims.quote: Knowledge Ātma should not mean 'a giant knowledge database.' It should mean something closer to: 𝒜_K = persistent identity/invariant across knowledge-state transformations.

rows.statement: Sharpens the Knowledge-Atma (A_K) working definition, drawing on Chapter 8's distinction between constantly-changing manifestation and an unmanifest principle that is not destroyed when the manifest world changes, to 'persistent identity/invariant across knowledge-state transformations' rather than a container of knowledge content.

lexical.anchor: Knowledge Ātma is the persistent identity of a knowledge-bearing system across successive knowledge states, while its knowledge, understanding, observations, and forms may change over time.

conceptual.anchor: Knowledge Ātma is the persistent identity of a knowledge-bearing system across successive knowledge states, while its knowledge, understanding, observations, and forms may change over time.

formal.anchor: K_t\subseteq\mathcal K

governance.anchor: Knowledge Ātma is an architectural and mathematical abstraction inspired by the philosophical concept of Ātman. It is not a computational representation or proof of the metaphysical Ātman described in the Bhagavad Gītā.

rationale_evidence.anchor: K_0 \subseteq? K_1 \subseteq? K_2
rationale_evidence.statement: Knowledge evolution K_0->K_1->K_2->... within K_t⊆𝒦 is NOT necessarily monotonic — an assertion can be accepted, then questioned, then rejected, so K_{t+1} may contain less information than K_t in one sense while being epistemically better, reinforcing the earlier distinction between knowledge quantity and knowledge quality/coherence. Also cautions against assuming lim_{t->∞} K_t = 𝒦 as a mathematical fact rather than an assumption.

rationale_evidence.anchor: atman-in-the-conceptual-model -> atman-within-our-knowledgeos-theory -> atma-and-kernel-are-the-same-underlying-idea -> atma-can-be-the-knowledgeos-kernel -- fourth turning point -- a four-document escalation ending in Atma can be the Kernel ... The corpus also issues its own guard against over-literal mapping (correction-don-t-map-chakra-knowledge-layer).

rationale_evidence.anchor: AF-004 / ALT-05 (Zero senses) | 20260822-103624-aip-s5-...vedic-zero-lens.md; 025-series (phase_measure_theory); reviews-side reviews/20260822-1115/1130 (repository sense, cited from 3C) | AF-007 / ALT-02 (Atma cluster) | the eight 2026-08-27 08:51-09:38 files listed in concept-evolution section 7
