rationale_evidence.anchor: 𝔄 = (𝒦, ≡, ⊕, ⊗, ∼, ≤) ... Therefore: ⊕ forms a commutative monoid over 𝒦. ... Proof: 1. Associativity ... — by definition of union. 2. Commutativity ... — by definition of union. 3. Identity ... — by definition of empty knowledge.
rationale_evidence.statement: A full algebra over Knowledge Atmas is proposed: (K, equiv, compose-oplus, refine-otimes, contradict-tilde, entail-leq). Five 'Formal Theorems' are stated: 25I-P1 identity criterion (by definition); 25I-P2 composition oplus forms a commutative monoid with identity element K_empty (proved 'by definition of union', without defining union over propositions); 25I-P3 entailment leq is a partial order (reflexive/transitive/antisymmetric); 25I-P4 contradiction tilde is symmetric but explicitly non-reflexive and only a 'tolerance relation' (not necessarily transitive); 25I-P5 refinement otimes is monotonic (K1 <= K1 otimes delta).

rationale_evidence.anchor: | Identity check | O(n) | Compare propositions, refs, truth conditions | ... | Contradiction detection | O(n²) | Check logical consistency |
rationale_evidence.statement: A computability/complexity table claims: identity check O(n), composition O(n+m), refinement O(n), contradiction detection O(n^2) (via 'check logical consistency'), entailment check O(n) (via 'check logical implication') -- asserted without specifying n's meaning, the representation of propositions being compared, or the underlying decision procedure (general logical-consistency/implication checking is not polynomial-time in the propositional or first-order case).

rationale_evidence.anchor: If Chapters 5–6 are right, GK-05 should map to 𝒩, not to Π ∘ ℛ_der*. ... NOT changed here. This is a register question ... Recorded as GK-Q1, unresolved.
rationale_evidence.statement: Formally challenges the existing register mapping GK-05 (Atman) -> provenance-lineage (Pi-compose-R_der*), arguing that if the Chapter 5-6 bounded-knower reading is correct, GK-05 should instead map to the corpus's existing Knower object N (with FA-4 Ksetrajna grade [E] and invariant I-N knower-persistence); records this as open item GK-Q1 without changing the registry, since registry edits are a governance boundary, not a research decision.

assumption_register.statement: the composition operation's associativity/commutativity/identity follow automatically from an unspecified underlying 'union of knowledge' operation

sources.note: S0900's Step 25H: the first fully formal, falsification-tested treatment of Sarathi specifically as a governed decision operator distinct from Lord, contrasted in an explicit Lord-vs-Sarathi comparison table; extends B0021's broader decision-theory-action-selection-sarathi (S0871/Step 15) object.

rows.anchor: Lord = selects the next useful action ... Sarathi = determines what decision should be made
rows.statement: Opens by distinguishing Lord ('selects the next useful action,' e.g. 'perform a restore test') from Sarathi ('determines what decision should be made,' e.g. migrate/postpone/change plan/stop given resulting knowledge).

rows.anchor: D=\{Migrate,Postpone,ChangePlan,Reject\} ... Decision\neq Action
rows.statement: Defines the decision set D (e.g. {Migrate, Postpone, ChangePlan, Reject}) as distinct from the executable action set A (e.g. a single decision d=Migrate may require several actions {Backup, RestoreTest, FirewallValidation, Approval, Migration}) — Decision ≠ Action.

rows.anchor: Lord: (K,Z,G,C)\rightarrow A ... Sarathi: (K,G,D,C,P)\rightarrow d
rows.statement: States the precise operator distinction: Lord: (K,Z,G,C)->A (chooses what to do next to advance the process); Sarathi: (K,G,D,C,P)->d (chooses which decision is justified given current knowledge and decision model P).

type_signature.domain: KnowledgeState x Goal x DecisionSet x Constraints x Policy

rows.anchor: Consequences(d_1) ... OutcomeModel(d,K)
rows.statement: Decision reasoning requires knowing Consequences(d) (e.g. for d1=Migrate: Success, Failure, DataLoss, Downtime, Rollback), formalized as requiring an OutcomeModel(d,K).

rows.anchor: U(Success)=+100, U(Failure)=-50, U(DataLoss)=-1000 ... illustrative only ... must never be invented by the AI and presented as organizational truth
rows.statement: Introduces a utility function U(o) over outcomes with illustrative example values, explicitly warning these numbers 'must never be invented by the AI and presented as organizational truth.'

rows.anchor: EU(d\mid K)=\sum_o P(o\mid d,K)U(o) ... d^*=\arg\max_d EU(d\mid K) subject to governance and safety constraints
rows.statement: Defines expected utility EU(d|K)=sum_o P(o|d,K)U(o) and d*=argmax_d EU(d|K), explicitly subject to governance and safety constraints — 'a mathematically well-defined decision mechanism.'

rows.anchor: P(o\mid d,K) cannot reasonably be established. We must not invent it ... Preference(d_1,d_2) or Dominates(d_1,d_2)
rows.statement: When probability cannot reasonably be established, prohibits inventing it and instead allows qualitative Preference(d1,d2) or Dominates(d1,d2) (e.g. 'if migration is unauthorized, postponement dominates migration' — no probability necessary).

rows.anchor: Feasible(d,K,C) ... Migrate requires RollbackVerified=True ... Feasible(Migrate)=False ... should not matter how attractive migration appears economically
rows.statement: Before utility calculation, Sarathi must determine Feasible(d,K,C); e.g. Migrate requiring RollbackVerified=True is Feasible=False when RollbackVerified=Unknown, regardless of economic attractiveness.

rows.anchor: Hard constraint C(d)=True ... Preference d_1\succ d_2 ... Constraints filter; Utility/preferences select
rows.statement: Distinguishes hard constraints (must hold, e.g. ProductionChangeAuthorized) from preferences among permissible decisions (e.g. prefer lower expected downtime): 'Constraints filter; Utility/preferences select.'

rows.anchor: EU(Migrate)=95 ... EU(Postpone)=60 ... Authorized(Migrate)=False ... Migrate is eliminated before utility optimization ... Utility cannot override governance
rows.statement: Worked example showing higher expected utility (Migrate=95 vs Postpone=60) does not matter once Authorized(Migrate)=False eliminates it before optimization — 'Utility cannot override governance.'

rows.anchor: DecisionModel=(Outcomes,Constraints,Preferences,Utilities,Uncertainty,Policy) ... Sarathi(K,D,DecisionModel)\rightarrow DecisionResult
rows.statement: Defines a six-component DecisionModel=(Outcomes, Constraints, Preferences, Utilities, Uncertainty, Policy) and Sarathi(K,D,DecisionModel)->DecisionResult.

rows.anchor: Decision: POSTPONE ... Reason: rollback capability not established ... Blocking requirements: RollbackVerified ... Evidence basis: E17,E22,E31 ... Now the decision is auditable
rows.statement: Worked full auditable DecisionResult record for a POSTPONE decision containing reason, blocking requirements, alternative feasibility, evidence basis, decision model version, and authorization status — contrasted with returning a bare 'MIGRATE' label.

rows.anchor: DecisionProvenance(d) ... K_t+Contract+Policy+Model+Evidence\rightarrow d ... Decision must be reproducible
rows.statement: Requires DecisionProvenance(d) tracing K_t+Contract+Policy+Model+Evidence -> d, so 'Decision must be reproducible.'

rows.anchor: Decision_t remains associated with K_t ... Decision_{t+1} is calculated from K_{t+1} ... Decision is time-indexed
rows.statement: A historical decision (e.g. today's Postpone) must not be rewritten when tomorrow's new evidence would produce Migrate; Decision_t stays tied to K_t, and Decision_{t+1} is separately computed from K_{t+1} — 'Decision is time-indexed.'

rows.anchor: Stability(d,K) as sensitivity to plausible changes in the knowledge state
rows.statement: Defines decision Stability(d,K) conceptually as sensitivity to plausible changes in the knowledge state, motivated by the concern that small evidence changes flipping Migrate<->Postpone indicate an unstable decision.

rows.anchor: P(Success)=0.91 ... threshold 0.90 ... Migrate ... if a small uncertainty could make P(Success)=0.88 ... DecisionFragility=High
rows.statement: Worked example: a decision that barely clears its threshold (P(Success)=0.91 vs threshold 0.90) but could plausibly drop to 0.88 under small uncertainty should be reported as DecisionFragility=High rather than simply 'Migrate.'

rows.anchor: P(Success)\ge\theta ... \theta must come from governance/domain policy. The AI cannot invent it
rows.statement: Formalizes threshold decisions P(Success)>=theta (e.g. theta=0.95: P=0.97=>Migrate, P=0.72=>Postpone), explicitly requiring theta to come from governance/domain policy — 'the AI cannot invent it.'

rows.anchor: Probability=Unknown ... We should not substitute P=0.5 ... Unknown+CriticalRisk\rightarrow Postpone
rows.statement: When P(Success) cannot be estimated, prohibits substituting an arbitrary P=0.5 as 'unjustified'; instead records Probability=Unknown and lets the decision policy handle uncertainty (e.g. Unknown+CriticalRisk -> Postpone).

rows.anchor: Absence of evidence \neq evidence of failure ... Required evidence absent \Rightarrow decision may be blocked
rows.statement: States a named KnowledgeOS principle: Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of failure, distinct from Required evidence absent => decision may be blocked — 'these are different.'

rows.anchor: Risk(d)=P(Loss\mid d,K)\times Impact(Loss) ... only appropriate where the probabilistic model is justified
rows.statement: Distinguishes Risk (consequences under uncertainty) from Uncertainty (what we do not know), giving a common quantitative formalization Risk(d)=P(Loss|d,K) x Impact(Loss), qualified as appropriate only where the probabilistic model is justified.

rows.anchor: RiskLevel\in\{Low,Medium,High,Critical\} ... Risk can be quantitative or qualitative
rows.statement: Offers a qualitative RiskLevel enum {Low, Medium, High, Critical} as acceptable when defined by the organization's risk framework — 'Risk can be quantitative or qualitative.'

rows.anchor: d_1 more expensive, more risky, no more beneficial than d_2 ... d_2\succeq d_1 ... We don't need precise utility numbers
rows.statement: Defines decision dominance: if d1 is more expensive, more risky, and no more beneficial than d2, then d2 ⪰ d1 without requiring precise utility numbers — 'valuable when data is incomplete.'

rows.anchor: Objectives=\{Cost,Risk,Time,Quality,Compliance,Architecture\} ... Pareto set \mathcal P(D) ... Three decisions are Pareto-optimal; organizational preference is required
rows.statement: For multi-objective enterprise decisions (Cost, Risk, Time, Quality, Compliance, Architecture) that cannot honestly be reduced to one scalar, defines a Pareto set P(D) of non-dominated decisions; Sarathi can report multiple Pareto-optimal decisions requiring organizational preference — 'far better than arbitrary AI selection.'

rows.anchor: HumanChoiceRequired ... occurs when multiple decisions are equally defensible; utility weights undefined; governance unresolved; critical uncertainty cannot be reduced; authorized human judgment explicitly required
rows.statement: Defines the terminal state HumanChoiceRequired, triggered by five listed conditions, explicitly framed as itself 'a computed result,' not a failure.

rows.anchor: DecisionAvailable or DecisionNotComputableFromCurrentKnowledge or HumanDecisionRequired ... much more rigorous than pretending every question has an AI answer
rows.statement: States 'perhaps the most important finding in 25H': the system need not always produce a decision, only determine which of DecisionAvailable / DecisionNotComputableFromCurrentKnowledge / HumanDecisionRequired applies — more rigorous than pretending every question has an AI answer.

rows.anchor: Mode 1 Deterministic decision K+Rules\rightarrow d ... Mode 2 Model-based K+Probability+Utility\rightarrow d ... Mode 3 Human escalation K+Constraints\rightarrow HumanChoiceRequired
rows.statement: Defines three Sarathi operating modes: Mode 1 deterministic-rule decision, Mode 2 probability/utility model-based decision, Mode 3 human escalation.

rows.anchor: Rollback=verified, Firewall=verified, Security=approved, Architecture=approved ... Sarathi\rightarrow Migrate ... Rollback=unknown ... Sarathi\rightarrow Postpone ... Architecture policy=conflicting, No authority precedence ... Sarathi\rightarrow HumanDecisionRequired
rows.statement: Three parallel worked scenarios producing three different Sarathi outcomes (Migrate; Postpone due to blocking unknown rollback; HumanDecisionRequired due to unresolved conflicting policy with no authority precedence) — 'three different outcomes from three different epistemic conditions.'

rows.anchor: LLM(K,D)\rightarrow CandidateDecisionReasoning ... The LLM cannot manufacture Utility or Authority
rows.statement: The LLM may propose CandidateDecisionReasoning, but Sarathi validates it against Contract/Constraints/Evidence/Policy/Authorization; 'the LLM cannot manufacture Utility or Authority.'

rows.anchor: | | Lord | Sarathi | ... Main question What next? / What decision? ... Human escalation Possible / Central when choice is irreducible
rows.statement: Presents a clean eight-row comparison table distinguishing Lord vs Sarathi across Main question, Input, Main concern, Output, Information acquisition, Utility, Governance, and Human escalation — 'this separation is architecturally valuable.'

rows.anchor: Knowledge\rightarrow Zero\rightarrow Lord\rightarrow Evidence/Action\rightarrow Knowledge ... until sufficient knowledge exists ... Knowledge\rightarrow Sarathi\rightarrow Decision\rightarrow Authorization\rightarrow Execution ... Lord and Sarathi are not competing agents. They form a sequence
rows.statement: Composes the complete agent loop: an inner Knowledge->Zero->Lord->Evidence/Action->Knowledge cycle runs until sufficient knowledge exists, then Knowledge->Sarathi->Decision->Authorization->Execution follows — Lord and Sarathi 'are not competing agents. They form a sequence.'

rows.anchor: Sarathi\rightarrow Lord ... Migration decision cannot be made because rollback evidence is insufficient ... Sarathi\rightarrow KnowledgeGap\rightarrow Lord
rows.statement: Identifies a feedback path: when Sarathi discovers a decision cannot yet be made, it can hand back to Lord (Sarathi -> KnowledgeGap -> Lord), giving the architecture a genuine feedback loop rather than a one-directional pipeline.

rows.anchor: WORLD -> Observation -> EVIDENCE -> KNOWLEDGE STATE -> {EPISTEMIC CONTRACT->ZERO->LORD, DECISION MODEL} -> SARATHI -> {Decide, Escalate, More Knowledge} -> AUTHORIZATION -> EXECUTION -> WORLD
rows.statement: Presents the full architecture diagram integrating Lord and Sarathi as parallel downstream branches from Knowledge State (Epistemic Contract->Zero->Lord vs Decision Model), converging at Sarathi with three exits (Decide/Escalate/More Knowledge), then Authorization->Execution->WORLD — 'now the loop is almost complete.'

rows.anchor: constraint satisfaction; rule evaluation; expected utility; preference ordering; Pareto analysis; graph traversal; threshold evaluation; provenance; versioned state ... ordinary computational operations
rows.statement: Lists Sarathi's computational primitives (constraint satisfaction, rule evaluation, expected utility, preference ordering, Pareto analysis, graph traversal, threshold evaluation, provenance, versioned state) as ordinary operations runnable on a normal workstation even for moderately complex decision models.

rows.anchor: LargeScaleMonteCarlo or ComplexOptimization or LargeCausalModels ... optional specialized engines. The Sarathi abstraction does not require them
rows.statement: Identifies potentially expensive optional add-ons (large-scale Monte Carlo, complex optimization, large causal models) as specialized engines the Sarathi abstraction itself does not require.

rows.anchor: Should the company accept a politically sensitive strategic risk? ... ValueModelUnderspecified. That is a correct result
rows.statement: Worked example of a genuinely non-computable decision: when the utility function depends on an unspecified human value judgment (e.g. accepting a politically sensitive strategic risk), Sarathi should return ValueModelUnderspecified rather than force an answer — 'a correct result.'

rows.anchor: 1. Missing knowledge Zero\neq\varnothing 2. Conflicting knowledge Conflict\neq\varnothing 3. Missing decision model Utility/PreferenceUndefined 4. Irreducible human authority HumanDecisionRequired
rows.statement: Distinguishes four fundamentally different reasons KnowledgeOS may fail to produce an automatic decision: missing knowledge, conflicting knowledge, missing decision model, and irreducible human authority — described as 'the deepest result so far.'

rows.anchor: Decision unavailable because: 1. Rollback evidence is insufficient. 2. Architecture policy conflict remains unresolved. 3. No authorized utility preference exists between options A and B ... vastly more useful
rows.statement: Contrasts vague 'the AI is uncertain' with a structured, itemized 'decision unavailable because...' explanation citing the specific unresolved reasons — 'vastly more useful,' arguing 'AI uncertainty' is too vague a category.

rows.anchor: S(K,G,D,M,C)\rightarrow DecisionResult ... DecisionResult\in\{Decision,HumanDecisionRequired,InsufficientKnowledge,GovernanceBlocked,ModelUnderspecified\}
rows.statement: Defines the formal 25H operator S(K,G,D,M,C) -> DecisionResult with a five-value result enum {Decision, HumanDecisionRequired, InsufficientKnowledge, GovernanceBlocked, ModelUnderspecified} — 'computationally explicit.'

type_signature.domain: KnowledgeState x Goal x DecisionSet x DecisionModel x Constraints

rows.anchor: Test A: all requirements satisfied and one decision dominates ... S\rightarrow d. PASS
rows.statement: Falsification Test A: when all requirements are satisfied and one decision dominates, S->d — PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: A dominant, feasible decision should be selected.
experiment.setup: All requirements satisfied; one decision dominates.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply S operator
experiment.result: S -> d
experiment.interpretation: Baseline positive case.

rows.anchor: Test B: blocking knowledge missing ... S\rightarrow InsufficientKnowledge. PASS
rows.statement: Falsification Test B: blocking knowledge missing yields S->InsufficientKnowledge — PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: Missing blocking knowledge should prevent a decision.
experiment.setup: Blocking requirement unresolved.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply S operator
experiment.result: S -> InsufficientKnowledge
experiment.interpretation: Confirms Zero-gap gating of decisions.

rows.anchor: Test C: governance conflict unresolved ... S\rightarrow GovernanceBlocked. PASS
rows.statement: Falsification Test C: unresolved governance conflict yields S->GovernanceBlocked — PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: Unresolved governance conflict should block, not force, a decision.
experiment.setup: Governance conflict present, unresolved.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply S operator
experiment.result: S -> GovernanceBlocked
experiment.interpretation: Confirms integration with governance-conflict-resolution-algebra's Unresolved state.

rows.anchor: Test D: two decisions equally valid, no preference ... S\rightarrow HumanDecisionRequired. PASS
rows.statement: Falsification Test D: two equally valid decisions with no preference yields S->HumanDecisionRequired — PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: An undecidable tie between decisions should escalate.
experiment.setup: Two decisions equally valid, no preference defined.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply S operator
experiment.result: S -> HumanDecisionRequired
experiment.interpretation: Confirms indeterminate-preference escalation for decisions, mirroring Lord's tie-breaking.

rows.anchor: Test E: utility model absent where utility is necessary ... S\rightarrow ModelUnderspecified. PASS
rows.statement: Falsification Test E: a necessary but absent utility model yields S->ModelUnderspecified — PASS.

experiment.hypothesis: An undefined necessary utility model should be reported explicitly, not guessed.
experiment.setup: Utility/preference model required but not defined.
experiment.assumptions: n/a
experiment.method: apply S operator

aliases: Madhyamaka -- time-indexed K_t losing a determination not emptiness

sources.note: Reads Nagarjuna Madhyamaka four-alternatives (Asti/Nasti/Ubhaya/Nobhayam) as disciplined structural inspiration for a time-indexed knowledge-transition theory. Distinguishes three kinds of emptiness (representational R(x)=empty; epistemic Determine(x,K_t)=empty, not non-existence; relational, identical to the existing Transformation-relative Zero), time-indexes Zero (Zero_t(x)!=Zero_{t+1}(x)), reframes K_t->K_{t+1} as purification (scope down, validity up), proposes knowledge transition algebra KA_T=(K,T,Delta,Gamma,equiv,Pi) with idempotent-purification (P^2=P) and non-reversibility candidate properties, introduces question-relative Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) explicitly not implying K_t is the empty set, and specifies experiment KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 (status discrimination, purification stability, differential tracking).

rows.anchor: K_{t+1} = Pres(K_t) + Rev(K_t) + New(K_t) - Rejected(K_t). The critical question becomes: What is the status of what has been removed? Is it zero? No -- not necessarily.
rows.statement: Replaces the naive additive knowledge-transition model K_{t+1}=K_t+DeltaK with a richer decomposition K_{t+1}=Pres(K_t)+Rev(K_t)+New(K_t)-Rejected(K_t), posing the critical open question of what status the rejected/removed portion actually has -- explicitly not assumed to be zero.

rows.anchor: Asti (exists), Nasti (does not exist), Ubhaya (both), Nobhayam (neither). The important conceptual move is that Sunya is not simply the fourth object 'nothing.' ... absence from knowledge != non-existence. [Causes of absence: rejected, superseded, unresolved, irrelevant, redundant, outside the curre
rows.statement: Reads Nagarjuna's four alternatives (Asti/Nasti/Ubhaya/Nobhayam) as showing Sunya is not simply the fourth alternative 'nothing', extracting the KnowledgeOS principle that absence from knowledge is not non-existence, since a proposition's absence from K_{t+1} can have at least nine distinct causes (rejected, superseded, unresolved, irrelevant, redundant, outside the current question, deliberately abstracted away, contradicted, never established).

rows.anchor: K_t = P_t union R_t union E_t where P_t=preserved knowledge, R_t=revised/transformed knowledge, E_t=eliminated/removed content. Then ask: What is E_t? This is where emptiness might enter.
rows.statement: Partitions a knowledge-transition step into preserved (P_t), revised (R_t), and eliminated (E_t) content, posing the question of what E_t actually is as the entry point for the emptiness discussion.

rows.anchor: A. Representational emptiness: R(x)=empty set, ordinary absence. B. Epistemic emptiness: Determine(x,K_t)=empty set. This does not mean x does not exist. It means knowledge has no justified determination of x. C. Relational emptiness: Pi(T(D))=Pi(T(D\x)). That is precisely our existing Transformatio
rows.statement: Distinguishes three kinds of emptiness -- Representational (ordinary absence, R(x)=empty set), Epistemic (no justified determination, Determine(x,K_t)=empty set, not implying x does not exist), and Relational (the pre-existing Transformation-relative Zero, Pi(T(D))=Pi(T(D\x))) -- concluding Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D) is neither x=empty-set nor x=false.

rows.anchor: Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_t) but after a challenge or new evidence: not Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_{t+1}). Then Zero is clearly state-relative and time-relative: Zero_t(x) != Zero_{t+1}(x). ... consistent with what our experiments already suggested about contextual Zero.
rows.statement: Time-indexes the existing Zero definition (Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_t) vs Zero_{T,Pi}(x;K_{t+1})), demonstrating Zero is both state-relative and time-relative (Zero_t(x) != Zero_{t+1}(x)), consistent with and extending the already-established contextual-Zero finding that an element can be eliminable in one context and not in another.

rows.anchor: Perhaps some knowledge-state questions cannot be represented adequately by a binary present/absent state. Status_t(x) in {Established, Rejected, Unresolved, Qualified}. Or perhaps, more fundamentally, Status_t(x|Q,C,E). The status is relative to question Q, context C, evidence E, time t.
rows.statement: Proposes replacing a binary present/absent knowledge-state representation with a richer status typing Status_t(x) in {Established, Rejected, Unresolved, Qualified}, or more fundamentally Status_t(x|Q,C,E) relative to question, context, evidence, and time.

rows.anchor: K_t: 'X is always true.' Challenge discovers an exception. K_{t+1}: 'X is true under conditions C.' We lost information, in one sense: scope(K_{t+1})<scope(K_t). But we may have gained epistemic quality: Validity(K_{t+1})>Validity(K_t). So the removed part is not simply 'negative knowledge.' It is u
rows.statement: Illustrates K_t->K_{t+1} as a purification process with a worked example: a universal claim 'X is always true' becomes the qualified 'X is true under conditions C' after a challenge, so scope decreases (scope(K_{t+1})<scope(K_t)) while validity increases (Validity(K_{t+1})>Validity(K_t)), with the removed part being unsupported structure, not negative knowledge.

rows.anchor: Knowledge Difference != Knowledge Loss. Knowledge Reduction != Epistemic Degradation. A transition can reduce representation while preserving the question (D->R) or reduce claim scope while improving epistemic validity (K_t->K_{t+1}). These are two completely different reduction processes.
rows.statement: Distinguishes Knowledge Difference from Knowledge Loss and Knowledge Reduction from Epistemic Degradation, noting representation reduction (D->R, preserving the question) and knowledge-state reduction (K_t->K_{t+1}, improving validity while shrinking scope) are two completely different reduction processes that must not be conflated.

rows.anchor: Loss_t = K_t \ K_{t+1}. But some x in Loss_t may have different statuses: Rejected_t, Superseded_t, Redundant_t, Unresolved_t, Irrelevant_t, Purified_t. So the space between K_t and K_{t+1} is not necessarily empty. It may contain epistemic transition structure. K_t --tau_t--> (K_{t+1}, Delta_t, Gam
rows.statement: Investigates a 'knowledge vacuum' hypothesis: the loss set Loss_t=K_t\K_{t+1} may partition into six distinct statuses (Rejected, Superseded, Redundant, Unresolved, Irrelevant, Purified), so the space between K_t and K_{t+1} contains epistemic transition structure rather than being empty, formalized as K_t--tau_t-->(K_{t+1}, Delta_t, Gamma_t) carrying both the change and its justification.

rows.anchor: KA_T = (K, T, Delta, Gamma, equiv, Pi) where K=knowledge states, T=admissible transformations, Delta=state difference/residue, Gamma=justification of transition, equiv=epistemic equivalence, Pi=observations/contractions. Can transitions compose? Is there an identity transition I(K)=K? Are there inve
rows.statement: Proposes a candidate knowledge transition algebra KA_T=(K,T,Delta,Gamma,equiv,Pi) (knowledge states, admissible transformations, state residue, transition justification, epistemic equivalence, observations) rather than beginning with (K,+), posing four experimental questions: whether transitions compose, whether an identity transition exists, whether inverse transitions exist (probably not, since knowledge revision is usually not reversible), and whether purification is idempotent (P(P(K))=P(K), potentially yielding P^2=P as an experimentally supported property).

rows.anchor: I would not currently write Sunyata=Zero. That would collapse very different concepts. Instead: Sunyata leads to research inspiration for relational non-substantiality, while our formal Zero remains Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D). rows.statement: Explicitly refuses to write Sunyata=Zero (which would collapse distinct concepts), positioning Sunyata only as research inspiration for relational non-substantiality while the formal Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D) remains unchanged, and introduces a new predicate Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) (the current knowledge state contains no justified determination relevant to Q) that does not imply K_t is the empty set -- a knowledge state can be enormous while empty with respect to one particular question.

rows.anchor: Elimination Zero / Balance Zero / Epistemic Emptiness, corresponding to representation / contribution / knowledge state, connected by time K_t --challenge/evidence/revision--> K_{t+1}. Knowledge Algebra is fundamentally an algebra of transitions and preserved/revised relations, not an algebra of sta
rows.statement: Identifies a research triangle of three Zero-adjacent notions -- Elimination Zero (representation), Balance Zero (contribution), and Epistemic Emptiness (knowledge state) -- connected by the temporal transition K_t->K_{t+1}, proposing as a hypothesis (not conclusion) that Knowledge Algebra is fundamentally an algebra of transitions and preserved/revised relations, not an algebra of static knowledge objects.

rows.anchor: Do not identify what is absent from a representation or determination with what does not exist. Epistemic absence != ontological non-existence. And an even stronger one: A zero result is always zero relative to a specified state, transformation, question, and observation.
rows.statement: Turns Nagarjuna's warning into two KnowledgeOS research principles: epistemic absence is not ontological non-existence, and a zero result is always zero relative to a specified state, transformation, question, and observation -- consistent with the direction the Zero experiments have already forced.

rows.anchor: KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 -- Knowledge State, Emptiness and Purification, testing whether K_t -> K_{t+1} can empirically distinguish removed, rejected, unresolved, redundant, purified, and question-empty states without conflating them.
rows.statement: Commissions experiment KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 (Knowledge State, Emptiness and Purification) to test whether a knowledge-state transition K_t->K_{t+1} can empirically distinguish removed, rejected, unresolved, redundant, purified, and question-empty states without collapsing them into one generic category.

rows.statement: Consolidates three key epistemic principles with formal signatures: Epistemic Absence != Ontological Non-Existence (Determine(x,K_t)=empty-set does not entail falsity or non-existence), Knowledge Difference != Epistemic Degradation (scope reduction under challenge is the formal mechanism of Purification, since scope can shrink while validity rises), and an 'Epistemic Triad of Zero' table mapping Representation/Elimination-Zero, Contribution/Balance-Zero, and Knowledge-State/Epistemic-Emptiness each to a precise formal signature.

rows.statement: Finalizes three formal candidate properties for empirical verification: idempotency of purification (P(P(K_t)) equiv_Q P(K_t), giving P^2=P once a challenge-relative purification stabilizes), non-reversibility of revision (tau^{-1}(K_{t+1}) != K_t in general, due to loss of unrectified assumptions), and question-relative emptiness invariance (Empty_Q(K_t) never implies K_t is the empty set).

rows.statement: Specifies three primary objectives for KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01: status discrimination (programmatically distinguishing Rejected/Superseded/Redundant/Unresolved/Purified states without collapsing them into a generic null/false/deleted category), purification stability (testing convergence of challenge-driven revision sequences to an idempotent state P^2=P), and differential tracking (validating that retaining the transition residue (Delta_t,Gamma_t) prevents information loss during non-monotonic updates).

rows.anchor: Residue(tau_t,K_t,K_{t+1}) because two transitions can produce the same final state while having completely different histories. ... a claim was falsified; superseded; evidence was withdrawn; a redundant representation was removed; a claim was narrowed through qualification. rows.statement: Establishes that the residue can be more important than the endpoint difference: since multiple distinct epistemic histories (falsification, supersession, evidence withdrawal, redundancy removal, qualification) can all produce the same final state K_{t+1}, the endpoint state alone does not fully characterize the epistemic state transition.

Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) means: not-exists d [Determine(d,Q,C,K_t)]. But this does not imply K_t=empty-set. And it certainly
rows.statement: Fixes a three-level distinction that must remain separate: knowledge-state emptiness (K_t=empty-set), question-relative epistemic emptiness (Empty_{Q,C}(K_t), formally not-exists d such that Determine(d,Q,C,K_t)), and transformation-relative eliminability (Zero_{T,Pi}(x;D)) -- Empty_{Q,C}(K_t) implies neither K_t=empty-set nor that Q itself has no answer.

These are epistemically very different. Empty_Q(K_t) should not mean merely 'there is no answer.' We need to know why there is no de
rows.statement: Adds a fourth critical concept distinguishing Unexamined (nothing investigated) from Unresolved (investigated but inconclusive) as epistemically very different causes of Determine(x,K_t)=empty-set, requiring a typed EpistemicStatus(x,Q,C,t) rather than a simple Boolean 'no answer'.

rows.statement: Redefines purification away from simple removal (K minus bad content) to a three-stage process -- Challenge -> Qualification/Revision -> Preservation of justified content -- allowing scope to shrink while justification and potentially validity increase, explicitly kept as an experimental hypothesis rather than an axiom.

rows.statement: Splits the purification idempotency claim into operational idempotence (P(P(K))=P(K), a strict internal-state equality) and observational idempotence (P(P(K)) equiv_Q P(K), a weaker contract-relative equality), recommending testing the weaker observational form first since internal states can differ while being indistinguishable under the epistemic contract -- mirroring the kernel-minimality semantic-equivalence discipline.

Instead define reversibility: Rev(tau,K_t) iff there exists an admissible tau^{-1} such that tau^{-1}(tau(K_t)) equiv K_t. Then test whether revision transformations are reversible. Some transf
rows.statement: Replaces the unjustified hypothesis tau^{-1}(K_{t+1})!=K_t (which presumes an inverse is meaningful) with a proper reversibility predicate Rev(tau,K_t) iff an admissible tau^{-1} exists with tau^{-1}(tau(K_t)) equiv K_t, opening a three-way classification of transformations as reversible, partially reversible, or irreversible.

If yes, we have composition T x T -> T, possibly giving us a transition algebra. ... transitions have domains and codomains: tau: K_i -> K_j. That starts looking more naturally like a cate
rows.statement: Proposes that the deepest candidate mathematical object may be a transition monoid/category rather than an ordinary algebra, since transitions have explicit domains and codomains (tau:K_i->K_j) resembling a category of knowledge-state transitions, deliberately leaving open whether composition, identity, inverses, associativity, invariant preservation, and typed domains/codomains actually hold, to be discovered experimentally.

rows.statement: Formalizes the revised KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 objective (determine whether knowledge states are better modeled as non-monotonic transition systems with explicit residues and justification traces than static additive sets) and its core object, the transition record TR_t=(K_t, tau_t, K_{t+1}, Delta_t, Gamma_t), with a non-exclusive seven-tag status annotation.

rows.anchor: H1 -- Non-monotonicity: exists tau_t s.t. K_{t+1} not-superset-eq K_t. H2 -- Quality-preserving reduction: Scope(K_{t+1})<Scope(K_t) while contract preserved/improved. H3 -- Residue necessity: TR_1 != TR_2 with K_{t+1}^(1)=K_{t+1}^(2) but different histories/justifications -- if yes, endpoint state
rows.statement: Specifies six core hypotheses for KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01: H1 non-monotonicity (a transition need not preserve K_t as a subset), H2 quality-preserving reduction (scope can shrink while the epistemic contract is preserved or improved), H3 residue necessity (identical endpoints with different histories prove endpoint state alone is insufficient), H4 purification stability (testing both operational and observational idempotence), H5 emptiness distinction (Empty_Q(K_t) without K_t=empty-set, separated from Rejected/Unresolved/Irrelevant), and H6 transition composition (associativity, identity, reversibility, invariant preservation).

rows.anchor: Knowledge is not only a state; knowledge is also the justified history of transitions between states. rows.statement: Proposes the profound (explicitly [HYPOTHESIS], not [LAW]) KnowledgeOS principle that knowledge is not only a state but also the justified history of transitions between states (KnowledgeState != KnowledgeTransition, but KnowledgeSystem=(States,Transitions,Residues,Justifications)), concluding there is no single 'nothing' -- Representational Zero, Elimination Zero, Balance Zero, Question-relative Emptiness, Unresolvedness, and Rejectedness must not collapse into the same state.

rows.statement: Finalizes a six-row 'taxonomy of non-being in knowledge systems' table, giving each mode (Representational Emptiness, State Emptiness, Epistemic Emptiness, Elimination Zero, Balance Zero, Unresolvedness) a precise formal signature and description, consolidating the entire Zero/emptiness research thread into one reference table.

rows.statement: Provides a concrete JSON schema for logging KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 transition records in an actual implementation, with fields for the transition identity, transformation type, tripartite residue (removed/transformed-with-prior-and-updated-values/acquired), justification (challenge ID, evidence reference, applied rule), and non-exclusive status-tag annotations per affected item -- illustrated with a worked example qualifying a universal claim under a discovered counterexample condition.

rows.statement: Illustrates Sunya as a transitional epistemic space via a worked example: a universal claim challenged by a counterexample transitions Universal(C)->Sunya->Conditional(C), where the prior universal determination becomes empty while a qualified determination has not yet been established -- not 'there is nothing' but a state between two determinations.

rows.anchor: Determination -> Challenge -> Sunya -> Revision -> New Determination. The negative contribution can create a temporary epistemic Sunya from which a better determination emerges. ... Argument -> Challenge -> Sunya -> Qualification -> Purified Knowledge. The challenge removes the false certainty, not
rows.statement: Inserts Sunya into the purification cycle as an intermediate transitional stage (Determination->Challenge->Sunya->Revision->New Determination, equivalently Argument->Challenge->Sunya->Qualification->Purified Knowledge), proposing the candidate interpretation that Knowledge Sunya is not the absence of knowledge but the absence of unjustified determination -- the challenge removes false certainty, not the underlying subject matter -- kept as a candidate interpretation pending testing.

rows.anchor: Elimination Zero: representation. Balance Zero: contribution. Knowledge Sunya: determination. Purification: transition. They interact, but we don't yet know whether they are manifestations of one deeper mathematical structure. That should be discovered, not assumed.
rows.statement: Consolidates the four Zero-adjacent research threads by their domain -- Elimination Zero (representation), Balance Zero (contribution), Knowledge Sunya (determination), Purification (transition) -- explicitly leaving open, as a discovery question rather than an assumption, whether they are manifestations of one deeper mathematical structure.

rows.anchor: \Delta_t=(\Delta_t^{-},\Delta_t^{\circ},\Delta_t^{+}) where removed/rejected/superseded, transformed/qualified, newly acquired material.
rows.statement: Corrects Delta_t=K_t\K_{t+1} (captures only removal) into a three-part residue (removed/transformed-qualified/acquired), motivated by qualification examples like 'X is always true' becoming 'X is true under C'.

rows.anchor: K_{t+1} alone does not fully characterize the epistemic state transition. ... Residue(tau_t,K_t,K_{t+1})
rows.statement: States that the same endpoint K_{t+1} can be reached via distinct epistemic histories (falsified, superseded, withdrawn evidence, redundancy removal, narrowing), so the endpoint alone is insufficient -- motivating H3 (Residue Necessity).

rows.anchor: K_t = \varnothing (knowledge-state emptiness) ... Empty_Q(K_t) (question-relative epistemic emptiness) ... Zero_{T,\Pi}(x;D) (transformation-relative eliminability) ... these should remain separate.
rows.statement: Keeps three emptiness notions formally separate and adds a fourth 'unresolved' status distinction (Unexamined vs Unresolved) since Determine(x,K_t)=empty can arise for epistemically different reasons.

rows.anchor: TR_t=(K_t,\tau_t,K_{t+1},\Delta_t,\Gamma_t) ... test six hypotheses: H1 Non-monotonicity ... H6 Transition composition
rows.statement: Specifies KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01's six hypotheses (non-monotonicity, quality-preserving reduction, residue necessity, purification stability P(P(K))=P(K) vs P(P(K)) equiv_Q P(K), emptiness distinction, transition composition) and frames the resulting object as possibly a transition monoid/category rather than an additive algebra.

rows.anchor: Knowledge is not only a state; knowledge is also the justified history of transitions between states. ... KnowledgeSystem=(States,Transitions,Residues,Justifications).
rows.statement: States, as a [HYPOTHESIS] not [LAW], that a KnowledgeSystem is properly a tuple of states, transitions, residues and justifications rather than a set of states alone.

rows.anchor: Śūnya is not simply the fourth object "nothing." ... absence from knowledge \neq non-existence.
rows.statement: Uses Nagarjuna's four-alternatives structure to argue that a proposition's disappearance from K_{t+1} must not be automatically read as false or non-existent; enumerates several distinct causes (rejected, superseded, unresolved, irrelevant, redundant, outside scope, deliberately abstracted, contradicted, never established).

rows.anchor: K_t = P_t \cup R_t \cup E_t where P_t preserved, R_t revised/transformed, E_t eliminated/removed content.
rows.statement: Partitions a knowledge-state transition into preserved/revised/eliminated components and asks what E_t (eliminated content) actually is, as the entry point for emptiness.

rows.anchor: Zero_{T,\Pi}(x;K_t) but after a challenge ... \neg Zero_{T,\Pi}(x;K_{t+1}). Then Zero is clearly state-relative and time-relative: Zero_t(x) \neq Zero_{t+1}(x).
rows.statement: Time-indexes the existing Transformation-relative Zero, extending it with an explicit temporal argument on top of the already-established transformation/observable/contract relativity.

rows.anchor: scope(K_{t+1}) < scope(K_t). But we may have gained epistemic quality: Validity(K_{t+1})>Validity(K_t). ... that is purification.
rows.statement: Reframes K_t->K_{t+1} under challenge as purification: representational scope may shrink while epistemic validity rises (e.g. a universal claim narrowed to a conditional one), distinguishing Knowledge Difference from Knowledge Loss and Knowledge Reduction from Epistemic Degradation.

rows.anchor: KA_T=(K,\mathcal T,\Delta,\Gamma,\equiv,\Pi) ... Can transitions compose? Is there an identity transition? Are there inverse transitions? ... Are there idempotent purification operations? P(P(K))=P(K)
rows.statement: Proposes a candidate knowledge transition algebra KA_T and a corresponding empirical checklist (composition, identity, inverse, idempotent purification) to determine what algebraic structure, if any, the transition system actually has.

rows.anchor: Does KnowledgeOS require a non-monotonic extension of information-algebra closure? ... Closure idempotency <-> Purification idempotency ... but the semantic direction is different.
rows.statement: Compares the article's closure operator C(C(X))=C(X) (monotone, knowledge->everything entailed) to the corpus's own purification idempotence hypothesis P(P(K))=_Q P(K) (knowledge->justified residue), arguing they are structurally analogous but semantically opposite, and posing whether KnowledgeOS needs a non-monotonic closure extension as open.

lexical.anchor: K_{t+1} = Pres(K_t) + Rev(K_t) + New(K_t) - Rejected(K_t). The critical question becomes: What is the status of what has been removed? Is it zero? No -- not necessarily.

conceptual.anchor: Perhaps some knowledge-state questions cannot be represented adequately by a binary present/absent state. Status_t(x) in {Established, Rejected, Unresolved, Qualified}. Or perhaps, more fundamentally, Status_t(x|Q,C,E). The status is relative to question Q, context C, evidence E, time t.

formal.anchor: K_{t+1} = Pres(K_t) + Rev(K_t) + New(K_t) - Rejected(K_t). The critical question becomes: What is the status of what has been removed? Is it zero? No -- not necessarily.

operational.anchor: KR-STATE-TRANSITION-01 -- Knowledge State, Emptiness and Purification, testing whether K_t -> K_{t+1} can empirically distinguish removed, rejected, unresolved, redundant, purified, and question-empty states without conflating them.

rationale_evidence.anchor: Asti (exists), Nasti (does not exist), Ubhaya (both), Nobhayam (neither). The important conceptual move is that Sunya is not simply the fourth object 'nothing.' ... absence from knowledge != non-existence. [Causes of absence: rejected, superseded, unresolved, irrelevant, redundant, outside the curre
rationale_evidence.statement: Reads Nagarjuna's four alternatives (Asti/Nasti/Ubhaya/Nobhayam) as showing Sunya is not simply the fourth alternative 'nothing', extracting the KnowledgeOS principle that absence from knowledge is not non-existence, since a proposition's absence from K_{t+1} can have at least nine distinct causes (rejected, superseded, unresolved, irrelevant, redundant, outside the current question, deliberately abstracted away, contradicted, never established).

notations: commuting square F o That = T_i o F

sources.note: Step 259's formal congruence/commuting-diagram criterion for testing whether a candidate Knowledge-State abstraction F:H->K is sufficient for KnowledgeOS's mandatory transformations; distinguishes local (tested) from global congruence and is the recurring test used across the B0040 verification/phase_measure_theory files.

rows.anchor: The governing criterion is: F_i(H_1)=F_i(H_2) must imply F_i(\widehat T(H_1,c)) = F_i(\widehat T(H_2,c))
rows.statement: A candidate Knowledge-State abstraction F_i:H->K_i is sufficient for a mandatory transformation T over admissible context c iff F_i(H1)=F_i(H2) implies F_i(That(H1,c))=F_i(That(H2,c)); strengthened to require an actual state-level transformation T_i:K_i x C -> K_i such that F_i(That(H,c)) = T_i(F_i(H),c) for all admissible H,c (a commuting square between history-level and state-level transformations).

rows.anchor: In particular: Definition of K != Adequacy of K, and: Congruence criterion valid != KnowledgeOS satisfies congruence.
rows.statement: Self-correction of the immediately preceding step: a mathematical definition of K, a candidate representation of K, an abstraction F:H->K, and the claim that F is sufficient for the transformation family are four distinct claims that must not be conflated; Step 258 wrongly treated K as already a well-defined state abstraction.

lineage_claims.quote: The previous Step 258 discussion treated K as though it were already a reasonably defined state abstraction. That was too early.

rows.anchor: Not every operation has the form: T:K -> K. ... Assess:K x X -> Assessment ... Authorize:Actor x Action x Policy -> Decision
rows.statement: Operations must first be classified into (1) knowledge-state transformations, (2) epistemic assessments, (3) governance operations, (4) audit/history operations, (5) observation operations; not every legitimate KnowledgeOS operation is an endomorphism T:K->K — e.g. Assess:K x X -> Assessment and Authorize:Actor x Action x Policy -> Decision are non-state-closing operations, and only state-transforming operations enter the primary congruence test.

rows.anchor: Now introduce a revision rule dependent on lineage: Revise(x_1,x_2) is permitted only if: Origin(x_1) in ApprovedSources.
rows.statement: Conditional counterexample sketch for candidate F_A (artifact-set state) under Revise: if revision eligibility depends on Origin(x1) (an approved-sources lineage rule) while F_A discards origin, two histories with equal F_A images can differ in whether a subsequent Revise is valid, which would falsify F_A's congruence — but this is CONDITIONAL, not PROVEN, unless the corpus actually establishes that revision eligibility depends on origin.
missing: corpus evidence that revision eligibility actually depends on origin

experiment.hypothesis: F_A (artifact-set-only state) is congruent under Revise
experiment.setup: H1 with Origin(x1)=A vs H2 with Origin(x1)=B, both mapping to the same F_A(H)={x1}
experiment.assumptions: Revise(x1,x2) permitted only if Origin(x1) in ApprovedSources
experiment.inputs: two synthetic histories differing only in recorded origin
experiment.method: compare validity of Revise(x1,x2) under H1 vs H2 given F_A(H1)=F_A(H2)
experiment.result: if origin-dependence is real, Revise(H1) valid and Revise(H2) invalid despite F_A(H1)=F_A(H2)
experiment.interpretation: F_A fails congruence: same state, different next-state validity
experiment.limitations: origin-dependence of Revise eligibility is not yet established by the corpus

rows.anchor: Merge is the strongest initial discriminator ... If the resulting provenance must distinguish Source_1 from Source_2, then F_A(\widehat{Merge}(H_A)) != F_A(\widehat{Merge}(H_B)).
rows.statement: Conditional counterexample sketch for candidate F_A under Merge, described as the strongest initial discriminator among the tested operations: if two histories reach the same artifact x1 from different sources (Source_1 vs Source_2) with F_A(H_A)=F_A(H_B)={x1}, and a subsequent Merge(x1,x2) must record provenance distinguishing Source_1 from Source_2, then F_A fails congruence — again only if provenance is established as semantically observable by Merge, which the governing prompt requires testing (alongside evidence, replay, validation, implementation needs) before deciding whether Evidence/provenance belongs inside or outside K.
missing: establishing that provenance is semantically observable by Merge

experiment.hypothesis: F_A is congruent under Merge
experiment.setup: H_A: Source1->x1, H_B: Source2->x1, both giving F_A={x1}; then Merge(x1,x2)
experiment.assumptions: Merge's resulting provenance must distinguish Source1 from Source2
experiment.inputs: two synthetic single-artifact histories with different declared sources
experiment.method: compare F_A(Merge-result) across H_A and H_B
experiment.result: differ if provenance must be preserved by Merge
experiment.interpretation: would falsify F_A's sufficiency for Merge

rows.anchor: All transformations are K -> K | REFUTED as a universal assumption
rows.statement: The results table explicitly marks the assumption that all KnowledgeOS transformations have signature K->K as REFUTED as a universal assumption (distinguished from the still-CANDIDATE status of F:H->K as a useful abstraction model, and from several UNRESOLVED items: whether history can be discarded, whether provenance must be inside or can remain outside K, whether the transformation family is closed, whether current K is globally sufficient, whether a minimal K exists).

rows.anchor: We cannot perform a valid global congruence proof until the mandatory transformation family is itself sufficiently closed. ... the quantifier forall T in T has no determinate meaning if T is incomplete.
rows.statement: Central negative result of the step: a valid global congruence proof is impossible while the mandatory transformation family T is not itself closed, because the universal quantifier 'for all T in T' is not well-defined over an incomplete set; this reinforces the required sequencing Transformation Inventory -> Semantic Classification -> Congruence, rather than jumping to K -> Congruence in isolation.

rows.anchor: A finite test set can establish: Congruent_{tested}(F). It does not automatically establish: Congruent_{global}(F).
rows.statement: Local/tested congruence (survival of a finite, executed test set) must be distinguished from global congruence (a formal proof over the fully specified domain and transformation family); an executed test yields only 'evidence of survival', never 'proof of universal congruence'.

rows.anchor: This also explains why Step 260 must come after Step 259. Minimality asks whether K* is the coarsest sufficient abstraction. But we cannot establish sufficiency until we know which operations must be preserved.
rows.statement: Sequencing principle: no valid minimality proof (Step 260, testing whether K* = H/equiv is the coarsest sufficient state abstraction) can precede the operation registry and congruence-matrix analysis (Step 259), since minimality presupposes knowledge of which operations a sufficient state must preserve.

rows.anchor: A bounded context state is legitimate only if its externally observable behavior does not depend on information that the context has discarded. ... K1 equiv_K K2 must imply identical behavior under the context's published operations.
rows.statement: DDD interpretation of the congruence criterion: a bounded-context state representation is legitimate only when its externally observable behavior under the context's published operations does not depend on information the context's state has discarded — i.e. the congruence test is a rigorous check for an accidentally omitted domain invariant, not mathematical decoration.

rows.anchor: We must not assume: Statistical Sufficiency => KnowledgeOS Operational Sufficiency. That requires proof.
rows.statement: Statistical interpretation: two histories can produce the same estimated distribution P_theta under a distributional candidate state F_E, yet still be distinguishable by a future transformation dependent on information not identifiable from that distribution; statistical sufficiency must not be assumed to imply KnowledgeOS operational sufficiency without separate proof.

rows.anchor: Step 259 establishes the formal mechanism by which candidate Knowledge-State abstractions can be falsified, but it does not yet establish that any candidate abstraction is globally sufficient. ... if the quotient does not exist in the required usable form, that is a valid research result.
rows.statement: Conservative step verdict: the congruence-falsification mechanism is established but no candidate is proven globally sufficient; Step 260 is set up to test — not assume — existence, uniqueness, representability, computability, decidability, composability, equality, membership and identity of the candidate minimal quotient K*=H/equiv (H1 equiv H2 iff no mandatory operation can distinguish them), explicitly allowing a negative result (the quotient not existing in usable form) as a valid outcome.

rows.anchor: H1 ≈ H2 iff every permitted observation produces the same result: ∀O∈𝒪: O(H1)=O(H2). ... This is the relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient.
rows.statement: Observational equivalence for histories (H1 approx H2 iff every permitted observation O produces the same result) and for states (K1 approx K2 iff every permitted state observation agrees) is identified as the same relation already underlying Step 260's behavioral quotient; notably it does not require internal representations to be identical.

rows.anchor: K1 ≡_K K2 ⟺ ∀O∈𝒪_K: O(K1)=O(K2) ... 𝒪_K is not yet completely closed. Therefore this is a candidate formal definition, not a completed theorem.
rows.statement: Candidate formal definition of Knowledge-State equality as purely observational/behavioral: K1 equiv_K K2 iff every permitted state observation O in the (not-yet-closed) set O_K agrees on K1 and K2; explicitly a candidate, not a completed theorem, because O_K is not yet closed.
missing: closure of O_K, the permitted-observation set

rows.anchor: Equality → Congruence → Quotient → Minimality. This is the correct dependency direction.
rows.statement: If K1 equiv_K K2 (no permitted observation distinguishes them) and all mandatory operations preserve that equivalence, equiv_K becomes the congruence relation needed for the minimal quotient K*=H/equiv (Step 260) — establishing the dependency direction Equality -> Congruence -> Quotient -> Minimality as correct.

rows.anchor: Transformation-sufficiency test F(H1) = F(H2) ⇒ F(T(H1,i)) = F(T(H2,i)) — executed, congruent for every input tested. See artifact F.
rows.statement: The transformation-sufficiency (congruence) test F(H1)=F(H2) => F(T(H1,i))=F(T(H2,i)) was executed and found congruent for every tested input, with full detail deferred to a separate artifact F — direct empirical support for the K=(A,R) abstraction passing the Step-259 congruence criterion.

rows.anchor: The model is executable, so removal is testable. The phrase MINIMAL KERNEL is therefore earned — but only in the sense step 254 names: Minimality(K | 𝒯), relative to the transformation set. Not ontological necessity. A richer 𝒯 could force more.
rows.statement: Minimality caveat: the removal-based necessity audit only earns Minimality(K|T) relative to the specific tested transformation set T (per step 254's framing), never ontological necessity of the components — a richer transformation set could force additional components to become necessary.

rows.anchor: F(Hx) = F(Hy) ? False — different states, so congruence is NOT tested by this pair ... A congruence test requires two DIFFERENT histories producing the SAME state. Two of my first three attempts were vacuous, and would have "passed" while proving nothing.
rows.statement: Self-disclosed methodological failure: two of the first three attempted congruence-test constructions used history pairs that already produced different F-images, meaning congruence was never actually being tested (a vacuous pass); a valid congruence test requires two DIFFERENT histories that fold to the SAME state F(H1)=F(H2).

rows.anchor: Hr = [assert A1, assert A4] ; Hs = [assert A4, assert A1] ... F(Hr) = F(Hs) = True ... i = relate(A1,A4,supersedes) -> congruent: True ... i = assert A2 -> congruent: True ... i = relate(A4,A1,refines) -> congruent: True ... F(H1) = F(H3) where H3 re-asserts A1 (idempotence) -> congruent: True. No c
rows.statement: Valid executed congruence test: order-reversed histories Hr=[assert A1, assert A4] and Hs=[assert A4, assert A1] satisfy the precondition F(Hr)=F(Hs); three different subsequent operations (relate-supersedes, assert, relate-refines) are each tested and found congruent, plus an idempotence test (re-asserting A1); no counterexample is found across these tests.

experiment.hypothesis: K=(A,R) is congruent for the tested operation set
experiment.setup: order-reversed and idempotent history pairs over assertions A1,A2,A4
experiment.assumptions: F=fold(T,empty,H)
experiment.method: apply relate/assert operations after confirming F(H1)=F(H2), compare resulting F images
experiment.result: congruent: True in every tested case
experiment.interpretation: no counterexample found under the tested domain
experiment.limitations: finite, executed test set, not a closed-domain proof

rows.anchor: T's derived signature is 𝕂 × Op × Policy × Authority ⇀ 𝕂 × Outcome. History is not in its domain. A function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. Congruence therefore holds by construction, under exactly two assumptions: A1 · T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN ... A2 · no operat
rows.statement: Structural (by-construction) explanation for why congruence held in every test: T's derived signature K x Op x Policy x Authority -harpoon-> K x Outcome does not include History in its domain, so T cannot depend on it — a function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. This holds under exactly two assumptions: A1 (T reads only K, Policy, Authority — PROVEN by elimination of actor/time/evidence/context during signature derivation) and A2 (no operation consults order-of-arrival — HOLDS for the twelve derived operations because A and R are sets, making order structurally unobservable).

rows.anchor: A2 is the one that could fail. Any future operation reading insertion order — "the first assertion wins", "the most recently added is authoritative" — breaks congruence immediately. That is a design constraint the theory now states explicitly rather than assumes silently.
rows.statement: Explicit forward-looking design constraint: assumption A2 (no operation consults insertion order) is violable by future design — any future operation implementing 'first assertion wins' or 'most recently added is authoritative' semantics would break congruence immediately; the theory now states this as an explicit constraint rather than a silent assumption.

rows.anchor: SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS. Not sufficient unqualified: the assumptions are real and A2 is violable by future design. Not insufficient: no counterexample exists and none can, given A1. Not unknown: the test was constructed correctly and executed.
rows.statement: Final classification: the Knowledge-State/History sufficiency question is SUFFICIENT UNDER ASSUMPTIONS — deliberately neither 'sufficient unqualified' (the assumptions A1/A2 are real and A2 is violable), nor 'insufficient' (no counterexample exists, and none can given A1), nor 'unknown' (the test was validly constructed and executed).

rows.anchor: Knowledge State is sufficient for FUTURE COMPUTATION. It is NOT sufficient for GOVERNANCE AUDIT. ... Who asserted this, and when? NO ... Was every admission properly authorised? NO — GovernanceValid(K,Γ) needs History ... What did we believe last March? NO — needs History
rows.statement: The state/history sufficiency boundary is drawn precisely: K alone answers what is currently held, what follows from an operation (congruence), whether structural/semantic invariants hold, and current epistemic status (recomputable from e); K alone CANNOT answer who asserted something and when, whether every admission was properly authorised (GovernanceValid(K,Gamma) needs History), or what was believed at a past point in time (needs History or a bitemporal interpretation of t).

rows.anchor: K answers what is known. History answers how it came to be known and by whom. Neither reduces to the other, and T needs only the first.
rows.statement: Governing principle stated as the resolution of the state/history boundary the programme has circled since the executed History(K)!=K counterexample: K answers what is known; History answers how it came to be known and by whom; neither reduces to the other, and the transformation function T needs only K.

rows.anchor: Step 253 places H inside Structure(X,R,Q,H,…). This result shows why that is unnecessary for computation: congruence holds without it. ... it destroys equality ... VERDICT on D-1: the corpus's inclusion of H in K is REFUTED for computation and REFUTED for equality, while remaining CORRECT as an obse
rows.statement: Definitive verdict on disagreement D-1 (does History belong inside K?): step 253's inclusion of H inside Structure(X,R,Q,H,...) is REFUTED for computation (congruence holds without H) and REFUTED for equality (including H would make two identical-content states with different histories unequal, breaking merge/dedup/replay-verification coherence), while remaining CORRECT only as an observation that governance needs history; the resolution is to pair (K,History) as a system rather than merge History into K, with K alone sufficient for T.

lineage_claims.quote: VERDICT on D-1: the corpus's inclusion of H in K is REFUTED for computation and REFUTED for equality, while remaining CORRECT as an observation that governance needs history.

rows.anchor: deterministic YES ... closed YES ... total NO — deliberately partial ... composable YES, associatively ... identity element YES — noop ... idempotent (assert, relate, merge) YES ... monotone NO ... invertible NO ... congruent w.r.t. history YES, structurally
rows.statement: Algebraic property table for T: deterministic (executed), closed (T(K,.) in K by construction), deliberately NOT total (three rejection kinds executed), composable associatively (Replay=fold(T,empty,H)), has an identity element (noop), idempotent for assert/relate/merge (set semantics, executed), NOT monotone (retract shrinks A), NOT invertible (retract's cascade is lossy), and congruent with respect to history (structurally, because T's domain contains no History — per artifact F).

rows.anchor: G(π1)=G(π2) ⇒ ∀o,K: T(K,o,π1,α)=T(K,o,π2,α) and similarly for assessment: G(π1)=G(π2) ⇒ Assess(x,π1)=Assess(x,π2). If two policies are indistinguishable under all mandatory operations, then they may belong to the same semantic equivalence class. This gives us a route to a minimal Policy semantics ra
rows.statement: Proposes a Policy congruence criterion directly analogous to the Step-259 state congruence criterion: if a candidate policy abstraction G maps two policies to the same value, then they must be indistinguishable under every mandatory transformation and assessment — giving a principled route to minimal Policy semantics rather than premature policy-language design.

rows.anchor: EV-B3 (DERIVED). The terminal form K=(𝒜,ℛ) is strictly poorer than #8 and #9. Q6's (𝒜,ℛ,ℰ,ℋ,𝒵,ℒ) carries evidence, history, zero and lineage as first-class components; (𝒜,ℛ) carries neither evidence nor history nor status. ... The corpus arrived at its smallest K by relocating components, but the re
rows.statement: Finding EV-B3, directly qualifying the K=(A,R) minimality narrative used throughout this batch: the terminal K=(A,R) is strictly poorer in stated components than earlier Q6/Q13 candidates (which carried evidence, history, zero-findings and lineage as first-class parts of K itself); the reduction to (A,R) worked by relocating those components elsewhere (into Assertion internals, external History, external Policy), but the relocation targets were fixed AFTER the reduction rather than justified before it, and whether (A,R) is actually SUFFICIENT is exactly the still-open Step 259/260 congruence question.

rows.anchor: Semantic minimality ≠ syntactic compactness. ... ≡ must be a congruence for 𝒯, not just an equivalence relation. DERIVED, and correctly so. Reflexivity PROVISIONALLY DERIVED ... symmetry and transitivity DERIVED under ordinary equality. This session checked the three proofs: they are correct but tri
rows.statement: ARC E (State vs History, called 'the deepest and most honest arc') is independently checked and found genuinely sound where claimed: semantic minimality is correctly distinguished from mere syntactic compactness; the requirement that the equivalence relation be a congruence (not merely an equivalence) for the transformation set is correctly derived; the reflexivity/symmetry/transitivity proofs are verified correct but trivial (holding for any observational equivalence, establishing nothing KnowledgeOS-specific) — and importantly, the corpus itself does not overclaim them; hash identity is correctly kept distinct from semantic identity.

rows.anchor: EV-E1 (DERIVED, CRITICAL). Step 260.16: membership requires the equivalence test — H∈[H₀] ⟺ H≡H₀. Step 260.9: ≡ quantifies over the whole transformation algebra 𝒯. Step 266: 𝒯 is not closed. Therefore ≡ is defined by a universal quantification over a set that has never been enumerated. It is not mer
rows.statement: Finding EV-E1 (CRITICAL), sharper than the corpus's own Step 260 gate: since the semantic-equivalence relation equiv is defined by universal quantification over the mandatory transformation algebra T, and T itself is not closed/fully enumerated (per Step 266), equiv is not merely undecidable — it is NOT YET A WELL-DEFINED RELATION, because its defining quantifier ranges over an open, unenumerated collection; every object depending on it (the minimal quotient K*, membership A in K, state equality K1=K2, and the Step 259 sufficiency/congruence theorem) inherits this indeterminacy, undermining the confidence level of the congruence-based results relied on throughout the batch's canonical-K work.

rows.anchor: H1 (Step 255 Class I): a CONTENT-ONLY abstraction is not sufficient. H2 (Step 265 verdict): placing provenance INSIDE the assertion repairs H1. H3 (Steps 262-269): K=(A,R) with in-assertion provenance IS a sufficient abstraction of history. H4 (this session, EV-E1): the answer to H3 is not determine
rows.statement: Four explicit, corpus-cited hypotheses are set up for direct executable testing: H1 (content-only state abstraction is insufficient), H2 (placing provenance inside the assertion repairs H1), H3 (the terminal K=(A,R) with in-assertion provenance is a sufficient history abstraction), and H4 (this session's own claim that H3's truth is undetermined because it depends on the never-closed mandatory operation set) — using the Step 259/260 sufficiency-plus-congruence criterion as the formal test.

rows.anchor: ## E. What SURVIVED — the load-bearing positives
rows.statement: Sixteen results are registered as SURVIVED and load-bearing for any successor theory, including: provenance must be carried not derived (S-01); lineage is computable in O(n+m), the one unambiguously decidable relation in the theory (S-02); 𝒦=(K,H) is necessary, 4 audit questions unanswerable from K alone (S-03); Evidence(O,P,C,R) is a relation not a substance (S-04); admission≠truth (S-05); P≠A makes independent corroboration representable (S-06); no scalar operator suffices for evidence aggregation (S-08); K=(𝒜,ℛ) is instantiated and running — 40 assertions, 59 typed relations (S-12); two orthogonal status axes are running and schema-enforced (S-13); a real constitutional self-amendment rule exists (S-14).

rows.anchor: Step 259 s259.7 partitions operations into five classes ... Only state-transforming operations enter the primary congruence test.
rows.statement: Corpus-stated five-class operation partition: (1) knowledge-state transformations (Add, Remove, Revise, Transform, Supersede, Merge, Split, Reject, Withdraw, Promote, Reintroduce), (2) epistemic assessments (Validate, Assess), (3) governance operations (Authorize), (4) audit/history operations (Replay, EverContested, RevisionCount), (5) observation operations (none named); with s259.8's rule that only class-1 operations enter the primary congruence test, class 2 uses a determination test, and class 3 is not a state-closure question.

rationale_evidence.statement: Structural (by-construction) explanation for why congruence held in every test: T's derived signature K x Op x Policy x Authority -harpoon-> K x Outcome does not include History in its domain, so T cannot depend on it — a function cannot depend on an argument it does not receive. rows.statement: Zero-Lens result on Williamson: after removing beliefs, documents, language, databases, probabilities, possible worlds, embeddings, topics, LLMs, what survives is minimal: 'A participant is related to a proposition/content in a world/context/time such that the proposition is true and the participant is in a factive state of knowing.' Knowledge itself should not be reduced to its representations.

rows.anchor: 1. Participants make commitments. 2. Commitments have inferential consequences. 3. Some commitments are supported/entitled...
rows.statement: Zero-Lens extraction on Brandom (removing language/English/sentences/speech/Frege/Wittgenstein/philosophy) yields ten survivor claims: participants make commitments; commitments have inferential consequences; some commitments are supported/entitled; commitments can conflict; participants assess one another's commitments; new actions alter the state; implicit relations can become explicit; concepts are characterized partly by inferential roles; objectivity can emerge within social assessment; a claim is not merely a string but a position in a normative/inferential structure.

rows.anchor: Unknown is not simply an error state. It is a legitimate epistemic condition.
rows.statement: ASP answer-set semantics give TRUE/FALSE/UNKNOWN query results and ground at least three distinct kinds of 'unknown': unknown because alternatives remain (P and ¬P both possible), unknown because the agent is unaware (neither represented), and unknown because a default was blocked (an exception/missing condition prevented an otherwise-applicable default). The earlier flat UNKNOWN category should become an Epistemic Status taxonomy: true/false/unresolved-alternatives/not-represented-unaware/defeasibly-inferable-but-blocked/etc; the exact taxonomy remains a research question but the distinction itself is now strongly grounded.
missing: a finalized taxonomy

rows.anchor: Absence must not silently become an epistemic state.
rows.statement: Danger flagged in the Projection model: 'If Projection P2 doesn't contain X, therefore X is false' would be wrong, since absence from a projection could mean not relevant, not visible, not assessed, outside scope, unavailable, superseded, or genuinely no longer justified — these are different meanings. This connects to the ZERO lens: absence must not silently become an epistemic state, giving another reason to preserve ZERO discipline within the Projection idea.
invariants: absence must not silently become an epistemic state

rows.statement: Unknownness U(e) is proposed not as a Boolean but a classification (alternative / unrepresented / blocked-default / outside-scope / computationally-unresolved), with the exact taxonomy left empirical and countable for future statistical analysis.

rows.anchor: 1. There is an underlying world/domain. 2. A participant has beliefs/knowledge about it. 3. Only part of that knowledge may be explicitly represented...
rows.statement: Zero-Lens extraction on Brachman & Levesque (removing FOL/Prolog/frames/description logic/SAT/default logic/Bayesian networks/STRIPS/GOLOG) yields twelve survivor claims: an underlying world/domain exists; a participant has beliefs/knowledge about it; only part is explicitly represented; representation is a mapping between domains; reasoning derives implicit content from explicit content; meaning depends on interpretation/context; different representation languages have different expressive power; reasoning capability is resource-limited; knowledge changes and can be revised; uncertainty/vagueness require richer representations; the same knowledge may have different representations; action depends on knowledge — described as extraordinarily close to the current model.

rows.anchor: what survives across *both* phases is: **a knower/participant · something known · a ground · and a record that the two were connected.**
rows.statement: Zero-Lens applied across both phases: after stripping optional attributes, what survives universally is a knower/participant, something known, a ground, and a record that the two were connected — every phase and nearly every model retains those four; nothing else survives universally. The corpus distinguishes 'nothing exists' from 'we do not know' (0258: 'Knowledge is not only about what exists'; formal law §9: unknown≠absent≠false). Whether UNKNOWN is the absence of Knowledge or a state of an identified object is NOT resolved by the corpus: formal law (⟨Z-1⟩) says UNKNOWN/ABSENT/FALSE/REJECTED are states of an identified epistemic object, while kernel document 125708 §17 pushes the other way ('UNKNOWN must not be a single epistemic state', eight readings) — no new state proposed here.

rows.anchor: The adjacent states — an inheritance
rows.statement: The ladder answers how far admitted, never in what condition held. The ratified Final Architecture layers the constitutional state vocabulary beside it: REJECTED (failed reasoning preserved, never silently discarded), CONFLICTED (contradictory knowledge coexisting until governed resolution, the conflict record surviving resolution), and the evidence-layer triple UNKNOWN != ABSENT != FALSE. These are not extensions bolted on: the archaeology dated them to the programme's first weeks, before the ladder existed -- inherited from the constitutional side rather than invented to fill the gap.

rows.anchor: unqualified Zero means the L2 gap operator of this chapter, and nothing else. What the three share is a refusal... and that shared refusal, not any shared definition, is why one word kept being chosen.
rows.statement: Resolves the one-name-three-referents naming collision on "Zero" via the ratified terminology register (D-FA-3): unqualified Zero means only this chapter's L2 gap operator; Z-KOS-001 is the repository-side ratified meta-principle (explicitly not a kernel object, epistemic status, or implementation); the absence-lens Zero of the early corpus is historical only; fixed chronology places the meta-principle and absence-lens as the older senses (2026-08-22) and the computable gap operator as the youngest (2026-08-27); the three share only a refusal to treat not-knowing as either nothing or falsehood, not a shared definition, which explains why one word kept being chosen for all three.
